复制为 Markdown 进阶 你已经选好了模型。但真正包裹模型的那个程序 —— 读取文件、制定计划、运行命令、检查自身工作并重试的那个循环 —— 是一个独立的选择，而且它的重要性至少不亚于模型本身。社区把这个外壳称为 harness（或 agent），同一个模型在一个 harness 里可以表现得极其出色，在另一个里却平平无奇。本页梳理 2026 年的终端编程 agent、真正拉开它们差距的因素，以及如何保持配置的可移植性，让切换成本始终维持在低位。 What you'll learn 分清两个常被混为一谈的选择：模型本身，以及驱动它的 harness 掌握每个主流 CLI agent 的持久形态 —— Claude Code、Codex CLI、Gemini CLI，以及开源阵营 在真正起决定作用的维度上做选择：自主性、开放性、模型无关性、沙箱与生态 用 AGENTS.md 让你的配置可移植，这样切换 agent 时无需重写项目上下文 最后验证时间：2026-07-08。 本页上的 star 数量、版本号、基准分数、价格以及套餐/层级可用性变化很快 —— 编程 agent 的排名几乎每月都会重新洗牌，厂商也会在几乎没有预告的情况下改动免费层级。请把下文的原型与维度当作持久内容；在做决定之前，请对照每个项目自己的仓库或文档（在“来源”中给出链接）重新核对任何具体数字。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: 编程 Agent CLI 横向对比

documents.t: 前沿模型是一个文本预测器。而编程 agent是围绕它的 harness：系统提示词、工具集（读取、编辑、运行 shell、搜索）、规划循环、上下文管理策略、权限与沙箱模型，以及重试逻辑。改变 harness 就会改变结果 —— 贯穿 2026 年的从业者报告都描述过：同一个模型在真实仓库任务上的表现，会因为驱动它的 agent 不同而波动几十分。 这带来两个现实后果： 一个基准数字是一个组合，而不是模型分数。“Terminal-Bench 上 83%”是一个模型 + harness + 脚手架的结果。换掉其中任何一部分，它都会变化。 **你的循环才是真正的比较单位。**最好的 agent，是在你的技术栈、你的终端里、以你能接受的价格表现最好的那一个 —— 这和挑选编程模型的逻辑一模一样。模型这一半的决策请见 Claude vs GPT vs Gemini 编程对比；本页讲的是 harness 这一半。

终端 agent 领域分成了两大阵营：针对某个实验室模型调优的第一方 agent，以及可以指向任何模型（或本地权重）的模型无关 agent。 Agent 出品方 开放性 模型 形态 Claude Code Anthropic 闭源 Claude（第一方） 自主、agentic 的多文件工作；操作系统级强制沙箱；深厚的 skills/MCP/subagent 生态 Codex CLI OpenAI 开放（Apache-2.0，Rust） GPT（第一方） 自主终端 agent；原生 Windows 沙箱；广泛的平台覆盖 Gemini CLI Google 开源 Gemini（第一方） 大上下文 agent，与 Google 生态深度绑定（见下方时效性提示） opencode 社区（anomalyco） 开放（MIT，TypeScript） 任意（模型无关） star 数最高的开源 agent；CLI + 桌面端；自带模型 Aider 社区 开放（Apache-2.0） 任意，含本地模型 git 原生的结对编程伙伴，而非完整的自主编排器 Cline / Goose / 其他 社区 开放 任意 编辑器内嵌（Cline）或通用开源 agent（Goose）；模型无关 最后验证时间：2026-07-08。 **Gemini CLI 正处于变动之中。**2026 年年中，Google 改动了免费层级的访问方式，并把部分用户引向了一个独立的“Antigravity”CLI。究竟 Gemini CLI、Antigravity 还是某个更新的东西才是正确的 Google 入口，正是那种会迅速过时的事实 —— 在投入之前，请在 Google 自己的文档上确认当前状态。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.

先把排行榜放一边。这些才是持久的问题： Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1第一方还是模型无关？⌄ 第一方 agent（Claude Code、Codex CLI、Gemini CLI）针对自家模型调优，通常能给出最顺滑的巅峰体验。模型无关 agent（opencode、Aider、Cline）让你可以更换模型 —— 今天用前沿模型，明天用便宜的或本地的 —— 而无需更换工具。如果避免被锁定、或运行本地权重对你很重要，就选模型无关的。 ←PreviousNext→ 2你想要多少自主性？⌄ Aider 是结对编程伙伴：专注、文件级、git 原生的编辑，每次提交你都在环内。Claude Code 和 Codex CLI 是编排器：给一个目标，它们就会在众多文件和 shell 命令上规划并执行。更高的自主性意味着更大的杠杆，也意味着更需要护栏。 ←PreviousNext→ 3影响半径有多大？⌄ 一个能运行 shell 命令的 agent 可以删除文件、推送代码或花掉钱。相比“相信我”，更应优先选择操作系统级强制沙箱和明确的权限模型。Claude Code 和 Codex CLI 在 2026 年都带有沙箱；在让任何 agent 无人值守运行之前，先确认它能触及什么。 ←PreviousNext→ 4生态是否契合你的工作？⌄ 在核心循环之外：用于工具的 MCP 服务器、可复用的 skills、subagent、hooks、IDE 集成、CI actions。一个搭配顶级模型的“更薄”agent，可能会输给一个搭配“够用就好”模型的“更厚”agent，因为生态承担了更多工作。 ←PreviousNext→ 5在“你的”循环里它要花多少钱？⌄ 订阅制还是 API 计量、上下文窗口、缓存，以及 harness 有多“话痨”，都会影响真实账单。一个便宜的模型放进吞 token 的 harness 里，可能比一个更贵的模型放进精简 harness 里花得更多。 ←PreviousNext→ Pro tip 不要凭一个头条基准分数就买下一个 harness。要凭一次 30 分钟的试用来买它 —— 用你自己仓库里的真实任务来试，这正是那个能击败一切模型排行榜的“在你自己的代码上做评测”的做法。 开放性是一种对冲，而不是你每天都会用到的功能。它的价值会在价格改动或免费层级消失、而你想搬家的那一天显现出来。
documents.s: 真正起决定作用的维度

documents.t: 最大的隐藏切换成本是你的项目上下文 —— 构建命令、约定、测试规则，以及那些 agent 无法自行推断的东西。2026 年这方面有了一个事实标准：AGENTS.md，一个放在仓库根目录的纯 Markdown 文件，由 Linux Foundation 旗下的 Agentic AI Foundation 维护，并被 Codex、Gemini CLI、Cursor、Aider、Copilot 的 coding agent、opencode、Goose 以及另外 20 多种工具原生读取（已有 6 万多个仓库采用）。 AGENTS.md = 跨工具的项目上下文。写一次；大多数 agent 都会读取。 CLAUDE.md = Claude Code 自己的项目记忆文件（见 CLAUDE.md）。你可以保留一个指向 AGENTS.md 的小型 CLAUDE.md，或者两者都维护。 SKILL.md = Anthropic 用于打包可复用 skills 的独立规范，带 frontmatter 和捆绑脚本。它与 AGENTS.md 是互补关系，而非竞争者 —— 一个描述项目，另一个打包可复用的流程。 把上下文放在 AGENTS.md 里，意味着你尝试另一个 agent 的那天，你的项目规则会免费一起跟过去。 精简版 AGENTS.md —— 只写 agent 无法推断的内容 CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # AGENTS.md ## Setup - Install: `pnpm install` - Dev server: `pnpm dev` (port 3000) ## Build & test (run before every commit) - Typecheck: `pnpm typecheck` - Lint: `pnpm lint` - Tests: `pnpm test` — all must pass ## Conventions - TypeScript strict; no `any`. - Components in `src/components`, one per file. - Never edit files under `generated/` by hand. ## Constraints - Do NOT run `git push` or open PRs without being asked. - Secrets live in `.env.local`; never commit them. Watch out 只在 AGENTS.md 里放 agent 无法自行发现的内容。重述显而易见的事实会在每次运行时消耗 token，并把真正重要的规则淹没。要手工整理它 —— 自动生成的上下文文件往往都是噪音。
documents.s: 可移植性：上下文只写一次

documents.t: 需要深度、自主的 Claude 工作，配上最丰富的工具生态 → Claude Code。 想要一个绑定 GPT、拥有强大平台/Windows 覆盖的开源第一方 agent → Codex CLI。 想要自由更换模型或运行本地权重 → opencode 或 Cline。 谨慎、git 原生、人在环内的编辑 → Aider。 押注庞大的 Google 生态上下文 → Gemini CLI（先确认当前访问方式）。 无论你选哪个，都把项目上下文放在 AGENTS.md 里，并在投入之前用你自己仓库里的一个真实任务来验证这个选择。 Check yourself 0/4

复制为 Markdown 高级 What you'll learn Understand the three-tier trick — dense weights in RAM, routed experts on disk, optional VRAM tier — and why MoE makes it possible at all Read the benchmark table honestly: which hardware gets 0.1 tok/s, which gets ~2, which gets ~6, and why NVMe bandwidth, not CPU, is the ceiling Know the four gotchas that cost people days: int8 MTP heads, O_DIRECT on the wrong drive, speculative decoding that loses, and SSD wear Get from git clone to a first streamed token on GLM-5.2 or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Decide when Colibrì beats a GGUF-plus-Ollama offload, when to rent a GPU instead, and when a hosted API is simply the right answer On July 1, 2026 a developer publishing as JustVugg pushed a repository with a one-line promise: run frontier MoE models on hardware you already own — pure C, zero deps, experts streamed from disk. The Show HN thread hit 453 points nine days later. By mid-September the project is at 30.8k stars and version 1.11.0, released September 13, added a ninth model family (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 552B) that reads the published checkpoint natively with no conversion step. It is the top AI repository on GitHub's daily trending list as this page is written. The pitch sounds like a trick, and in a sense it is one. This page explains the trick precisely enough that you can predict what it will do on your machine before you download 370 GB.
documents.s: Colibrì: Run a 744B MoE From Your SSD (and What It Really Costs You)

documents.t: A mixture-of-experts model only touches a small slice of its weights per token, so Colibrì keeps the always-used part (attention, embeddings, shared experts) resident in RAM and reads the rarely-used part (the routed experts) from NVMe on demand — trading tokens per second for the ability to run a 744-billion-parameter model on a laptop.

Take GLM-5.2 as the reference case, since it is the model the project was built around: Quantity Value Total parameters 744B Active per token ~40B Dense (always-on) parameters ~17B → ~9.9 GB resident as int4 Routed experts roughly twenty thousand across all layers → ~370 GB on disk as int4 Expert weight that changes token to token (cold) ~11 GB Minimum RAM / comfortable RAM 16 GB / 24 GB Every token needs the dense 9.9 GB plus the handful of experts the router picks in each layer. The dense part fits in RAM. The experts do not — but you only need a few of them at a time, and the next token often reuses many of the same ones. So the engine treats VRAM, RAM and NVMe as one memory hierarchy: a per-layer LRU cache of recently used experts in RAM, a learned "pinned hot-store" of experts that are used most often, an optional VRAM tier if a GPU is present, and the disk as backing store for everything else. The design choice that makes it a single C file per model rather than a framework: no BLAS, no Python at runtime, no GPU required. The GLM engine started at about 1,300 lines of C. Zero dependencies also means the OS page cache becomes a free second cache layer for expert reads.

The expensive part of streaming is waiting for disk. Colibrì runs a lookahead thread (enabled with PILOT=1) that predicts which experts the next layer will need and starts the reads early. The README's measured figure is that routing decisions are 71.6% predictable one layer ahead, which is enough to hide a large share of the I/O latency behind compute. This is why "tok/s after warmup" is a very different number from "cold tok/s".
documents.s: 1. Router lookahead: routing is 71.6% predictable one layer ahead

documents.t: Put a full copy of the model on a second NVMe and the engine streams from both at once. Each expert hashes deterministically to one drive, weighted by each drive's measured bandwidth, so there is no duplicate caching and the effective read bandwidth is roughly the sum of the two. The DeepSeek V4 Flash benchmark below (RTX 5080 plus two NVMe drives, ~1.6 tok/s) is a dual-drive configuration.
documents.s: 2. Dual-SSD streaming: two drives, one model, summed bandwidth

documents.t: Models with multi-head latent attention (MLA) let Colibrì store a compressed KV state — 576 floats per token instead of 32,768, a 57× reduction. The engine persists that state to a .coli_kv file, so reopening a conversation after a restart does zero re-prefill and is byte-identical to a session that never stopped. On a machine where prefill runs at streaming speed, not re-prefilling a long context is the difference between usable and not.
documents.s: 3. Compressed KV state that survives a restart

documents.t: The project's stated contract: insufficient fast memory only makes it slower; precision and router behavior never silently change. The forward pass is validated token-exact against a transformers oracle. This is the opposite trade from most "fits on a laptop" quantization stories, where you get speed by accepting a different model.
documents.s: 4. Semantics are guaranteed, speed is not

documents.t: Numbers from the project's README (GLM-5.2 unless stated), warm cache where noted: Hardware Tok/s What it means 6× RTX 5090, full expert residency in VRAM 5.8–6.8 (TTFT ~13 s) The ceiling: no disk I/O at all. This is a GPU rig, not "hardware you already own". 128 GB RAM desktop, CPU only, warm cache ~1.8 The realistic best case for a fat workstation without GPUs. Single RTX 5070 Ti (~24 GB VRAM tier) 1.07 A laptop-class GPU roughly doubles the cold-disk floor. RTX 5080 + 32 GB RAM + 2 NVMe, DeepSeek V4 Flash ~1.6 at 3k context, after warmup The dual-SSD path on a smaller model. 25 GB RAM laptop, slow NVMe, cold 0.05–0.1 The headline "744B on 25 GB" configuration. About one token every 10–20 seconds. The variable that decides your number is random-read bandwidth from the drive, not CPU. A cold token needs on the order of 11 GB of expert reads; a PCIe 5.0 NVMe at 13–15 GB/s therefore caps a cold, unprefetched setup near 1 tok/s, and lookahead plus cache hits are what get you above that. Commenters in the launch thread reported cache hit rates around 23% on a 128 GB Apple M5 Max and 0.091 tok/s on an old dual-Xeon with 192 GB of DDR3 — "viable for overnight jobs". So the honest use cases are: overnight or asynchronous batches, private offline experiments with a frontier-class model, research into how MoE inference actually behaves, and warm multi-turn chat on a machine with 100 GB+ of RAM. Interactive pair-programming on a 32 GB laptop is not on the list.

Model Total / active Disk RAM min Notes OLMoE 7B / 1B ~7 GB 8 GB The "does my build work" model Qwen3.6 35B / 3B ~20 GB 24 GB (full RAM residency) Optional GPU; 7× speedup measured on dual 8 GB cards Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 125B + 51B n-gram / 6B ~185.5 GB 16 GB CPU only DeepSeek V4 Flash 284B / 13B ~167 GB 16 GB Native fp4 experts; GPU optional (Pascal or newer) GLM-5.3-Flash 321B / 40B ~195 GB 25 GB Vision-capable DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 552B / 16B ~203 GB 16 GB New in 1.11.0; reads the released checkpoint with no conversion GLM-5.2 / 5.3 744B / 40B ~372 GB 16 GB The reference model; MIT-licensed weights Inkling 975B / 41B ~469 GB 25 GB bf16 dense is 49.4 GB resident by default; an int4 tool brings it to 25 GB hosts Kimi K3 2.8T / 104B ~1.6 TB 32 GB+ Native MXFP4; requires the raw checkpoint, no conversion available Quantization is per family, not one global setting: int4 group-scaled for GLM and Inkling, int8 or block-FP8 for OLMoE and Qwen3.8, native MXFP4 for Kimi K3, native fp4 experts with fp8-e4m3 dense for the DeepSeek V4 line. If you already have Kimi K3 or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash weights from a vLLM deployment, Colibrì reads those same files.
documents.s: Nine model families, and what each one costs in disk

documents.t: MTP heads must be int8. Multi-token-prediction draft heads quantized to int4 give 0–4% draft acceptance — speculative decoding silently does nothing (issue #8). The pre-converted GLM-5.2 container on Hugging Face is int4 for the model and int8 for MTP for exactly this reason. O_DIRECT helps on some drives and hurts on others. Bypassing the page cache measured +34% on NVMe drives with a DRAM cache and bandwidth headroom, and neutral-to-negative on QLC, DRAM-less and virtualized disks. Benchmark both on your drive; do not copy someone else's flag. Speculative decoding is often a net loss on real chat. On multi-turn conversations the MTP and grammar drafters accepted roughly 1–10 of every 24 tokens, and replaying the engine's recurrent attention state for rejected suffixes cost more than the accepted drafts saved. For DeepSeek V4 the project measured 495 seconds of rejected-suffix replay and ships with both drafters off by default (V4_DRAFT=0, V4_MTP=0). Turn them on only if you measure a win. SSD wear is real. Heavy expert reads drive page-cache churn; the README warns about wear on consumer drives, and the launch thread's advice was to disable swap and consider a read-only mount for the model directory. A 370 GB model streamed for hours per day is a workload consumer NVMe was not sold for. One more, less a gotcha than a limitation: the learned expert pinning can overfit to your routing history. It helps repeated workloads; the maintainers say it still needs held-out, cross-session A/B tests before you should trust the gains on new prompts.
documents.s: Four gotchas that cost people days

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Build (checks gcc and OpenMP, compiles, runs self-tests)⌄ git clone https://github.com/JustVugg/colibri && cd colibri/c && ./setup.sh — then make -C c glm for GLM-5.2, or make -C c inkling / make -C c kimi_k3 for the others. Start with OLMoE (7 GB) to prove the build before committing hundreds of gigabytes of downloads. ←PreviousNext→ 2Get the weights in Colibrì's container format⌄ ./coli convert --model /nvme/glm52_i4 downloads and converts shard by shard, one time. For GLM-5.2 a pre-converted int4 container with int8 MTP heads exists on Hugging Face (mastouri/GLM-5.2-colibri-int4-g64-with-int8-mtp). DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Kimi K3 need no conversion: point the engine at the released checkpoint. ←PreviousNext→ 3Check placement before you wait⌄ COLI_MODEL=/nvme/glm52_i4 ./coli plan shows which tensors land in VRAM, RAM and disk for your machine; ./coli doctor runs a readiness check. If plan says most experts will be cold on a slow drive, you now know your tok/s before spending an evening on it. ←PreviousNext→ 4Run: TUI, or API with a dashboard⌄ COLI_MODEL=/nvme/glm52_i4 ./coli chat for a terminal chat. ./coli web --model /nvme/glm52_i4 starts an API server plus a dashboard that shows tier placement, cache hit rate and disk I/O live; ./coli serve is the headless variant. Enable PILOT=1 for router lookahead on any setup that streams from disk. ←PreviousNext→ 5Tune the two knobs that matter, and measure⌄ Try O_DIRECT on and off on your specific drive. Leave speculative decoding off until a benchmark on your own prompts shows it winning. If you have a second NVMe, mirror the model onto it for dual-drive streaming. ←PreviousNext→ A minimal first run on GLM-5.2 (Linux, one NVMe) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ git clone https://github.com/JustVugg/colibri && cd colibri/c ./setup.sh make -C c glm ./coli convert --model /nvme/glm52_i4 # one-time download + convert COLI_MODEL=/nvme/glm52_i4 ./coli plan # see what lands where COLI_MODEL=/nvme/glm52_i4 PILOT=1 ./coli chat # first streamed tokens

Path What it is good at Where Colibrì differs llama.cpp / Ollama with GGUF offload (our Ollama guide) Huge model catalog, GPU offload, mature tooling; the GLM-5.2 page covers the 239 GB dynamic 2-bit GGUF route GGUF offload needs the whole quantized model in RAM plus VRAM (256 GB for GLM-5.2 at 2-bit). Colibrì needs 16–24 GB of RAM and a big disk, at the same precision the lab released, not 2-bit. vLLM / SGLang on rented GPUs (Kimi K3 deploy guide) Dozens of tokens per second, batching, multiple users Fast because everything is resident in HBM. Colibrì exists for the case where that hardware is not available or not allowed. Hosted API (DeepSeek, Z.ai, Moonshot) Cheapest per token by far, no hardware The only reason to prefer Colibrì is that the weights and the prompts must never leave the machine, or you want to study MoE inference itself. The right way to think about Colibrì is not "a faster llama.cpp". It is the tool that makes a frontier-sized open model available on a machine that could not otherwise load it, at a speed you schedule around rather than wait on. For a privacy-first stack that mixes a small fast local model for interactive work with a large slow one for batch jobs, see A private local AI stack. What you'll learn Understand the two-agent split (shopping vs merchant) and why Anthropic did NOT use an intent router or domain subagents Learn the staged-write guardrail: how no model tool call ever moves money or mutates the store — every write ends at a human-approved surface See the three runtime paths (Messages API, Agent SDK, Managed Agents) and how the SAME core code plugs into all three Steal three transferable patterns for any agent that touches a real business system: server-issued IDs, fenced third-party text, and prompt-vs-skill split On September 2, 2026 Anthropic published anthropics/commerce-agents — an Apache 2.0 reference blueprint for building shopping and merchant agents on Claude. It ships two working agents, four vertical examples (retail, travel, telecom, entertainment), and — crucially — a set of guardrail patterns implemented in code, not in prompts. Anthropic states the repo is a reference implementation they will not maintain as a product and does not accept outside contributions. The interesting thing is not that you can now build a shopping bot. The interesting thing is the shape: an unusually opinionated take on how an agent that touches real business systems should be structured. Everything below is transferable to any agent that has to write to a real backend — inventory, customer records, banking, ops tooling.

Anthropic ships one shopping agent (customer-facing) and one merchant agent (staff-facing), each with its own backend interface (StorefrontBackend and MerchantBackend) and its own set of skills. They deliberately did not build: an intent router that dispatches to sub-agents per-domain subagents (a "cart agent" + "returns agent" + "search agent") one monolithic agent that does both consumer and staff work Instead: one unified agent per audience, in a standard agent loop, with skills and tools. Their guidance in the anatomy of effective commerce agents post: "anything the agent needs on most turns generally goes in the system prompt" — so for a shopping agent, catalog search lives in the prompt because it's on nearly every turn. "The rest goes in skills." Customer care, personalization, returns — skills. This is a strong opinion. Intent routers and domain subagents are the default architecture in a lot of tutorials, and Anthropic is telling you: for a single audience with tightly coupled sessions, don't.
documents.s: The split: two agents, not one

documents.t: Pro tip The single most important line in the blueprint: 'No model tool call moves money or changes the business.' Every mutation goes through a server-controlled approval step. If you take one thing from the repo, take this. The blueprint enforces safety in code, not prompts. The mechanism has three parts: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 11. Server issues every ID the model is allowed to reference⌄ The server maintains a per-session record of every product ID, SKU, campaign ID, and price ID it has handed the model. Writes and renders will ONLY accept IDs from that record. If the model hallucinates a SKU, the harness refuses — no prompt engineering required. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Every write is staged, never applied⌄ Order placement, payments, refunds, price changes, and campaign launches all end in a server-generated draft with its own approval ID. The tool call returns the draft ID and a preview. Nothing is live yet. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Approval happens on a real human surface⌄ A staged change only succeeds when the approval ID is signed off through a real UI — a button in the operator's portal, a confirmation in the CLI. The agent cannot self-approve; the approval endpoint doesn't accept model-generated identity. ←PreviousNext→ The blueprint also handles two other classic footguns: Regulated content: for fees, disclosures, and price-shown-to-consumer, the model chooses which product to disclose; the words come from server-supplied approved copy. The model never writes disclosure text. Third-party text sanitization: any user-generated content (reviews, seller notes, messages) is wrapped in "fenced text" markers before it reaches the model, so it can't smuggle instructions into the prompt.

The blueprint places no orders and charges no cards. Checkout is rendered for the host application to complete. In Anthropic's words, this "keeps payment handling, fraud rules and credentials outside the agent." Visa, Mastercard, and Accenture are named partners on the announcement, but the payment step lives in your existing checkout or an agentic payments provider — never in the model's tool surface. This is another opinionated line: if it can lose money in one shot, the model doesn't touch it.

The repo splits every agent into a core package (types, backend interface, prompt, tool contracts) and separate runtime packages that adapt the core to different serving surfaces: Messages API — the reference loop CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from shopping_agent import ShoppingAgentConfig from shopping_agent_runtime import ShoppingAgent agent = ShoppingAgent( backend=your_backend, skills_dir=Path("shopping-agent/skills"), config=ShoppingAgentConfig(brand_name="Your Store"), ) async for event in agent.stream_turn(messages, session, state): # yields: text_delta | tool_call | ui | cart_update | turn_complete ... await agent.update_memory(messages, session) Agent SDK — with a local console CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ python shopping-agent/runtime-agent-sdk/main.py \ --once "a two-person tent under $250" python merchant-agent/runtime-agent-sdk/main.py # prints staged changes and waits for y/n approval Managed Agents (beta) — hosted CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ scripts/deploy_managed_agent.sh \ shopping-agent/managed-agents/shopping-agent # The manifest declares tools + a storefront MCP server; # Anthropic hosts the loop. The same core/ code runs under all three, which is the actual portable pattern: keep the agent's contract (tools, prompt, backend interface) separate from the serving harness. If you swap Messages API for Managed Agents six months from now, only the runtime package changes.

Long-term memory (preferences, past orders, service notes) is persisted in your existing databases, not in model context. Extraction happens asynchronously after the conversation ends — you don't pay latency to update memory on the hot path. On the next turn, the runtime hydrates relevant memory into the system prompt. This is worth internalizing even if you're not building commerce: shoving conversation summaries into context on every turn is a common performance mistake. The blueprint's shape — write async, read on turn-start — is the cheaper one.

examples/ includes end-to-end demos for four verticals, each with a different structural wrinkle you can copy: Retail — the base case. Standard catalog, cart, checkout. Travel — date-bound inventory (a flight seat expires), itinerary presentation with multi-leg comparison. Telecom — account context ("your current plan is X"), plan matrices, regulated fee disclosure. Entertainment — timed holds on tickets, waitlists, venue seat maps. If your product isn't commerce but has any of these traits (expiring inventory, regulated disclosure, timed holds), the matching vertical is worth reading before you design your own agent.
documents.s: The four verticals (and why they differ)

documents.t: Clone, install, run one vertical CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ git clone https://github.com/anthropics/commerce-agents.git cd commerce-agents python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env # add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (cd examples && npm ci) python scripts/run_demo.py retail # API on :8000, storefront on :3000 The repo verifies with ruff check . && ruff format --check . && pytest && python scripts/check.py, and there's a python scripts/verify_all.py for the comprehensive pass.

复制为 Markdown 高级 Every major lab now ships a model that can look at a screen and click on it. Anthropic's computer use tool, OpenAI's computer tool, and Google's computer_use tool all solve the same shape of problem — take a screenshot, decide an action, execute it, screenshot again — and all three are wire-incompatible with each other in ways that are not obvious until your clicks start landing 40 pixels off. This page is the harness-level guide, not the leaderboard. The leaderboard changes monthly; the failure modes below have been the same since the first preview shipped. Related security reading When the screen an agent drives is a browser, the agent also lands above a boundary the web has relied on for 30 years — see Agentic Browsers Break the Same-Origin Policy for the UW findings on Atlas, Comet, Gemini in Chrome and Claude for Chrome. Related pattern For the shared-login variant — an agent that drives a real Chromium session with your cookies inherited, via ego lite and its ego-browser skill — the loop above collapses into a JavaScript-per-turn model and the security posture inverts (the agent has your privileges by design). What you'll learn Understand the agent loop all three providers share — and the three places they diverge Fix the coordinate bug that silently breaks most first attempts (Retina, downscaling, and image size limits) Know each provider's safety gate, because it is part of the protocol, not an optional add-on Read OSWorld honestly: what the human baseline actually means Pick reasoning effort correctly — the cheapest setting is not the one you would guess 最后验证时间：2026-07-14。 Model names, beta headers, pixel limits and benchmark scores in this space move fast, and every provider still labels its computer-use surface as preview or beta. The mechanics below are durable; re-check any specific number, header or model id against the provider docs linked in Sources before you ship. 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.

Strip away the branding and all three are the same state machine: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Send the task plus a screenshot⌄ The model gets your instruction and an image of the current screen. Some providers also want the current URL or a short history of recent actions. ←PreviousNext→ 2The model returns an action, not a result⌄ Click at (x, y). Type this. Scroll here. It is a request for your code to do something — the model cannot touch the machine itself. ←PreviousNext→ 3Your harness executes it⌄ You own this. Anthropic states it plainly: your application must run the tool; Claude cannot run it directly. You implement the screenshot capture, the mouse, the keyboard. ←PreviousNext→ 4Screenshot again, feed it back⌄ The new screen goes back as a tool result. The model sees the consequence of its own action — this is the entire feedback signal. ←PreviousNext→ 5Repeat until no action comes back⌄ Termination is the absence of a further action request, not a 'done' flag. Your loop needs its own step cap and stall detection. ←PreviousNext→ The consequence people miss: the model's only perception of the world is the image you send it. Every failure below is really a failure of that image, or of the coordinate space it implies.

The divergence is not "which one is smarter." It is the contract. Anthropic (Claude) OpenAI (GPT) Google (Gemini) Action space Raw desktop primitives: screenshot, left_click, type, key, scroll, drag, hold_key, wait, plus zoom on the newest tool version Structured UI actions: click, double_click, scroll, type, keypress, drag, move, wait, screenshot Semantic actions: not just click/type but navigate, go_back, go_forward, open_app, long_press — the browser and mobile concepts are first-class Coordinates You send pixel dimensions; the model returns raw pixel coordinates in that space Same pixel contract, with recommended desktop sizes Same, with an intent field explaining the reasoning behind each action Loop plumbing Tool result blocks carrying an image computer_call → computer_call_output keyed by call_id; previous_response_id carries history so you don't resend it Function call → function_result with a fresh screenshot Safety gate Injection classifiers run automatically on screenshots pending_safety_checks you must explicitly acknowledge safety_decision with policy categories Sweet spot General desktop / OS-level control Desktop and browser, plus a code-execution path Browser-first; strong on mobile; explicitly not optimized for desktop OS control That last Anthropic/Google row is the one that decides architecture. Google's action space is semantic — go_back is a concept the model can name. Anthropic's is mechanical — going back means the model must find and click the back button, or press the right key combination. Semantic actions are more reliable inside a browser and useless outside one. Mechanical primitives work anywhere and fail more often. So: porting a computer-use agent between providers is not a model swap. It is rewriting the harness's action executor. Budget accordingly. (Same lesson as Coding Agent CLIs Compared: the harness, not the model, is the thing you're actually married to.)

This is the single highest-value thing on this page, because almost everyone hits it and the symptom looks like "the model is bad at clicking." It is not bad at clicking. Your image and your coordinate space disagree. Three independent causes, which stack:
documents.s: The coordinate bug that eats your first week

documents.t: macOS Retina displays capture screenshots at a device pixel ratio of 2 — the image is twice the resolution of the logical screen coordinates. Send that raw and the model reasons about a 2880-wide image while your click executor thinks in 1440-wide logical points. Every click lands at roughly half the intended position, consistently, in one direction. Fix: downscale by 2 before sending, or halve the coordinates the model returns. Not both.

Models have image size limits — and they differ between models from the same lab. Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8 and Opus 4.7 accept up to 2576 pixels on the long edge; earlier Claude models accept 1568 pixels and roughly 1.15 megapixels total. Here is the trap: if you send something bigger, the API downscales it for you rather than erroring. The model then returns coordinates in the space of the image it saw — and you never learned the scale factor, because the resize happened server-side. Only genuinely enormous images (over ~8,000 px on a side) get rejected outright with a validation error. So the "helpful" behavior is the bug. Always resize client-side, set display_width_px/display_height_px to the dimensions you actually sent, and scale returned coordinates back up yourself.
documents.s: 2. The API silently downscales oversized images

documents.t: On OpenAI's tool, screenshots should use detail: "original" — both "high" and "low" degrade click accuracy for this task specifically. And if you resize without preserving aspect ratio, clicks land in the right region and miss the target. Coordinate scaling — the shape of the fix CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Before sending: shrink to fit the model's image limit, remember the factor. LONG_EDGE_LIMIT = 2576 # check YOUR model's limit; older Claude models: 1568 scale = min(1.0, LONG_EDGE_LIMIT / max(width, height)) sent_w, sent_h = round(width * scale), round(height * scale) # -> send the resized image, and declare display_width_px=sent_w, display_height_px=sent_h # After the model replies: map its coordinates back to the real screen. real_x, real_y = model_x / scale, model_y / scale # On a Retina capture you did NOT pre-downscale, divide by the device pixel ratio too.

Symptom Almost certainly Clicks consistently offset in one direction Your declared display_width_px/display_height_px don't match the image you actually sent Clicks land in the right area but miss small targets Detail lost to downscaling, or aspect ratio distorted on resize Accuracy poor everywhere Resolution too low — try 1280x720 as a floor Model misreads tiny text (tab titles, filenames, line numbers) It needs to zoom, and you didn't enable it Resolution guidance, from the vendors themselves: Anthropic suggests 1024x768 or 1280x720 for general desktop, 1280x800 or 1366x768 for web apps, and explicitly says to avoid going above 1920x1080. OpenAI recommends 1440x900 or 1600x900. Bigger is not better — you pay tokens for pixels and then throw the detail away in the downscale.

Claude's newest computer tool version (computer_20251124) adds a zoom action, off by default — you must set enable_zoom: true. With it on, Claude zooms into a region when it needs to read small text that isn't legible at the screenshot's base resolution: sidebar filenames, tab titles, status-bar text, line numbers, button labels. Non-obvious operational note: if Claude isn't zooming when you expect it to, the fix is usually to ask about a specific region or element rather than about the screen as a whole.

Do not treat this as a bolt-on. In all three APIs, the safety mechanism changes the shape of your loop. Anthropic trained the model to resist prompt injection and runs classifiers over your prompts automatically when the computer-use tools are in play. When a classifier spots a likely injection in a screenshot, it steers the model to ask the user for confirmation before the next action. That is great with a human present and actively wrong for an unattended pipeline — which is why there is an opt-out, gated behind contacting support. OpenAI surfaces pending_safety_checks that your code must explicitly acknowledge (acknowledged_safety_checks) before the loop proceeds. The gate is in your hands, and skipping it is a decision you make in code. Google returns a safety_decision — allowed, require_confirmation, or blocked — driven by policy categories including FINANCIAL_TRANSACTIONS, COMMUNICATION_TOOL, ACCOUNT_CREATION, SENSITIVE_DATA_MODIFICATION and LEGAL_TERMS_AND_AGREEMENTS. Prompt-injection screening of screenshots is available as an opt-in. The threat is real and specific: a screenshot is untrusted input. Text rendered on a webpage, in an image, in a PDF the agent opened — all of it reaches the model through the same channel as your instructions. Anthropic's own docs note that Claude will, in some circumstances, follow instructions found in content even when they conflict with yours. Every provider's mitigation converges on the same three rules: isolate the environment, keep a human on high-impact actions, and treat everything on screen as hostile. If the agent must log in, that risk goes up sharply — credentials plus injectable content is the worst combination in this space. See Securing Local and Hybrid Agents and Prompt Injection for the defensive playbook.
documents.s: Safety gates are part of the protocol

documents.t: OSWorld is the shared yardstick, and it's a good one because it's hard to fake: it drops an agent into a real OS with real applications, and grades with execution-based verification — a script checks whether the file actually got saved, not whether the agent claimed it did. The benchmark spans 369 tasks (361 in the standard evaluation set, since a handful of Google Drive tasks need manual setup) and ships 134 execution-based evaluation functions. OSWorld-Verified is the cleaned-up revision, with community-reported broken examples fixed and evaluation time cut to about an hour on AWS. Two numbers worth holding together: The human baseline is ~72.4%. Not 100%. These tasks are genuinely fiddly, and humans fumble them too. When OSWorld launched, the best model scored 12.24%. Frontier agents now report scores in the 70s and up — which means the headline "agents have reached human level on computer use" is arithmetically defensible and practically misleading. A benchmark score is a model + harness + scaffold result, exactly like a coding benchmark (see The Capability–Reliability Gap). Your harness is not their harness. And a 75% success rate on single tasks compounds brutally: an eight-step workflow where each step is 95% reliable succeeds about 66% of the time. Treat OSWorld as evidence the capability exists, and your own eval set as the only evidence that your product works.

For Claude computer use specifically, Anthropic's internal benchmarking gives guidance that inverts the usual intuition: Opus 4.7: high effort as the default; drop to low for high-throughput or cost-sensitive workloads. Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6: medium is the best accuracy-to-cost ratio. Avoid max — on UI tasks it adds token cost without improving accuracy. The counterintuitive one: on those models, low effort uses fewer output tokens than disabling thinking entirely. A little thinking prevents mistakes, and mistakes cost you retries — and retries cost far more tokens than the thinking did. So "turn thinking off to save money" is, for computer use, often wrong. Cheapest is a little thinking. One more model-selection wrinkle: mechanical click precision is not the same axis as intelligence. Sonnet 4.6 is more mechanically precise at clicking than Opus 4.6, and more robust when screenshots have been heavily downscaled. Opus 4.7 narrows that gap and raises the pixel limit, so it needs less downscaling in the first place.

Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Sandbox first, always⌄ A container or VM with nothing valuable in it. Every provider says this and they all mean it: the agent will eventually click something you did not intend. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pin the coordinate space⌄ Capture, resize client-side to your model's limit, declare the exact dimensions you sent, and keep the scale factor. Write this once and never think about it again. ←PreviousNext→ 3Cap the loop⌄ Termination is 'no further action returned' — which never fires if the agent is stuck in a modal it can't dismiss. Add a max-step budget and a stall detector (identical screenshots N times running). ←PreviousNext→ 4Decide your safety-gate policy explicitly⌄ Human-in-the-loop, or unattended with an opt-out and a narrower blast radius. Do not discover this by accident when a confirmation prompt deadlocks your cron job. ←PreviousNext→ 5Build a ten-task eval before you build feature two⌄ Execution-verified, like OSWorld does it: check the world changed, not that the agent said it did. This is the only number about your system that means anything. ←PreviousNext→ 6Prefer the API to the pixels where you can⌄ The most reliable computer-use agent is the one that doesn't have to use the computer. If the target has an API, an MCP server, or a CLI, that path is faster, cheaper and orders of magnitude more reliable. Screens are the fallback, not the goal. ←PreviousNext→ That last step is the strategic one. Computer use is the universal adapter for software with no API — legacy desktop apps, vendor portals, anything behind a login with no integration story. It is a magnificent hack, and it is still a hack. Reach for MCP and real tools first. Check yourself 0/5

复制为 Markdown 高级 At 09:08 UTC on 20 October 2026, a link titled "DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models" hit Hacker News and settled at 2,251 points and 856 comments — the biggest AI story on the site that week. The repository, deepseek-ai/DeepInfer, had been created four days earlier and collected 16,337 stars and 1,620 forks by the following morning. Apache 2.0. Written in Python. The framing everywhere was "DeepSeek open-sources the engine that runs DeepSeek." That framing is true and almost useless. The 856-comment thread is a near-perfect demonstration of the gap: it is an extended argument about whether inference is profitable for frontier labs, and contains essentially no discussion of what the code does. Nobody in it reports trying to run it. So this page does the unglamorous part. Four things in DeepInfer's own documentation materially change what you should conclude from the release, and none of them made the coverage: It is a vLLM fork, by its own acknowledgments — not a clean-room engine. "NVIDIA SM100" rules out every H100 and every consumer card. Most readers cannot run this at all. Its headline decode throughput is computed under full-acceptance accounting — it counts speculative draft tokens regardless of the true acceptance rate. Its most durable contribution, batch-invariant inference, is turned on by a flag that turns off DeepInfer's own speculative decoder. Speed and reproducibility are an either/or here. What you'll learn Describe accurately what DeepInfer ships and what it explicitly withholds — a KV cache system, prefill/decode disaggregation and DP load balancing are all absent, so this is an engine, not a server Decode the hardware line: SM100 means datacenter Blackwell, which excludes SM90 (H100/H200) and SM120 (RTX 50-series), and pair that with ~763 GB of FP8 weights to size a real deployment Explain why temperature 0 was never deterministic — and why the popular 'GPUs plus floating point are random' explanation is wrong Apply DeepInfer's deterministic-sampling recipe, and recognise the cost: the same flag disables the variable-length MTP path that DSpark rides on Read the published prefill/decode numbers correctly, including full-acceptance accounting, per-GPU normalisation, and why the profiler traces must never be used to derive steps-per-second Set the two configuration values that corrupt output or waste capacity when you get them wrong: SWA replay keep-tokens and EPLB redundant experts 最后验证时间：2026-10-21。 Star counts, the supported-model list (today: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash only), the pinned dependency versions and the environment-variable names here were read from the repository on 21 October 2026, four days after it was created. A four-day-old repo with 172 open issues and no tagged release will move fast — re-read the README and examples/README.md before you commit a deployment to any of it. 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: DeepInfer: DeepSeek's Own Inference Engine, Read Honestly

documents.t: DeepInfer is the offline inference path of DeepSeek's production stack, extracted and published. It runs exactly one model family — DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash — on two hardware targets, with DeepSeek's own kernel libraries wired in: FlashMLA for multi-head latent attention, DeepGEMM for matrix multiply, DeepEP for expert-parallel communication, DeepSelect for sparse-attention and sampler top-k, and TileKernels plus in-tree TileLang kernels for the rest. Those five repos are not new — FlashMLA, DeepGEMM and DeepEP all date to February 2025 and carry 13.1k, 9.1k and 10.3k stars respectively; DeepSelect is from September 2026 and has 510. DeepInfer is the thing that was always missing: the scheduler and runtime that assembles them.
documents.s: What it is, in one paragraph

documents.t: Straight from the acknowledgments: DeepInfer "was originally built primarily on vLLM, with additional inspiration from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM." That is worth sitting with. The dominant reading of this release was a frontier lab rejected the open-source serving stack and built its own. The opposite is closer to true: DeepSeek took vLLM, specialised it hard for one architecture on one class of accelerator, and gave the result back under the same permissive terms. If you already run vLLM, DeepInfer is a statement about what a vLLM derivative looks like when you delete all generality — not a competitor you must evaluate.

The README has a section most summaries skipped, titled "Required for a complete inference service (not included in this release)": a KV cache system VE/prefill/decode disaggregation (DeepSeek notes most of the engine-side functionality is implemented, but the orchestration is not) load balancing across data-parallel replicas, for both prefill and decode There is no OpenAI-compatible HTTP server here to point your client at. Every example is python examples/offline_inference.py. If your mental model was "swap vLLM out, swap DeepInfer in, same endpoint" — three of the hardest pieces of a serving platform are the ones you would be writing yourself. Watch out "Offline inference" is doing real work in that sentence. DeepInfer is a batch engine with the serving layer removed, which is exactly the shape you want for evals and for RL rollouts — and exactly the wrong shape for a production API without months of platform work.

The README lists two targets: NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs. One line, and it quietly excludes almost everyone. SM100 is CUDA compute capability 10.0 — datacenter Blackwell, the B100/B200 class. It is not: Your hardware Arch Listed? H100 / H200 SM90 (Hopper) No RTX 5090 / 50-series SM120 (consumer Blackwell, cc 12.0) No B200 / B100 SM100 Yes Ascend 950 CANN 9.2 Yes And the two Blackwells are not interchangeable: there is no binary compatibility between sm_100 and sm_120, because datacenter Blackwell kernels use the tcgen05 instruction and TMEM — dedicated tensor memory that consumer Blackwell does not have at all. A kernel written for SM100 does not "run slower" on an RTX 5090; it does not run. The pinned dependency list says the same thing in a different dialect. requirements-nvidia.txt is three lines: torch==2.13.0+cu132, flash-attn-4==4.0.0b34, and the dev requirements — and build.sh then force-reinstalls nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.32.3 over whatever came with Torch. A beta FlashAttention-4 build, CUDA 13.2, and a hand-patched NCCL. This is a stack pinned to the exact machines in DeepSeek's own racks.

DeepInfer's default checkpoint is deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 — MIT-licensed, FP8, published 17 October 2026, spread over 48 safetensors shards. Hugging Face reports roughly 763 billion parameters for it. At FP8 that is on the order of 763 GB of weights before any KV cache, which is why the examples are written as --ep 8 and the decode benchmark runs on 64 GPUs. Eight 80 GB cards (640 GB) cannot hold it. You are looking at eight B200-class GPUs as a floor, inside a single scale-up domain, plus the three platform components DeepSeek didn't ship. Pro tip This is the practical answer to "should I switch?" for 99% of readers: you can't, and that's fine. The transferable value of this release is the three ideas below, each of which applies to the engine you actually run. If you want DeepSeek V4.1-Flash on hardware you own, the serving paths in our V4.1-Flash field guide (vLLM, SGLang, hosted API) still apply — and the -1017 checkpoint is a later revision than the September launch weights, so re-check its card rather than assuming parity.

This is the part of DeepInfer worth your attention even if you never run it. Set temperature=0, send the same prompt twice, get two different answers. Everyone has seen it. The explanation you have probably read — including in our own sampling-controls lesson, which this page sharpens — is "batching and floating-point non-determinism on the server side." That is the right neighbourhood and the wrong mechanism, and the distinction is what makes the bug fixable.
documents.s: Batch invariance: why temperature 0 was never deterministic

documents.t: "GPUs are parallel and floating-point addition isn't associative, so results wobble" implies the wobble is inherent. It isn't. Run the identical matrix multiplication on the identical data on the identical GPU as many times as you like and you get bitwise identical results every time. The kernel is deterministic. Concurrency is not the culprit.
documents.s: The wrong half of the explanation

documents.t: The culprit is batch invariance — or rather its absence. A GPU kernel picks its reduction strategy based on the shape of the work it's given. Multiply a single row (batch of 1) and the accumulation happens in one order; multiply that same row as part of a 32-row batch and the kernel splits the reduction differently, so the floating-point additions land in a different order, so the result differs in the last bits. Each run is deterministic. The shape is not. Then comes the part that makes it feel haunted: your batch size is decided by other people's traffic. A shared inference server batches your request with whatever else arrived in the same window. You changed nothing; the load did; your numerics moved. The forward pass is deterministic and your experience of it is not. In transformers, three reduction-based operations need fixing: RMSNorm, matrix multiply, and attention. The recipe is to keep each reduction inside one core where possible, refuse split reductions whose shape depends on batch size, and use a single kernel configuration even when that leaves performance on the table.

Thinking Machines Lab measured this on Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507: the same prompt ("Tell me about Richard Feynman"), temperature 0, 1,000 tokens, 1,000 runs. Result: 80 unique completions. The most frequent appeared 78 times. And the shape of the divergence is the instructive bit — all 1,000 completions are identical for the first 102 tokens, then split at token 103, where 992 runs say "Queens, New York" and 8 say "New York City." That is why equality assertions in LLM test suites are so treacherous. A short smoke test passes a thousand times and tells you nothing; the divergence was waiting at token 103. Fixing it is not free. On Qwen-8B over 1,000 sequences, Thinking Machines measured vLLM's default at 26 s, a naive deterministic build at 55 s, and 42 s once the attention kernel was improved — so roughly 1.6× slower for bitwise reproducibility. 最后验证时间：2026-10-21。 The 80-completions result, the token-103 divergence and the 26 s / 55 s / 42 s figures are Thinking Machines Lab's measurements on their hardware and kernels, not DeepInfer's. DeepSeek publishes no comparable before/after cost for its own batch-invariant path. Treat ~1.6× as the order of magnitude to budget for, not a number to quote about DeepInfer. 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: The number that should bother you

documents.t: Four reasons, in rough order of how much money they represent: On-policy RL stops being a lie. If your sampler and your trainer compute different numerics, your "on-policy" reinforcement learning is quietly off-policy. Thinking Machines showed that without deterministic inference you need off-policy correction to avoid reward collapse; with bitwise-identical results you get true on-policy RL and zero KL divergence between the sampling and training policies. For anyone doing RL on a large model, this is the headline, not a footnote. Regression tests can assert equality. DeepInfer leans on this hard: tests/models/offline_decode_ppl.json stores per-platform perplexity baselines that are compared exactly, sample by sample. That test design is only possible on a deterministic engine. Debugging an agent run becomes tractable. A failure you can replay bit-for-bit is a bug; one you can't is a ghost story. Audit and compliance. "Same input, same output, provably" is a requirement in some regulated settings and an impossibility without this.

Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Turn on batch invariance⌄ Set DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1. This holds each token's result bitwise identical regardless of what else shares its batch. NVIDIA only — the Ascend path does not offer it. ←PreviousNext→ 2Turn off the variable-length MTP path⌄ Set DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0. This is the same flag you set to 1 to enable DSpark speculative decoding, so by DeepSeek's own documentation the two features are mutually exclusive. ←PreviousNext→ 3Pin the sampler seed per sequence⌄ Pass a fixed seq_seed in SamplingParams. Identical input tokens plus identical sampling parameters then produce identical outputs. ←PreviousNext→ 4Decide which you actually need, per workload⌄ Determinism for evals, regression baselines and RL rollouts; DSpark for throughput on everything else. Running one cluster in each mode is a legitimate design, and cheaper than pretending one config serves both. ←PreviousNext→ DeepInfer: deterministic sampling (environment) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Deterministic sampling — NVIDIA only. # Note that MTP_VARLEN=0 is the same switch that disables DSpark, # so this configuration is deliberately the slow one. export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia export DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 export DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0 # ...and pass a fixed seq_seed in SamplingParams, e.g. # SamplingParams(temperature=0.0, seq_seed=42) python examples/offline_inference.py --ep 8 DeepInfer: DSpark speculative decoding (the other mode) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Throughput mode: draft tokens plus confidence-scheduled verification. # DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE sets the maximum draft length (default 5). export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia export DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1 export DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE=5 # Explicitly disable speculative decoding instead: # export DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE=0 python examples/benchmark.py The second mode is where DeepInfer's cleverest idea lives. Plain speculative decoding drafts n tokens and verifies them all. Confidence-scheduled verification uses the model's own confidence estimates to decide how much verification budget to spend — cheap where the draft is obviously right, expensive where it isn't. That is a scheduling idea, not a kernel idea, and it transfers to any engine with a draft path.

DeepSeek publishes two Pareto curves — prefill throughput vs latency, decode throughput vs per-user speed — rather than a headline tokens-per-second figure. That restraint is admirable and it means there is no single number to quote. It also means the methodology, documented in examples/README.md, is where the truth lives. Three things in it change how you read the charts.

This is the big one. The published decode throughput is computed as: decode_throughput = avg_SPS × decode_num_requests × (1 + nextn) / cp and the documentation states plainly that this is "under the full-acceptance accounting — 1 + nextn tokens per request per step, regardless of the true acceptance rate." nextn defaults to 5. So each request is credited with 6 tokens per decode step whether the speculative decoder's 5 drafts survived verification or not. With the default 64 requests, "the 64 requests of one decode step account for 384 tokens in total" — 64 × 6. Real acceptance rates for multi-token prediction are well under 100%. So the decode throughput on that chart is an upper bound that no real workload reaches, and the gap between the chart and your reality is exactly your rejection rate. Nothing here is dishonest — it is written down in the repo — but it is not what a reader glancing at a Pareto curve assumes, and nobody in 856 Hacker News comments mentioned it.
documents.s: 1. Decode throughput assumes every draft token was accepted

documents.t: Prefill was measured on 4 SM100 GPUs, decode on 64, "each within one scale-up domain" — i.e. inside a single NVLink fabric, not across an Ethernet cluster. Both throughput figures are then divided by the device count to give tokens/s/GPU. Per-GPU normalisation is the right way to publish this, and it is also the easiest thing in the world to misread. A per-GPU decode number obtained with 64 GPUs sharing one fabric does not survive being multiplied back up on your 8-GPU node, because the expert-parallel communication pattern that made it possible was the fabric.
documents.s: 2. The numbers are per-GPU, at a scale you don't have

documents.t: A detail I have not seen anywhere else, and a genuinely useful warning for anyone profiling their own engine. From the docs: step times inside a PROFILE=1 trace include profiler overhead of "up to nearly 50% inflation at bsz=1", and even after the profiler exits there is a residual slowdown of ~7–11% — which is why no measurement is allowed to be scheduled after the profiler section. The explicit instruction is to use traces for inspecting kernel composition and never to derive steps-per-second. The harness goes further than most: it drops any measurement interval that collides with a MoE load-balancer statistics flush (an expert-parallel all_gather with a dozen milliseconds of jitter), and it runs the measurement window twice — once with logging on to capture load-balancer values, once silently for the actual numbers. Pro tip Steal the two-stage eval design regardless of engine. DeepInfer's eval harness separates generation from scoring: generation writes raw outputs to disk, scoring reads them back. You can re-judge with a different grader without paying for inference again — and on a deterministic engine you can prove the outputs didn't move.
documents.s: 3. The profiler traces are not throughput data

documents.t: Worth knowing before you cite any accuracy number from this repo. It covers three benchmarks, all reported as Pass@1: AIME 2026 (30 tasks × 32 samples, mean accuracy), HLE (2,500 questions — 2,158 text and 342 image — single sample), and GPQA Diamond (198 tasks × 8 samples). The scripts deliberately do not download the datasets; you must fetch each one yourself and convert it to JSONL, and HLE is gated on Hugging Face. A benchmark harness that refuses to auto-download its own test sets is a small sign of seriousness about contamination.
documents.s: What the eval harness actually measures

documents.t: SWA bounded replay. DeepInfer reduces decoder prefill work by replaying only a bounded suffix of context, configured with DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact and DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140 for V4.1's defaults. The constraint is the interesting part: the retained suffix must cover the sliding-window-attention window plus the maximum backtracking length. That oddly specific 140 is not a tuning preference, it is a floor derived from the architecture. Lower it to save memory and you are not trading quality for speed — you are truncating context the model still needs. EPLB redundant experts. Expert-parallel load balancing is configured through DEEPINFER_OVERRIDE_NUM_EXTRA_EXPERTS, default 32. This is only a lower bound: the engine rounds num_routed_experts + num_extra_experts up until it divides evenly by ep_size, rounding the backbone and DFlash separately. So the value you set is frequently not the value in effect — and the records written to disk and the plots use the rounded figure that actually took effect. If you are comparing two runs, compare the logged value, not your environment.

Ask what accounting a throughput number uses. "Tokens per second" with a speculative decoder in the loop is ambiguous until someone tells you whether rejected drafts are counted. Ask it of every engine, including the one you run. Stop asserting equality on LLM output unless you've earned determinism. Temperature 0 is near-deterministic, not deterministic, and the failure mode is a divergence a hundred tokens in that your smoke test never reaches. Either make the engine batch-invariant and assert bitwise, or test with evals and distributions. The middle ground is a flaky suite that teaches your team to ignore red. "Open-sourced the engine" rarely means "open-sourced the service." Read for the absences — cache system, disaggregation, load balancing. The gap between a published engine and a running service is where all the platform work lives, and the README that tells you honestly which pieces are missing is doing you a favour. Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways DeepInfer is a hard-specialised vLLM derivative for one model on datacenter Blackwell or Ascend 950 — not a general engine and not a drop-in server. Most readers cannot run it, and that is the honest answer to "should I switch?" It withholds the KV cache system, prefill/decode disaggregation and DP load balancing by design. Read releases for what is absent, not just what is announced. Batch invariance, not floating-point randomness, is why temperature 0 drifts: kernels pick reduction orders by batch shape, and co-tenant traffic picks your batch shape. 1,000 temperature-0 runs produced 80 unique completions, identical for 102 tokens and then not. Reproducibility costs roughly 1.6× throughput in published measurements, and in DeepInfer it also costs you DSpark — the enabling flag for one disables the other. Run separate configs for evals/RL and for serving. Full-acceptance accounting means the published decode throughput counts drafted tokens whether or not they were accepted. Ask every engine which accounting its tokens-per-second uses. DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140 is an architectural floor, not a tuning dial; DEEPINFER_OVERRIDE_NUM_EXTRA_EXPERTS=32 is a lower bound the engine rounds up. Log the effective values before comparing runs.
documents.s: If you can't run it, take these three things
