复制为 Markdown 高级 DeepSeek Harness — the command is dsh — is DeepSeek's open-source agent harness. It appeared on GitHub on 13 August 2026, carries 242,626 stars and 29,081 forks as of today, is MIT licensed and written in TypeScript. On 1 October 2026 DeepSeek added signed desktop installers, which is what put it back on the Hacker News front page. Its one-line pitch is the repository description: "Everything is a Plugin." That phrase is on the README of roughly every agent framework ever published, and it almost always means "we have a plugin folder." Here it means something much stronger and much weirder, stated plainly in docs/architecture.md: the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log and the agent loop itself are plugins, "so each is replaceable from configuration." You can delete the agent loop from a YAML file and drop in your own without forking anything. That design has consequences — some excellent, some expensive. This page is about the ones you cannot read off the landing page. What you'll learn Understand what 'everything is a plugin' buys you here, and what Cordis — the framework underneath — actually guarantees Run your existing Claude Code hooks.json inside dsh, and know which subset survives the bridge Point dsh at Claude, GPT or a company gateway, and know why an OAuth subscription will not work Use PTC mode (run_code) deliberately instead of accidentally Read the three sandbox modes against the kernel primitive each one really uses Avoid the five configuration traps that cost an hour each 最后验证时间：2026-10-03。 Star counts, the npm version and the desktop installer matrix are perishable. The npm latest tag currently resolves to 0.2.0-rc.2 — a release candidate, not a stable release — and SAFETY.md describes the project as "experimental developer-preview software" that "has not undergone a security audit." The README warns of compatibility-breaking changes. Treat every file path, service key and config field below as true for the 0.2 line and re-check against the repository docs before you build on them. The architecture and safety claims here come from the repository's own documentation, not from secondary coverage. 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: DeepSeek Harness: the agent where the agent loop itself is a plugin

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Start it⌄ `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` boots the web profile, prints a URL — `http://127.0.0.1:3080` — and opens your browser. No clone, no build. The directory you invoke it from becomes the default workspace root, but a fresh Web UI has no workspace selected until you add one, and the composer stays disabled until you do. ←PreviousNext→ 2Give it a model⌄ Settings → Models. The DeepSeek card takes an API key from platform.deepseek.com. Add a third-party provider and the shipped catalog offers provider ids including `anthropic`, `openai`, `moonshotai` (Kimi) and `zai` (GLM). Model changes apply on the next request — no restart. ←PreviousNext→ 3Understand where it put things⌄ Keys land in `$DSH_HOME/.credentials.yaml`, write-only: the settings page gets a redacted descriptor back, never the secret, and your settings store only a credential reference. Everything else you change in the UI is written to `$DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml` — the same file you can hand-edit. ←PreviousNext→ 4Pick an entry mode⌄ `dsh web` is one of five shipped profiles. `dsh --profile headless "run the tests"` runs one persisted session, prints the final answer and exits — that is your CI entry point. `dsh --profile acp` serves automation clients over ACP stdio. `dsh --profile sdk` serves SDK clients over JSON-RPC stdio. The `desktop` name is reserved for the Electron app's own profile and the npm CLI refuses to boot it. ←PreviousNext→ 5Install plugins like npm packages⌄ `dsh plugin --profile web <pnpm args>` forwards straight to pnpm inside the profile directory. Plugins are ordinary packages in the profile's own `node_modules`. Community plugins are discoverable by the `dsh-plugin` GitHub topic. ←PreviousNext→

Underneath dsh is Cordis, a plugin framework vendored into the repository (vendor/) and described in an arXiv paper the project cites — A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability, arXiv:2608.25512, submitted 26 August 2026, from authors at Peking University and DeepSeek-AI. The paper's two ideas map directly onto how the harness behaves at runtime: Temporal composability — a component's side effects can be completely reversed when it is removed. In the harness this is ctx.effect(): prompt sections, tool schemas, model adapters, providers and listeners are all installed as reversible effects, so unloading a plugin unwinds its registrations in order rather than leaving orphans behind. Spatial composability — dependencies resolve reactively. A plugin names the services it needs via inject, and Cordis simply does not start it until those services exist. There is no boot sequence to maintain; load order is a consequence of declared requirements. A service claims a stable key on the shared context. The names are the architecture: Service key What owns it ctx.llm the LLM adapter registry — the model seam ctx.tools the tool registry and its scoped execution pipeline ctx.agentLoop the default agent-loop driver ctx.agents the live agent registry ctx.sessions the append-only SessionEvent log ctx.systemPrompt system-prompt assembly ctx.fs filesystem access ctx.subprocess subprocess execution ctx.sandbox subprocess confinement ctx.subagents subagent delegation ctx.ptcRuntime program execution for run_code ctx.credentials the credential seam The repository calls these capability seams, and splits every one into three roles: the package that declares the service, the packages that implement it, and the packages that consume it. ctx.sandbox is declared by packages/sandbox/sandbox, implemented by sandbox-local and sandbox-windows-acl, consumed by tool-bash and the PTC runtime. Replace the implementation and every consumer follows, with no consumer edits. Communication between plugins is typed events with five declared dispatch modes, and the mode is part of an event's public contract: Mode Awaited Order Returns a value emit no registration order no waterfall no registration order yes parallel yes all at once no serial yes registration order yes bail no registration order, stops at first bail yes waterfall is the interesting one: it is around-middleware. A listener gets (...args, next), calls next() to pass a possibly-wrapped result down the chain, or returns without calling next() to short-circuit. For single-decision events — "may this tool run?" — short-circuiting is the design: a policy listener that owns the decision returns without delegating, while a listener that merely annotates must delegate. If you have written a Claude Code hook that returns a deny decision, you already know this shape; the difference is that here it is the native extension mechanism rather than a shell-out. The agent loop runs turns (zero or more steps) and steps (one model request plus its tool calls), and the published extension sequence is agent/pre-step → agent/request → llm/stream → tools/* → step/end. Those are the hook points. You do not patch the loop; you listen to it.
documents.s: "Everything is a plugin" is a load-bearing claim

documents.t: This is the single most under-reported fact about dsh. packages/hooks ships three packages: hook-protocol (the shared engine), hooks-claude-code and hooks-codex. Point the Claude Code bridge at an existing hooks.json and your hooks run inside dsh when sessions start, prompts arrive, tools run and runs stop. The group README is explicit about what they can do: block prompts or tool calls with model-visible messages, add conversation context, or require the run to continue. The limit is equally explicit, and it is the thing to check before you plan a migration: each integration supports only the command-hook subset documented by its source tool. So your command-type hooks port. Anything that depends on Claude Code behaviour outside that subset does not. If you have a hooks layer you trust — see Claude Code hooks — this is a genuine "bring your guardrails with you" path, not a rewrite.
documents.s: 1. It will run your existing Claude Code hooks.json

documents.t: The provider list shipped in the installed catalog includes anthropic and openai by name. For anything not in the catalog — a relay, a company gateway, a self-hosted server — the custom-provider form asks for a Provider ID, a base URL, a credential and an API protocol, and offers exactly three: OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, and Anthropic Messages. In cordis.patch.yml these are stored as openai-completions, openai-responses and anthropic-messages. Two consequences people trip over: A provider speaks one protocol. A gateway that serves both OpenAI and Anthropic shapes needs two provider entries, not one. OAuth sign-in is not supported. The providers guide states it directly, using Codex as its example: providers that sign in with OAuth "are not supported here yet." That means API-key billing, not a seat you already pay for. If you were hoping to drive dsh off an existing assistant subscription, budget for metered tokens instead — the arithmetic is in what AI costs across providers. There is also a model-discovery button that asks your endpoint which models it serves. Useful, with a caveat worth internalising: a built-in provider is always answered from the installed catalog even when its base URL points at a gateway. So if you want to see what a gateway really serves, you have to add it as a custom provider. Otherwise you are reading DeepSeek's shipped list back to yourself.
documents.s: 2. You can point it at Claude — but not with your subscription

documents.t: packages/ptc-runtime is the capability family behind what the tool registry presents to the model as run_code. The contract: the model writes one program that calls host-provided functions as ordinary async calls, and only the program's printed output and return value come back. Not the intermediate tool results. Not twenty round-trips. The specifics: The TypeScript backend runs each program in a fresh managed Node process under the resolved sandbox policy. Each run starts with no state from earlier programs. There is no implicit REPL session to lean on; carry state through files or the return value. Failures come back as results, not exceptions, so a caller can diagnose them or hand them to the model. An experimental Python backend exists, owning an fd-3 wire protocol between the Node host and a CPython subprocess, for when you genuinely need CPython. If this pattern is new to you, the clearest write-up of why it saves so much context is on Pi 1.0 and the codemode trick: tool results that never enter the transcript cannot inflate it. The same logic applies here. The difference is that in dsh the program runtime is a swappable seam (ctx.ptcRuntime) rather than a fixed sandbox choice.
documents.s: 3. run_code is codemode, and it is a first-class runtime

documents.t: The three modes will look familiar if you have configured Codex: Mode What a subprocess may do to files read-only read only workspace-write write only under the session workspace danger-full-access unrestricted What is more interesting is the backend table, because it tells you what is really enforcing the policy on your machine: Linux — bwrap, then Landlock as the fallback rung. macOS — Seatbelt. Windows — a restricted token, with sandbox-windows-acl as the write-restriction backend: confined children may write only in the workspace and a private temp directory. A denied call can retry through a user-approved one-time escalation, so the policy is a prompt-and-proceed boundary rather than a hard wall. And then the caveat, which the package README states itself and which you should quote to anyone who tells you this is "sandboxed": confinement is same-world only. It shares the host kernel and the host filesystem. Real isolation — containers, microVMs, remote executors — does not register here at all; it replaces whole capabilities instead. SAFETY.md is unusually candid for a 242k-star repository, and worth reading before a first run rather than after. It says the harness can execute model-generated code, load third-party plugins, reach the network and touch processes, credentials and files; that there is no inherent guarantee that sandboxing, approval prompts and permission controls will prevent damage to anything reachable; and that the software "must not be treated as secure or production-ready." Its own recommendations are the boring correct ones: disposable VMs or containers, backups of anything inside the project scope, and no sensitive credentials unless you accept the risk. The same reasoning applies to any harness you run locally — see securing local and hybrid agents and sandboxing and credential masking. There is also a small guard group worth knowing about: timeout-policy and repeat-tool-reminder — the latter being a nudge for the failure mode where a model calls the same tool in a loop.
documents.s: The sandbox: three modes, three kernel primitives, one honest caveat

documents.t: dsh persists sessions as a versioned JSONL file — session.vN.jsonl[.zstd] — with migration chains between versions, through a ctx.sessionPersistence seam whose shipped implementation is session-persistence-jsonl. Committed events include turn/start, step/start, user/message, assistant/message, tool/result and turn/end. The invariant behind it is the part to steal even if you never run dsh: "model-visible means logged." Every input the model saw must be reconstructable from the log. Live events exist separately, for driving UI in real time; they are explicitly not the record of truth. That single rule is what makes the surrounding packages possible: session-query-sqlite — query sessions out of SQLite instead of grepping JSONL. dsh-session-projection with ctx.sessionProjections — fold session state incrementally rather than replaying from zero. llm-replay plus token-meter ("replay token measurement") — replay a recorded session and measure its token cost, which is how you compare two prompt or model changes on identical inputs instead of on vibes. compaction-tool-result-pruner — described as model-free tool-result pruning, i.e. shrinking the transcript without paying a model to summarise it. Compare with Claude's own approach in context compaction. If you have ever tried to debug an agent run and discovered your logs recorded the rendered UI rather than the bytes the model received, you already know why this invariant is worth more than most features.
documents.s: The session log is the product

documents.t: dsh speaks MCP over both stdio and Streamable HTTP, using the official SDK for negotiation, discovery, validation and cancellation. The design choices are unusual enough to list: Servers are opt-in, one plugin entry per server. You configure one @deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client entry per server in the Cordis scope you want it visible in. There is deliberately no shared ctx.mcp service: the client is a connection plugin and a consumer of the tool registry. No configured server means no MCP tax. A caller with no visible configured server receives no MCP prompt text and no MCP tools, in native or PTC mode. Zero bytes, not "a small section." That matters more than it sounds — see the real cost of MCP tools. Public tool names include the server name, so identically-named tools from two servers stay distinct. A serverName must be unique inside its registration scope, but separate agent scopes may reuse it. Server instructions join the logged system prompt, bounded by the client's maxInstructionBytes. A verbose server cannot quietly annex your prompt — but note that this is also the channel through which a malicious server speaks to your model. That is the attack surface described in MCP tool poisoning and rug pulls. A failed tool-list refresh retains the previous tool generation rather than dropping your tools mid-session, and there is no product setting that forces a protocol revision — negotiation follows the SDK's supported revisions.
documents.s: MCP here is a per-server plugin, not a global registry

documents.t: A profile directory holds a package.json — out-of-tree plugin dependencies plus a dsh.profile manifest with an ordered bundles list — and a cordis.patch.yml, your own patch layer. The composed tree is built over an empty root in this order: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Each bundle's patch, in `dsh.profile.bundles` order⌄ Bundles resolve from the dsh installation first — `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base`, `dsh-web-app`, `dsh-headless`, `dsh-sdk-app`, `dsh-sdk-minimal`, `dsh-acp-app` — then from the profile's own `node_modules`, where pnpm installs out-of-tree plugins. `dsh-base` is the shared floor: model adapters, tools, persistence, sandbox policy. A bundle declares itself through a `dsh` field in its `package.json`. ←PreviousNext→ 2Then the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`⌄ `$DSH_HOME/profiles/<profile>/cordis.patch.yml`. For a plain `dsh web` launch the profile is `web`. This is the file the Settings UI writes; you can edit it directly and the adapters re-read it on the next request. ←PreviousNext→ 3Then the home patch⌄ `$DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml` — cross-profile overrides. ←PreviousNext→ 4Then `--patch` overlays⌄ Command-line overlays, applied last. `config/examples/` ships opt-in overlays for GitHub review webhooks, memory MCP servers and runtime Cordis tools; they are never part of a default profile. ←PreviousNext→ 5Inspect before you boot⌄ `--dump-default-config` and `--dump-config` print the composed tree without starting anything — the fastest way to answer "which layer set this?" ←PreviousNext→ With HMR enabled in YAML, dsh-hmr watches the profile manifest and both patch files and recomposes every layer through one serialized reload. Without it, changes apply on restart.
documents.s: Configuration: five layers, and the override that eats your providers

documents.t: A Cordis config override replaces the complete entry config. The providers guide spells this out: when you edit an existing override, you must preserve the other fields and other providers yourself. Patch one provider carelessly and you have deleted the rest. This is the single most expensive mistake available in cordis.patch.yml. A Provider ID is permanent. Requests, saved sessions, model defaults and credential references all key off it. Renaming means adding a new provider and deleting the old one. Display name, base URL, protocol, credential and model list stay editable. --dump-config-schema imports plugin code. Unlike the other dump flags, it loads the composed tree's declared plugin schemas to print JSON Schema — so pointing it at untrusted plugins executes their import-time code. The CLI reference has a dedicated safety note on this. Treat it like reviewing third-party code, not like --help. Plugin version compatibility is enforced, and the escape hatch is explicit. Installation and profile startup check declared DSH peer ranges against the runtime version from dsh --version; an incompatible plugin requires an acknowledged exact-version exemption (allow-version, revoke-version). Good hygiene, surprising the first time a plugin refuses to load. A session that has already sent a request keeps the model recorded in its own log. Changing the default model does not retroactively move a live session, and if a saved default names a deleted provider the composer blocks input until you pick another. Both are correct behaviour; both look like bugs at 1 a.m.
documents.s: Five gotchas that will cost you an hour

documents.t: Start the Web UI, then a headless one-shot run — no clone, no build CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Web UI on http://127.0.0.1:3080, workspace defaults to the invoking directory npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web # One persisted session, final answer to stdout, then exit — the CI shape npx @deepseek-ai/dsh --profile headless "summarize this repo and list its main packages" # Serve automation clients over ACP stdio (editor integrations) npx @deepseek-ai/dsh --profile acp # Inspect the composed config tree WITHOUT booting it npx @deepseek-ai/dsh --profile web --dump-config # Manage a profile's plugins (forwards to pnpm inside the profile directory) npx @deepseek-ai/dsh plugin --profile web add some-dsh-plugin Point dsh at a gateway that speaks Anthropic Messages — in $DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # WARNING: a Cordis config override replaces the ENTIRE entry config. # Include every provider you want to keep, not just the new one. - id: llm-pi-ai config: providers: my-anthropic-gateway: apiKeyEnv: GATEWAY_API_KEY api: anthropic-messages # or openai-completions / openai-responses baseURL: https://gateway.example/v1 models: - id: some-text-model - id: some-vision-model input: [text, image] # omit to inherit the catalog's input types Bring your Claude Code guardrails across CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # The Claude Code hook bridge runs your existing command hooks inside dsh. # Only the command-hook subset documented by Claude Code is supported. # Hooks can: block a prompt or a tool call with a MODEL-VISIBLE message, # add conversation context, or require the run to continue. # # Check the bridge's own README for the current config field names before # wiring this up — the 0.2 line is a developer preview and they can move: # packages/hooks/hooks-claude-code/README.md # # Verify enforcement the same way you would in Claude Code: a hook that is # configured but never fires is worse than no hook, because you trust it.

If you are choosing a harness rather than studying one, the honest summary is: dsh is the most architecturally interesting open harness shipping right now and the least ready to be load-bearing. Its own safety file says so. The plugin model is genuinely stronger than its competitors' — ctx.agentLoop being replaceable is not a thing you can do in most harnesses at any price — and the hook bridges mean adopting it is not an all-or-nothing bet. Against that: a release-candidate latest tag, no security audit, promised breaking changes, and a provider story that assumes API keys. For a comparison across the field, see coding agent CLIs compared and local coding agents. For the models you would most plausibly drive it with, see DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Check yourself 0/7

SAFETY.md — what the harness can do to your machine, and the explicit "not secure or production-ready" statement. packages/sandbox/README.md — the three modes, the per-platform backends, escalation, and "same-world only". packages/hooks/README.md — the Claude Code and Codex hook bridges and the command-hook-subset limit. packages/ptc-runtime/README.md — the run_code contract, fresh-process execution, the experimental Python backend. docs/subsystems/mcp.md — per-server client plugins, scope rules, name namespacing, maxInstructionBytes, protocol negotiation. docs/user/guide/providers.md — provider ids, the three API protocols, OAuth limitation, credential storage, the override warning. apps/cli/README.md — entry modes, profile composition order, bundle names, dsh plugin, the dump flags, version exemptions. 复制为 Markdown 进阶 在很长一段时间里，“优秀 AI”的故事就是少数几个闭源前沿模型的故事——你只能通过 API 租用它们。如今这已不再是故事的全部。一波开放权重模型——许多来自中国实验室，比如 DeepSeek 和阿里巴巴的 Qwen，此外还有 Meta 的 Llama 和法国的 Mistral——已经变得足够好、足够便宜、足够小，以至于下载并运行你自己的高能力模型成为了一个真正可行的选项。本页是这一版图的持久地图：为什么会发生、“开放权重”到底意味着什么、相对闭源前沿模型的诚实取舍，以及今天如何真正地使用这些模型。 What you'll learn 理解开放权重模型为何变得有竞争力——单位成本的能力，以及开放的推理能力 厘清“开放权重”真正的含义——相对于开源和开放数据 识别几种原型：通用对话、推理、编程，以及小型/高效模型 权衡相对于闭源前沿的真实取舍——在最难任务上的能力差距，以及自行拥有基础设施与安全责任 了解真正使用它们的两种方式：托管 API，或通过 Ollama 自托管

三件事大约在同一时间发生了转变，它们合在一起弥合了日常使用中的大部分差距。 单位成本的能力急剧下降。 更好的训练方案、数据筛选，以及**混合专家（MoE）**架构（一个大模型中每个 token 只激活一部分参数）让实验室能够推出远超其成本的模型。对于很大一部分真实任务——起草、摘要、抽取、分类、常规编程——一个优秀的开放模型如今已“足够好”，而成本只是前沿 API 的一小部分。 开放的推理模型出现了。 DeepSeek 的推理系列是一个转折点：它表明“在回答前一步步思考”的能力——此前是少数闭源模型的护城河——是可以用开放权重训练并发布的。一旦某个实验室证明了这一点，开放生态系统的其余部分便纷纷跟进。 小模型变得真正可用。 100 亿参数以下、甚至 10 亿参数以下的模型变得连贯而有用，这意味着你可以在笔记本电脑或便宜的服务器上运行有能力的东西。这改变了隐私、延迟和规模的经济学。 净效应是：与闭源前沿的差距并没有消失，但对大多数工作而言，它不再是决定性因素。决定性因素变成了成本、控制权，以及你的数据存放在哪里。
documents.s: 开放权重模型为何突然变得有竞争力
documents.h: #开放权重模型为何突然变得有竞争力

documents.t: 这是整个领域中最容易被混淆的一点。“开放”一词以三种不同的方式承担了大量含义，而它们并不是一回事。 术语 你实际得到的 你通常得不到的 开放权重 训练好的模型文件（权重）。你可以下载、运行、微调并自托管。 训练数据，有时还包括完整的训练代码。使用可能受某种自定义许可证的约束。 开源（严格意义） 权重加上在 OSI 风格许可证下的训练/推理代码，可自由使用、修改和再分发。 通常仍然不包括训练数据。 开放数据 模型训练所用的实际数据集，公开发布。 对于前沿规模的模型这很罕见；大多数“开放”模型是开放权重，而非开放数据。 实用的要点是：人们所称的“开源”模型大多其实是开放权重。 你可以运行并改造它们，但通常无法从零复现它们，而且你必须阅读许可证。许可证各不相同： 有些采用宽松许可证（Apache 2.0、MIT），对商业使用而言很干净——例如 Qwen 和 Mistral 的模型历来使用 Apache 2.0，而 DeepSeek 的重要发布采用过 MIT。 有些采用带条件的自定义社区许可证——例如 Meta 的 Llama 许可证历来包含一条条款，限制（按月活跃用户计）规模最大的公司自由使用它。 在基于某个模型进行开发之前，务必查看该模型的具体模型卡以了解其许可证。中立但重要的一点：一个模型是开放权重，只告诉你你可以自行托管它；它并不告诉你法律条款，也不会让许可或数据驻留的问题消失——它只是把这些问题转移给了你。 最后验证时间：2026-06-28。 确切的当前模型版本、参数量、基准分数以及每 token 价格变化很快，本文有意不将其断言为永久事实。版图的持久形态——实验室、原型，以及开放权重 vs 开源 vs 开放数据的区分——是稳定的；而具体的排行榜数字则不然。请查看所链接的组织页面以了解当前情况。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
开放权重家族几乎总是以一个变体系列的形式出现，而不是单一的模型。学会这四种原型，你就能一眼读懂任何实验室的产品线。 单个家族——Qwen 是最清晰的例子——通常会给你整个阶梯：用于边缘和笔记本的微型模型、用于服务器的中型模型、用于最难任务的大型旗舰，外加专门用于编程和推理的变体。你挑选适合你硬件和任务的那一档，而不是“那个模型”。

开放权重模型并不是严格意义上的升级。它们是另一种交易。下面中立地摆出这笔取舍。 维度 开放权重（自托管或廉价托管） 闭源前沿（托管 API） 最难任务的能力 很强且正在快速追赶，但在最难的推理、长时程智能体和小众任务上，闭源前沿通常仍然领先 通常是最艰难任务的上限 规模化成本 可以显著更便宜，尤其是自托管或通过预算型托管 每 token 溢价；可预测但会累积 隐私 / 数据驻留 你可以把数据完全保留在你的环境内部 数据离开你的网络流向提供商 控制与定制 完全：微调、量化、锁定版本、离线运行 仅限于 API 所暴露的内容；版本可能在你不知情下发生变化 谁负责安全与运维 你自己——护栏、滥用过滤、正常运行时间、扩展和打补丁都是你的工作 由提供商运行基础设施并提供基线安全 最后一行是人们低估的那一项。当你自托管一个开放权重模型时，你也继承了前沿实验室通常替你承担的责任：内容安全和滥用缓解、保持部署已打补丁、容量和正常运行时间，以及自己评估每一个新的模型版本。“开放权重”为你买来了控制权，而控制权既是收益，也是成本。关于这笔取舍中 API 一侧的成本直觉，参见 Token 经济学。
documents.s: 相对于闭源前沿的诚实取舍
documents.h: #相对于闭源前沿的诚实取舍

documents.t: 恰好有两条路径，大多数团队在不同阶段都会两者并用。 托管 API — 许多提供商（包括实验室自身以及第三方推理托管方）在 API 后面提供开放权重模型，通常是与 OpenAI 兼容的。你以零基础设施工作获得开放模型的经济性。当你想要低成本又不想运行服务器时最合适，但请注意你的数据仍会离开你的网络。 自托管 — 下载权重并在你自己的环境中运行它们。最大的隐私和控制权，也是数据确实无法离开你网络时的唯一选项。最简单的入门方式是 Ollama，它用一条命令拉取并运行开放模型。
documents.s: 如何真正使用一个开放模型
documents.h: #如何真正使用一个开放模型

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1安装 Ollama⌄ 从 ollama.com/download 下载（macOS/Windows），或使用 Linux 安装脚本。这会给你 ollama 命令以及一个本地后台服务。完整讲解见“在本地运行模型”页面。 ←PreviousNext→ 2挑选你的机器能跑的尺寸⌄ 更小的模型需要更少的 RAM/VRAM。笔记本电脑可以轻松运行小型变体（几 GB）；大型旗舰需要一块真正的 GPU 或服务器。先从小的开始，确认一切正常，如果质量不够再往上扩。 ←PreviousNext→ 3用一条命令运行它⌄ ollama run <model> 会在首次使用时下载权重（数 GB），然后把你带入一个交互式聊天。首次运行较慢是因为它在拉取；之后的运行会从缓存中瞬间启动。 ←PreviousNext→ 4从你的代码中调用它⌄ Ollama 暴露了一个与 OpenAI 兼容的本地端点，因此你可以把现有的 OpenAI 风格 SDK 指向 localhost 而非云端。现在同一份代码就能针对一个私有的本地模型运行。 ←PreviousNext→ 用 Ollama 在本地拉取并运行一个开放模型 CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ ollama run qwen3 这一条命令会下载一个 Qwen 开放权重模型并启动一个本地聊天——无需 API 密钥，也没有数据离开你的机器。把 qwen3 换成另一个家族（例如某个 Llama、Mistral 或 DeepSeek 标签），就能在你自己的任务上比较它们。为给定的工作挑选合适的模型本身就是一项技能：参见 选择模型。
documents.s: 四步在本地试用一个模型

documents.t: 不要按排行榜来选。要按约束来选： 数据不能离开你的网络 → 自托管的开放权重就是答案，没有例外。 高流量、成本敏感、“足够好”的质量 → 开放权重（托管或自托管）通常在成本上胜出。 你需要在最难任务上做到绝对最好 → 闭源前沿仍然倾向于领先——在真正重要的地方使用它，并把较容易的流量路由到更便宜的开放模型。 你想微调、量化、锁定版本或离线运行 → 只有开放权重才能给你那种控制权。 最经久耐用的做法，是在你自己的真实数据上，对一个开放候选和一个闭源候选各跑一个小型评测。基准描述的是别人的任务；你的评测描述的是你的任务。 自我检验 0/3 Key takeaways 得益于单位成本的能力、开放的推理模型，以及真正可用的小模型，开放权重模型弥合了日常使用中的大部分差距 “开放权重” = 可下载、可运行、可微调的权重——但不一定意味着开源代码、开放的训练数据或宽松许可证；务必阅读模型卡 按原型读懂任何产品线：通用对话、推理、编程，以及小型/高效——大多数家族都提供完整的尺寸阶梯 取舍是真实的：开放买来的是成本、隐私和控制权，但闭源前沿通常仍在最难任务上领先，而且你要继承安全与基础设施的责任 使用它们的两种方式：一个（通常与 OpenAI 兼容的）托管 API，或用一条命令通过 Ollama 自托管——然后在你自己的数据上评测，而不是看排行榜

复制为 Markdown 进阶 At 04:00 UTC on September 10, 2026, DeepSeek flipped its API to a new model and published the weights the same day: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, served as deepseek-flash. It is the smallest member of a new architecture family, but it is not a small model: 552 billion parameters, a 1-million-token context, native vision, and a KV cache that costs 890 bytes per token. On DeepSWE v1.1, the long-horizon software-engineering benchmark both Google and Anthropic now headline, DeepSeek reports 74.2, one-fifth of a point above Claude Opus 5. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it reports 31.2 against Opus 5's 51.8. Both numbers are true, and the gap between them is the whole story. This page is the field guide for a Claude user: what actually changed, the routing change that quietly re-pointed every deepseek-v4-pro request, the effort dial and what it does to your bill, how to run the weights, and the workloads where Claude is still the right call. What you'll learn Read the V4.1-Flash launch numbers the way they deserve: tied with Opus 5 on DeepSWE, far behind on Terminal-Bench, and why that split is not a contradiction Understand the new Causal Encoder-Decoder + CSA2 design well enough to know what the 890-byte KV cache buys you (and what DeepSeek says it has not yet characterized) Use the 1–100 reasoning_effort dial deliberately — 25 vs 100 is an 8-point DeepSWE swing for ~2.5× the output tokens Do the honest cost math: $0.30 / $1.20 peak, half that off-peak, $0.003 per million on an off-peak cache hit — and the UTC peak window that decides which rate you pay Know the September 14 routing change: deepseek-v4-pro now silently serves V4.1-Flash until V4.1-Pro ships Pick a serving path (hosted API, vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner) and the sampling defaults DeepSeek recommends 最后验证时间：2026-09-15。 Model ID, routing dates, and pricing from DeepSeek's September 10 announcement and the API pricing page. Architecture, license, reasoning-effort range, and sampling defaults from the Hugging Face model card. Benchmark comparisons against Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol are DeepSeek's own launch table as reported by VentureBeat on September 10; treat them as vendor-run until an independent harness publishes. The 3.0/4.0 Terminal-Bench gaps come from the same table. DeepSeek's statement that the architecture has "robustness boundaries it has not fully characterized" is quoted from the same coverage. 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: A 1M-Context Open Weight That Ties Opus 5 on DeepSWE (Sep 2026)

documents.t: V4.1-Flash is DeepSeek's first model on a new architecture (a "Causal Encoder-Decoder" with Compressed Sparse Attention 2), released MIT-licensed with native vision, a 1M-token window, 384K max output, and a continuously controllable reasoning effort from 1 to 100. It replaces every V4-era Flash endpoint immediately and, since September 14, also answers every deepseek-v4-pro call at Flash prices until V4.1-Pro lands.

DeepSeek's launch table, in the columns that matter for an agent shop: Benchmark DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Claude Opus 5 GPT-5.6 Sol DeepSWE v1.1 (resolved) 74.2 74.0 73.0 Terminal-Bench 3.0 30.0 43.3 — Terminal-Bench 4.0 31.2 51.8 — CyberGym 88.1 — — AutomationBench 54.8 — — DeepSWE rewards a model that reads a repository, plans a patch, and lands it: long context, careful retrieval, a few large edits. Terminal-Bench rewards many short, adaptive shell turns where each decision depends on the last tool result. V4.1-Flash has 1M tokens of context and a cheap cache, so the first shape suits it. It runs 8B active parameters per token at prefill and 16B at decode, which is a lot less "thinking per step" than a dense frontier model, so the second shape hurts. If your work looks like a pull request, the parity claim is credible and worth an eval. If your work looks like an interactive terminal session, the 20-point Terminal-Bench gap is the number to budget around. The same split shows up in Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash launch a week earlier, and for the same architectural reasons. The base-model rows tell a quieter story: MMLU-Pro 74.1 (V4-Flash 68.3, V4-Pro 73.5), HumanEval 79.4 (V4-Flash 69.5), GSM8K 93.0 (V4-Flash 90.8). The new "Flash" is a better base than last month's "Pro", which is why DeepSeek was comfortable routing Pro traffic onto it.
documents.s: 1. DeepSWE parity and Terminal-Bench deficit are the same fact seen twice

documents.t: Unlike Claude's effort (low/medium/high/max), V4.1-Flash exposes an integer from 1 to 100. DeepSeek's own ablation on DeepSWE v1.1: effort 25 scores 66.0%, effort 100 scores 74.2%, and the top setting emits roughly 2.5× as many output tokens. They also say the 60–80 band delivers most of the maximum-effort accuracy at less than half the token budget. Every benchmark row above was run at reasoning_effort=100. So the parity number is the expensive number. Reproduce it at 100 first, then walk down to the cheapest setting your evals still pass at. That is the same discipline we recommend for thinking_level on Gemini and effort on Claude in Reasoning models compared.
documents.s: 2. The reasoning-effort dial is a real dial, and it is on your bill

documents.t: From September 10, deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp route to V4.1-Flash, billed at Flash rates. The V4-Flash-Vision-Exp page's numbers now describe the open weights, not the hosted endpoint. From 04:00 UTC September 14, every deepseek-v4-pro request also routes to V4.1-Flash at Flash rates, "until V4.1-Pro launches". If you have evals pinned to deepseek-v4-pro, your production model changed under you on Sunday morning. Re-run the suite. The upside is that the same call now costs roughly a quarter of the Pro rate; the downside is that any Pro-specific behavior you tuned for is gone. This is exactly the failure mode Porting prompts across models warns about when a provider aliases model IDs.
documents.s: 3. Two routing changes happened without a client-side change

documents.t: Spec DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash API model ID deepseek-flash Release September 10, 2026 (API + open weights same day) Parameters 552B total; 8B active at prefill, 16B at decode MoE layout 384 routed + 1 shared expert per MoE layer; 6 routed experts active per token Architecture Causal Encoder-Decoder, Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2) KV cache 890 bytes per token (FP4, E2M1): ~1/4 of V4-Flash in HBM, ~1/8 in SSD storage; global KV cache lifetime at least 72 hours Context / max output 1M tokens / 384K tokens Vision Native; DeepSeek-ViT trained from scratch, 2D-RoPE, 3×3 pixel-unshuffle downsampling Reasoning control reasoning_effort integer 1–100 License MIT Weights Safetensors in BF16, F32, F8_E4M3, I8 Serving vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner, Transformers; reference inference code in the inference/ folder Recommended sampling temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 or 1.0, context 1M API concurrency 2,500 The KV-cache line is the architectural headline. A 1M-token conversation at 890 bytes per token is under a gigabyte of cache, which is why DeepSeek can promise a 72-hour cache lifetime and price cache hits at fractions of a cent. Anthropic's answer to the same problem is a cheaper cache-read rate on Claude Fable 5.1; DeepSeek's is to make the cache physically small. Both push you toward the same habit: put the stable prefix first and never edit it mid-run. See Prompt caching.

DeepSeek keeps a two-rate schedule. Peak hours are 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC, Monday through Friday; everything else is off-peak at exactly half the peak rate. Per 1M tokens Peak Off-peak Input, cache hit $0.006 $0.003 Input, cache miss $0.30 $0.15 Output $1.20 $0.60 Two things follow. First, the "$0.003 per million" headline is the off-peak cache-hit price, the cheapest of six cells; a cold, peak-hour agent run pays 100× that on input. Second, the peak window is defined in UTC and covers the European morning and the tail of the U.S. night. A batch job scheduled at 09:00 UTC pays double what the same job pays at 11:00 UTC. If you can shift, shift. For a framework that puts these cells beside Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google list prices, use What AI costs across providers; current Claude list prices live on Models and pricing.

Hosted is right for almost everyone: the model is enormous, and the API is the cheapest thing on this page. Self-host when data cannot leave your network or when you want the effort dial and 1M window without a rate limit. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Decide hosted vs self-hosted honestly⌄ 552B parameters in BF16 is over a terabyte of weights; the F8_E4M3 and I8 safetensors halve or quarter that but still need a multi-GPU node. If you do not already run Kimi K3 or Colibrì-class MoEs, the hosted endpoint at $0.30 / $1.20 peak will beat your amortized hardware bill. See the hardware math on Running Kimi K3 locally. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick a serving stack the card actually names⌄ vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner, and Transformers are the four listed. The card ships no Jinja chat template; it uses a custom encoding implementation, so use the reference code in the repo's inference folder (or the deepseek-recipe toolkit) rather than hand-rolling the prompt format. ←PreviousNext→ 3Set the sampling defaults DeepSeek recommends⌄ temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 or 1.0, context window 1M. These are the settings the benchmark rows were produced with. Do not port a Claude-tuned temperature of 0.2 over blindly. ←PreviousNext→ 4Start at reasoning_effort=100, then walk down⌄ Reproduce DeepSeek's number on your own eval first. Then try 80, 60, 40 and record accuracy vs output tokens. Most teams will land in the 60–80 band the vendor itself points at. ←PreviousNext→ 5Test long-context retrieval before you trust it⌄ DeepSeek says the new architecture has robustness boundaries it has not fully characterized, specifically sparse retrieval over very long contexts. Run a needle-in-haystack and a multi-hop retrieval test at the context length you will actually use. Treat the 1M number as a ceiling, not a promise. ←PreviousNext→ Hosted call with the effort dial (OpenAI-compatible endpoint) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ curl https://api.deepseek.com/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEEPSEEK_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "deepseek-flash", "reasoning_effort": 70, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior engineer. Reply with a unified diff and one paragraph of rationale."}, {"role": "user", "content": "The test suite in ./tests fails on macOS only. Here is the log and the relevant module: ..."} ] }' Self-hosted with vLLM (shape only; check the model card for the exact flags) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # One node, tensor-parallel across all visible GPUs. # The card names vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner and Transformers as supported. vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --max-model-len 1000000 \ --trust-remote-code # Then hit http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions with the same body as above.

Pro tip Reach for V4.1-Flash: repository-scale coding tasks that look like DeepSWE (read a lot, edit a little), where you can run at effort 60–100 and the cost per resolved issue still undercuts Claude by an order of magnitude. Reach for V4.1-Flash: anything that needs a 1M-token window and a warm cache for days — a 72-hour global cache lifetime and 890-byte-per-token KV make 'keep the whole codebase in context' cheap. Reach for V4.1-Flash: self-hosted or data-residency workloads where MIT licensing matters and you already run a multi-GPU MoE stack. Stay on Claude: interactive terminal agents and any many-short-turns loop. A 20-point Terminal-Bench 4.0 gap (31.2 vs 51.8) is not noise, and it is the shape of most real Claude Code sessions. Stay on Claude: work that needs Anthropic's tool-use loop, prefilled assistant turns, structured-output strictness, or the safety and retention guarantees of a first-party API. The DeepSeek API is OpenAI-shaped and the model has documented, uncharacterized long-context failure modes. Cross-check both: for a coding agent, run your own eval at DeepSeek's effort=100 and Claude's default effort, then at the cheapest passing setting on each. The vendor tables were run at maximum effort; your bill will not be. For the durable framework behind that list, How to choose a model. For what changes when you move a prompt between an Anthropic-shaped and an OpenAI-shaped API, Porting prompts across models. For the Claude-side reference these comparisons hang off, Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways V4.1-Flash is a repository-shaped model: parity with Opus 5 on DeepSWE, a 20-point deficit on Terminal-Bench 4.0. Match it to work that reads a lot and edits a little. The 1–100 effort dial is the price lever. Every launch number is at 100; DeepSeek's own guidance is that 60–80 keeps most of the accuracy at under half the tokens. Six price cells, not one. The $0.003 headline is off-peak cache-hit input; a cold peak-hour token is 100× that. Peak is 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC on weekdays. Two silent routing changes: V4-Flash endpoints on Sept 10, deepseek-v4-pro on Sept 14. If you pinned Pro, your model changed — re-run evals. The 890-byte KV cache and 72-hour cache lifetime make long-lived 1M-token contexts cheap, but DeepSeek itself flags long-context sparse retrieval as uncharacterized. Test before you trust.

复制为 Markdown 进阶 At 00:00 UTC on August 31, 2026, DeepSeek quietly pushed a new repository to Hugging Face: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp. Ten days after the same model went live on their API (August 21), the weights are now MIT-licensed and public. This is the first V4-family model with native vision — not a text model with a bolt-on adapter, but a joint-trained multimodal MoE — and its agent scores on the vision side jumped from 26.2 to 36.5 on ApexBench without moving the text-only agent scores at all. On several agent benchmarks it now matches or edges past Claude Opus 4.8 while the API costs $0.22 per million input tokens. This page is the practical field guide the launch didn't come with: what changed architecturally, the numbers that matter, the one hard limit nobody warns you about, how to run it, and when Claude is still the right call. What you'll learn Understand what 'native vision' means here — the V4-Flash backbone plus a vision encoder + aligner trained together, not stapled on after Read the benchmark table the way the release intends: text-only agents preserved, vision agents up sharply, both within striking distance of Claude Opus 4.8 Know the hard 384-tokens-per-image architectural cap and why it changes how you prompt Do the honest cost math: $0.22 / $0.66 / $0.007 (cached) per million tokens vs Claude Opus 4.8 at $15 / $75 Pick the right serving path — hosted API for almost everyone, vLLM + DSpark for a real self-hosted run

documents.t: DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is a 305-billion-parameter sparse-MoE multimodal model — 13B active per token, 1.048M-token context — that adds joint-trained vision to the V4-Flash text backbone, ships open under MIT on Hugging Face on August 31 2026, and delivers agent-tier multimodal performance at roughly one-fortieth of Claude Opus 4.8's per-token price.

Every open lab that has bolted vision onto a strong text model has paid a tax on text benchmarks. DeepSeek's release table is the flex: on Terminal Bench 2.1 the vision model scores 83.9 (vs 82.7 for the text-only V4-Flash-0731); on DeepSWE it climbs to 59.3 (from 54.4); on Toolathlon-Verified to 75.9 (from 70.3). None of these are vision tasks — they're pure code and tool-use agent evals. The vision variant is better on text-agent work than the text-only checkpoint, not worse. This matters because it's the "prove-out" the field has been waiting for since Chameleon: you can jointly train a giant MoE for text and vision without the multimodal add causing text regression, as long as the vision head lands late enough and the router gets to keep specializing text experts.
documents.s: 1. Vision was added without breaking the text agents — that's the whole point

documents.t: This is the single most important thing to learn before writing your first prompt. The vision encoder in V4-Flash-Vision-Exp allocates at most 384 tokens per image — and that ceiling is architectural, not a commercial policy. There is no "high-detail" mode that unlocks more. Practical consequences: Big screenshots lose fine text. A 2560×1440 dashboard, a dense CSV rendered as an image, or a long PDF page will be encoded at whatever resolution 384 tokens of visual features can express — meaning small-font text will not survive round-trip. Crop, don't scale. If you need to read numbers off a chart, send the chart cropped to the region of interest, not the whole page. Multi-image beats one giant image. Split large documents into per-region tiles; each tile gets its own 384-token budget. This is why Chartography lands at 64.3 (competitive with Claude Opus 4.8's 65.0) but why the model will still miss a footnote in a 12-point font on a full-page screenshot. Every vision-agent workflow you build should assume this ceiling. 最后验证时间：2026-09-01。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: 2. The vision encoder has a hard 384-tokens-per-image budget

documents.t: Most published MoE recipes activate 8 experts of 32 or 64. V4-Flash-Vision-Exp uses a much wider expert bank: 256 routed experts + 1 shared expert, with only 6 routed experts firing per token — a 2.3% activation ratio. The model has 43 layers, hidden size 4,096, and the hybrid attention stack combines two mechanisms: Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) — sparse patterns for long-range reads. Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) — an aggressively compressed form for the deep-context tail. Wrapped over that, Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) replace the standard residual with a constrained-manifold projection, which the paper reports stabilizes signal propagation through the 43-layer stack. Together these are the reason the model can advertise a 1,048,576-token context window without the quadratic attention bill.
documents.s: 3. The MoE routing is unusually sparse — 6 of 256 experts fire per token

documents.t: Sticker prices, all per million tokens: Model Input Output Cached read DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp (API) $0.22 $0.66 $0.007 Claude Opus 4.8 $15.00 $75.00 $1.50 Kimi K3 (cache-miss / cache-hit) $3.00 / $0.30 $15.00 $0.30 Cached-read at $0.007/M is not a typo — that is roughly one two-hundredth of a cent per thousand tokens. For any workload where a repeating system prompt or long context is re-sent (agent loops, RAG over a static corpus, chat with a fixed persona) the effective input price collapses. This is the reason V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is showing up in agent-cost tables at a fraction of what Claude Opus 4.8 costs per task, even when the raw quality is within a few points. 最后验证时间：2026-09-01。 Prices, context window and MoE routing are from the official model card at release. documents.t: V4-Flash-Vision-Exp launched on the DeepSeek API on August 21, 2026, and only landed on Hugging Face as open weights on August 31. This ten-day gap is DeepSeek's new default. Compare Z.ai (GLM), which has been shipping API + weights simultaneously; DeepSeek is deliberately sequencing. The industry read: labs now agree that big open MoEs are shipping. The remaining question is when in the release cycle the weights arrive. For production planning that means: If you need on-prem from day zero, watch for GLM-family releases. If you can start on the API and cut over to self-hosted a week or two later, DeepSeek is the pattern.
documents.s: The release pattern — API first, weights ten days later

documents.t: There are three realistic paths. Pick by the two constraints that actually matter: whether the weights need to live on your infrastructure, and how much VRAM (or RAM) you can pay for. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Path A — DeepSeek's hosted API (default for almost everyone)⌄ OpenAI-compatible endpoint at api.deepseek.com. Model ID is deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp. Pricing is $0.22 / $0.66 / $0.007 per million tokens. This is the right answer unless you have a data-residency or air-gap constraint. ←PreviousNext→ 2Path B — vLLM on 4× GB300 (single-node self-host)⌄ The vLLM container ships day-0 support and the deepseek_v4 tool-call parser. You need one node with 4× GB300 (or equivalent B300 config). DSpark speculative decoding is enabled via --speculative-config. FP8 KV cache and block-size 256 are both required for the throughput numbers DeepSeek published. ←PreviousNext→ 3Path C — Community GGUF via llama.cpp / Ollama (workstation-class)⌄ unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp-GGUF ships two dynamic quants: UD-Q4_K_XL at 155 GB and UD-Q8_K_XL at 162 GB. Neither fits a single 24/48/80 GB GPU. What works is a fat workstation with 192 GB+ system RAM and offload, or a small multi-GPU rig with CPU spillover. ←PreviousNext→ Hosted API — Python (OpenAI-compatible) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import openai client = openai.OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_DEEPSEEK_KEY", base_url="https://api.deepseek.com/v1", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp", messages=[ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "What does this chart claim, and what's the one thing it hides?"}, {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/chart.png"}}, ], } ], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) Self-host — vLLM on 4× GB300 with DSpark CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 \ vllm/vllm-openai:deepseekv4-flash-vision \ deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --block-size 256 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' Local — Ollama with the community GGUF CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ ollama run hf.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_XL # Compact image syntax the model was trained to accept: # <image>path/to/screenshot.png</image> followed by your prompt

Reach for V4-Flash-Vision when: You need multimodal agent quality at roughly Opus-4.8 tier and cost is a factor. Cached-read pricing crushes anything on the closed frontier. The workload benefits from a 1M-token context (long-document VQA, whole-video-frame analysis, big-repo review with screenshots). You need open weights for compliance, air-gapped work, or fine-tuning, and you have (or rent) frontier-class hardware. You're building a chart-heavy or dashboard-parsing pipeline where you can control image tiling. Stay on Claude Opus 4.8 (or Sonnet 5) when: The job is whole-repository code translation or synthesis — NL2Repo is the outlier where the gap is real (57.7 vs 69.7). You need Claude-specific features: Extended thinking under budget, Skills, Sub-agent orchestration in Claude Code, or the Managed Agents session-budget controls. Your prompts contain images with tiny critical text and you cannot tile — you'll hit the 384-token cap and lose accuracy. You want a single vendor / SLA / support contact and are already invested in Anthropic tooling. For a broader model-choice framework, see How to choose a model. For a side-by-side of the whole open-weight wave, DeepSeek, Qwen & the Open-Weight Wave is the durable overview.
documents.s: When to reach for V4-Flash-Vision — and when to stay on Claude

documents.t: You will forget the 384-token cap. The first three vision agents you build will overshoot resolution and quietly lose accuracy on small text. Instrument for it: log per-image dimensions and downscale + tile deliberately. DSpark drops silently if you skip --speculative-config. Without the flag, vLLM will happily serve the model at 1/3 the throughput the release announced. Always pass the speculative config in production. The GGUF is not a laptop model. UD-Q4_K_XL is 155 GB. Community threads that show it "running" on smaller boxes are running it at fractional tokens/s via SSD swap — technically working, not usable. API vs weights version parity is not guaranteed. The API model can be silently updated; the Hugging Face weights are pinned to Vision-Exp. If a benchmark shifts a few points month-to-month on the API, that's why. Exp means experimental. The vision variant is not guaranteed to survive into production V4 releases. Do not build a critical pipeline on the assumption that this specific checkpoint will be around in a year.

复制为 Markdown 高级 最后验证时间：2026-11-02。 agent-desktop reached v1.0.0 on 28 October 2026 and v1.0.2 two days later. A project moving at that cadence will change command names, flags and error codes. Everything below is read from the repository's own README.md and CONCEPTS.md at the start of November 2026 — check agent-desktop --help and the CHANGELOG before you depend on a specific flag. The design model in the second half is the durable part and is worth reading even if you never install this tool. 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源. What you'll learn Understand what an accessibility-tree agent reads, and how it differs from a screenshot agent at the protocol level Learn the retry rule that most computer-use harnesses get wrong — and why 'did it fail?' is the wrong question See why refs are scoped to a snapshot, and what a harness should do instead of guessing when one goes stale Know the three-state property model that stops an agent acting on a failed read Spot the two failure modes this approach does NOT fix: truncated trees and apps with no accessibility surface Understand the security surface: everything on screen becomes agent input On 28 October 2026 Vercel Labs tagged v1.0.0 of agent-desktop, and by 31 October it was at the top of GitHub's trending list. It is a Rust CLI and C library, Apache-2.0, that gives an agent computer use on macOS, Windows and Linux by reading the operating system's accessibility tree — the same structure a screen reader consumes: AX API on macOS, UI Automation on Windows, AT-SPI on Linux. Vercel's own framing is "agent-browser, for your whole computer." Every write-up so far stops at the headline: trees instead of pixels, so clicks land where they should. That is true and it is the least interesting half. The interesting half is that the repository ships a CONCEPTS.md which is, in effect, a specification for how a computer-use harness should handle uncertainty — and it answers questions that the mainstream computer-use APIs leave entirely to you. If you build agent loops, read this page for the model even if you never install the tool. Our computer-use agents compared page covers the screenshot-based APIs from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google; this is the other architecture.

A screenshot agent gets an image and returns coordinates. The contract is: here are some pixels, tell me where to click. Everything the agent knows about the UI it has to infer visually, and every action is a bet on a coordinate. A tree agent gets structure. A snapshot returns JSON with a ref for every element the agent can act on, and actions name a ref rather than a point. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Observe⌄ Snapshot the accessibility tree of a window, app or surface. You get back JSON — roles, names, states — with a ref per actionable node, and a snapshot ID that the refs belong to. ←PreviousNext→ 2Resolve⌄ Before the action fires, the ref is re-matched against the CURRENT live tree using identity evidence stored at snapshot time. This step is the whole ballgame and is covered below. ←PreviousNext→ 3Act⌄ Dispatch under an interaction lease — machine-wide exclusivity over desktop input, held by one process at a time, so two callers cannot interleave synthetic input into each other's actions. ←PreviousNext→ 4Verify⌄ Re-read the element to confirm the change actually reached it. A mutation is only 'delivered' once a re-read says so. ←PreviousNext→ The practical differences that follow from this are larger than they look: Refs survive layout changes that break coordinates. A button that moves 200 px down the window is the same node in the tree. For a screenshot agent it is a new bet. It is headless by default. Input goes through the accessibility API without moving the system pointer or stealing focus, so the agent can drive apps while you keep using the machine. A --headed mode exists for physical input synthesis when an app ignores programmatic input. This is a genuinely different operating model from screenshot agents, which fight you for the cursor. Snapshots are text, not images. That matters for your bill and your context window — see why agents burn tokens. But it is not a free win, because dense trees get large; the repo's own answer is to map coarsely first (--skeleton --compact) and then drill into a region with --root. You still need screenshots sometimes. The tool ships screenshot alongside snapshot. Canvas-rendered apps, custom-drawn UIs and games have little or no accessibility surface, and no amount of tree-reading invents one. The minimal observe / act / verify loop CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ npm install -g agent-desktop agent-desktop version # macOS only: accessibility permission must be granted first agent-desktop permissions --guide # 1. observe — -i limits output to interactive elements agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # 2. act — the ref MUST carry its snapshot ID; a bare @e8 is rejected agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # 3. verify — re-snapshot and confirm the change landed agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # dense UI? map coarsely, then drill into one region agent-desktop snapshot --app Slack --skeleton --compact agent-desktop snapshot --root @s8f3k2p9:e42 Output is JSON with an ok boolean and either data or an error carrying a code, a disposition and a suggestion. The commands group into observe (snapshot, find, get, screenshot, list-surfaces), act-on-ref (click, type, set-value, scroll, toggle, expand), raw keyboard and mouse (press, hover, drag, key-down), window and app management (launch, focus-window, resize-window, list-apps), and system (permissions, status, batch, skills).
documents.s: What changes when you read the tree instead of the screen

documents.t: Here is the rule, and it is the single most useful thing in the repository: The distinction that matters is not success versus failure. It is delivered versus not delivered. Think about what an agent does when a type command returns an error. The instinctive harness behaviour — retry on error — is actively dangerous, because "error" conflates two completely different situations: The keystrokes never reached the field. Retrying is free. The keystrokes may have landed and the confirmation read failed. Retrying types everything twice. A harness that cannot tell these apart will silently double-submit forms, double-click Send, and duplicate rows. So agent-desktop classifies every mutation into three delivery states instead of a boolean: Delivery state Meaning Retry? Not delivered Argument error, access denial, or a read-only command — the action demonstrably never reached the target Safe. Retry freely Delivered unverified Input was posted but the effect is unconfirmed — the typical outcome of physical input synthesis Unsafe. Re-reading state is the only correct move Delivered Effect confirmed by re-reading the element Done; nothing to retry Reads get a parallel four-way classification, and the first one is the subtle one: Settled absence — the provider was asked and the target genuinely lacks that property or pattern. A final answer, never retried. Retryable failure — a transport fault such as a timeout or dropped connection. Worth repeating within a budget. Unavailable element — it disappeared. Settles as a stale ref if the element had been resolved; retryable if hit mid-walk. Terminal failure — a denial or an unclassified code. Final, surfaced as-is. The tool exposes this directly: you retry only when error.disposition.retry says safe. Key takeaways If you are writing your own computer-use loop today, port this one idea even if you port nothing else. Classify every action by whether it could have landed, and make 'may have landed' a distinct branch that re-reads state instead of retrying. Idempotency is not a property of your retry code — it is a property of each individual action, and only the tool layer knows which is which.
documents.s: The idea worth stealing: delivered, not successful

documents.t: In agent-desktop a ref looks like @e8, but you may never use it bare — a bare ref fails with INVALID_ARGS. It must be qualified by its snapshot ID: @s8f3k2p9:e8. That looks like friction. It is a deliberate type system. The stated reason: refs are deterministic inside one snapshot but are not stable across UI changes. The snapshot ID is a namespace, and every lookup is confined to the namespace it was created in — a snapshot taken under a session needs that same session scope later. So the awkward syntax makes a real category error unrepresentable. You cannot accidentally carry an identifier from an observation three actions ago and have it silently resolve to whatever now occupies that slot. Compare the screenshot world, where a coordinate from a stale screenshot is syntactically indistinguishable from a fresh one and resolves to something every time.
documents.s: Why refs are scoped to a snapshot

documents.t: When the action fires, the ref is resolved against the live tree through a graded sequence, and the ordering encodes a judgement about which evidence is trustworthy: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Walk the stored positional path⌄ Follow the path recorded at snapshot time down the current tree. ←PreviousNext→ 2Verify against stored identity evidence⌄ Check the candidate against what was recorded: native ID first, then role-conditional stable text. Position gets you to a candidate; identity decides whether it is the right one. ←PreviousNext→ 3Fall back to a bounded broad search⌄ If the path no longer exists, search more widely — but with a bound, not indefinitely. ←PreviousNext→ 4Only then, geometry⌄ Resolve by unique geometry as a last resort, and only when the ref has NO meaningful identity to match on. On Windows and Linux the stored bounds must be a positive-area rectangle — a zero-extent stored hash never promotes to a geometric match. ←PreviousNext→ The design commitment is in what happens when none of that produces a confident match: the resolution fails closed. Missing, stale and ambiguous matches are rejected — STALE_REF, AMBIGUOUS_TARGET — rather than resolved to a best guess. On macOS the implementation retains the native accessibility objects specifically so an element cannot be silently misidentified when tree ordering shifts underneath it. This is the opposite of how a pixel agent degrades. A stale coordinate always hits something; a stale ref returns an error. Trading a silent wrong action for a loud failure is the entire reliability claim, and it is the right trade for anything an agent does unsupervised. What you'll learn The same reasoning shows up in the repo's two-sided treatment of partial results: if a snapshot runs out of its time budget mid-walk, it returns what it observed rather than discarding the walk — but it reports completeness per node. A harness that ignores that field will confidently reason over a truncated tree and conclude a button does not exist. Check completeness before you conclude absence.

A smaller mechanism with outsized consequences. Properties are never collapsed to a boolean. Three states stay distinct: Known — a value was read. Absent — the provider was asked and genuinely has no value. Unknown — the read itself failed. Most harnesses flatten Unknown into false or null, and an agent then acts on a failed read as if it were a negative result: the checkbox "isn't checked" (we could not read it), the field "is empty" (the query errored). The repo's phrasing is that uncertainty must travel — when a higher-priority evidence source fails, that failure is carried forward rather than smoothed away. Accessible names are computed in the core from ranked slots rather than in each platform adapter, so shared logic never sees a platform-specific token and the same uncertainty rules apply everywhere. If you take two things from this page, take delivery semantics and this. They are both cases of the same discipline: do not let a failure to know masquerade as knowledge.

The interaction lease covers dispatch only. Input exclusivity is machine-wide and held by one process at a time, but the lease deliberately does not cover the waiting that precedes an action, because waiting for an element to become actionable can run long. The practical consequence: an element can become actionable and then change again between your wait and your dispatch. That is exactly why the verify step is not optional. Platform support is not uniform, and Linux is the ragged edge. Accessibility tree, clicking and typing work across all three OSes, but on Linux clicking and typing run through AT-SPI with X11/GNOME caveats, screenshots need X11 or a Wayland portal, the clipboard needs wl-clipboard under Wayland, app management is launch-and-list only, and notifications are GNOME Shell. macOS needs accessibility permission granted explicitly, plus a TMPDIR that is user-owned with mode 0700. Windows needs no special permission at matching terminal integrity level. Of roughly 60 commands, not all are operational on every platform — check agent-desktop status on the machine you actually plan to run on.

This needs stating plainly, because the convenience is seductive. An accessibility-tree agent reads the text content of applications, which is a strictly richer capture than a screenshot of the focused window — including, potentially, content that is on screen but not what you were looking at. The repo is explicit that snapshots, screenshots and clipboard contents can contain sensitive data and should be kept out of public logs. It does build in one real mitigation: secure fields. Once a platform marks an element secret, the read path withholds both its value and related text evidence, and the action path may write into it but never echoes the attempted or observed value. That protects passwords. It does not protect the open email, the Slack DM, or the customer record in the next window. Two consequences: Transcripts become sensitive artifacts. Agent logs from a desktop session are closer to a screen recording than to a terminal history. Treat them accordingly — see what your agent uploads. Every readable surface is an injection surface. Any text an app displays becomes agent input, so a crafted calendar invite, filename or chat message is a prompt-injection vector with no network request involved. The same reasoning as the web your agent reads applies to the desktop, and prompt injection is the primer. An agent with machine-wide input exclusivity and no pointer movement is also, by construction, one whose actions you will not see happening. Watch out Headless-by-default is a usability feature and a supervision hazard at the same time. Because the agent does not move your pointer or steal focus, there is no ambient signal that it is acting. If you run this unattended, the compensating control has to be the log and a scoped-down target app — not your attention. Our hardening-autonomous-runs page covers the general pattern.
documents.s: The security surface is the whole screen

documents.t: Situation Reach for Native desktop app with real accessibility support (Finder, Office, most Cocoa/WinUI apps) Tree agent. Stable refs, cheap text snapshots, no coordinate math Web app in a browser A browser-specific harness first — the DOM is a better tree than the browser's AX projection. See computer-use agents compared and shared-login browsers Canvas/WebGL app, game, custom-drawn UI, remote desktop Screenshot agent. There is no accessibility surface to read Agent must run while you keep working Tree agent, headless mode — no focus stealing, no pointer fight Unsupervised, repeated, mutating actions Tree agent, and honour the delivery semantics. This is the case the whole design exists for Visual verification ("does this look right?") Screenshot, regardless of harness. A tree cannot tell you the layout is broken Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways Accessibility trees replace a coordinate bet with a named reference, so layout changes that break a screenshot agent are a non-event — but canvas, games and custom-drawn UIs have no tree to read. Steal the delivery model: classify actions by whether they COULD have landed, not by whether they returned an error. 'May have landed' deserves a re-read, never a retry. Scoping refs to a snapshot is a type system, not friction — it makes stale-identifier bugs impossible to express rather than silently wrong. Fail-closed resolution is the reliability claim: a stale coordinate always hits something, a stale ref returns STALE_REF. Prefer the loud failure for anything unsupervised. Keep Unknown distinct from Absent. An agent that reads a failed query as a negative result will act confidently on nothing. Headless operation removes the ambient signal that an agent is working. If you run it unattended, logs and a scoped target app are the control — not your attention.
