复制为 Markdown 高级 Every model on AILmanac so far generates text the same way: one token, then the next, left to right, forever. A different family of models does not. It starts with a blank canvas of masked positions, predicts all of them at once, keeps the ones it is confident about, and repeats. Position 40 can be decided before position 7. The numbers are the reason anyone cares. Inception's Mercury 2 — a reasoning model — reportedly runs at 1,009 tokens/sec on Blackwell GPUs with 1.7 s end-to-end latency, roughly 8–14× faster than comparable reasoning-enabled competitors (The Decoder). Google's experimental Gemini Diffusion samples at 1,479 tokens/sec excluding overhead, against Gemini 2.5 Flash's 272.4 (Techmeme roundup). And yet the README of LLaDA — the 8B open-weight model that proved the approach at scale — tells you its quality peaks when the number of sampling steps equals the response length. One forward pass per token. Exactly like an autoregressive model, but without a KV cache, so slower. Both facts are true. This lesson is the bridge between them: what the algorithm actually does, which knob buys the speed and what it costs, the two structural limits that made early diffusion LLMs unusable and the fix that shipped, and the three gotchas (streaming, length billing, and a jailbreak class that does not exist on autoregressive models) you need before you put one in production. What you'll learn Describe masked-diffusion generation in terms of a canvas, a denoising pass, and a commit decision — and say what bidirectional attention buys and costs Use the steps knob correctly: compute tokens-per-forward-pass, and explain the conditional-independence failure that makes aggressive parallelism wrong rather than merely worse Explain why block diffusion is on every dLLM you can actually call today — it is what restored the KV cache, variable-length output, and token streaming Pick the jobs where a dLLM genuinely wins: infilling and any-order edits, latency-bound voice, and bounded decisions — not 'everything, but faster' Treat an open dLLM endpoint as unaligned at the boundary, because masked-infill prompts bypass alignment in a way autoregressive refusals cannot 最后验证时间：2026-10-02。 Every price, context window, tokens-per-second and latency figure here is perishable — this field is moving monthly and Inception's rate card currently carries promotional discounts. Check the vendor's own model page and the independent leaderboards before quoting any number in a decision. Research claims are cited to their papers; several are preprints, not replicated results. 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: Diffusion LLMs: The Models That Don't Write Left to Right

documents.t: An autoregressive (AR) model's loop is: read the whole prefix, emit a probability distribution over one position (the next one), sample, append, repeat. The KV cache is what makes this cheap — the keys and values for every earlier token were computed once and never change, because attention is causal and nothing to the right exists yet. A masked diffusion LLM inverts that. Attention is bidirectional: every position attends to every other position, in both directions. So in a single forward pass the model produces a distribution for every masked position simultaneously. Generation becomes an iterative refinement of a whole answer, not a walk along it. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Lay out a canvas⌄ Decide a generation length L. Fill all L positions with a special mask token. On a pure masked dLLM (LLaDA, Dream), L is fixed before the first forward pass — the model does not grow the sequence as it goes. ←PreviousNext→ 2One denoising pass predicts everything⌄ The transformer runs once over prompt + canvas and returns a distribution for every masked slot at once. Not 'the next token' — slot 3, slot 17 and slot 240, in the same pass. ←PreviousNext→ 3Commit a subset (this is the whole game)⌄ You unmask some of those predictions and freeze them as real tokens. Which ones, and how many, is the decoding policy: random order, highest top-1 confidence, largest top1−top2 margin, or lowest entropy. Everything else stays masked. ←PreviousNext→ 4Re-run with the committed tokens as context⌄ The next pass sees the frozen tokens and re-predicts the remaining masks — and because attention is bidirectional, a token committed at the END of the answer conditions the tokens still missing from the middle. This is what AR models cannot do. ←PreviousNext→ 5Stop when the canvas is full⌄ Total cost = (number of passes) × (one full forward pass). So tokens per forward pass = L / steps. That ratio, not the hardware, is where the headline tokens/sec comes from. ←PreviousNext→ That last line is the one worth memorising. An AR model is pinned at one token per forward pass. A diffusion LLM lets you choose. DiffusionGemma, Google's open-weight entry, reports roughly 20 tokens per forward pass while refining blocks of 256 in parallel, which is how it reaches ~1,500 output tokens/sec on a single H100 (DiffusionGemma Technical Report).
documents.s: The mechanism, in one diagram you have to imagine

documents.t: Dream 7B exposes the knob explicitly. Its diffusion_generate() documents steps as "diffusion timesteps" where max_new_tokens / steps tokens are produced per step, and notes plainly that fewer steps are faster but coarser (DreamLM/Dream, Apache-2.0). So why not always use few steps? Because the error it introduces is not noise — it is a specific, nameable bug. A single forward pass gives you, for each masked slot, a marginal distribution: the probability of a token at that position, averaged over everything still unknown. If you commit two slots from the same pass, you are sampling from the product of their marginals, not from their joint distribution. Any dependency between them is silently discarded. The Fast-dLLM authors state the root cause directly: generation quality degrades under parallel decoding because masked diffusion models sample tokens independently from marginal probabilities when the true joint distribution has dependencies (Fast-dLLM, arXiv:2505.22618). The intuition: ask for a city and two adjacent slots might score "New" and "Delhi" as the most likely token for their own position, because "New York" and "New Delhi" are both plausible. Commit both in one pass and you get neither. The failure mode of over-parallel decoding is not vaguer prose, it is confidently assembled nonsense at the seams. The fix that made the field practical is confidence-aware parallel decoding: compute a confidence per masked slot (typically the max softmax probability), commit only the slots above a threshold, and if none clear it, commit the single highest so the loop still makes progress. Tokens that are nearly independent get decoded together; tokens that depend on each other wait. Fast-dLLM reports up to 27.6× throughput improvement on LLaDA and Dream across benchmarks with minimal accuracy loss — training-free, just a decoding change. That is the shape of this entire research area: the parallelism is free, the independence is not, and the work is in detecting which tokens can safely go together. What you'll learn A confidence threshold is a quality dial you can actually reason about: higher threshold means fewer tokens committed per pass, more passes, slower, closer to AR quality. Fast-dLLM v2 reports a 2.6× speedup on GSM8K at threshold 0.9 with minimal accuracy loss — that is the kind of setting to start from, not 'commit everything'.
documents.s: The steps knob, and why cranking it is wrong rather than just lossy

documents.t: LLaDA's own repository lists its efficiency constraints without euphemism: fixed context length for sampling, no KV-cache support, and degraded performance when sampling steps drop below the response length. The authors frame it as deliberate — they wanted to find the ceiling of the approach before optimising it (ML-GSAI/LLaDA, MIT, ~4k stars, Base and Instruct weights plus LLaDA 1.5, LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B and iLLaDA variants). Stack those up and a pure masked dLLM is nearly unusable as a product: No KV cache. Bidirectional attention means every pass can change any token's context, so cached keys and values are invalid. You recompute the whole sequence every step. Fixed output length. You must pick L before generating. Too small truncates; too large wastes compute on positions you will throw away. Latency worse than AR. Points 1 and 2 together can make a "parallel" model slower end-to-end than the sequential one it replaces. Block diffusion resolves all three by refusing to be pure. Generate in blocks: condition on previous blocks autoregressively, run diffusion inside the current block. That gives flexible sequence length and KV caching between blocks — the BD3-LM formulation, an ICLR 2025 oral (arXiv:2503.09573, kuleshov-group/bd3lms). Fast-dLLM v2 (arXiv:2509.26328) shows what a tuned version looks like, and the details are worth knowing because they explain the vendor behaviour you will observe: Hybrid attention mask. Block-diagonal (bidirectional) within a block, block-causal (left-to-right) between blocks. Bidirectional context where it helps, AR semantics where the cache lives. Two cache levels. A block-level cache holding finished blocks as clean prefix context, plus a sub-block cache (DualCache) for the recomputation that intra-block decoding still needs. Complementary masking in training. Each sample is duplicated into two views with masks m and 1 − m, so every token is supervised both as a mask target and as context. Reported results. Up to 2.5× faster than standard AR decoding; 1.8× at batch size 64 on H100s; a 7B average benchmark score of 60.3 against Dream's 57.6, including HumanEval 63.4 vs 57.9 and GSM8K 62.0 vs 39.2. And the training cost is the detail that reframes the field: Fast-dLLM v2 reports fine-tuning from an AR model on roughly 1B tokens — about 500× less than Dream's 580B — a 7B trained in ~12 hours on 64 A100s.
documents.s: The two structural limits — and block diffusion, which is why you can call one today

documents.t: DiffusionGemma makes that point unmissable. It is not trained from scratch: it fine-tunes Gemma 4, a mixture-of-experts model with 3.8B activated and 25.2B total parameters, into a diffusion model using fewer than 10% of the starting AR model's total training token budget — supervised denoising fine-tuning, then reinforcement learning and sampler distillation (arXiv:2608.00146, CC-BY-4.0 weights). What survives the conversion is the surprising part. The report states it retains the base model's thinking mode, multimodal inputs and long contexts — and keeps the ability to generate autoregressively with only minor degradation. One set of weights, two decoding modes. If that result holds up, "diffusion LLM" stops being a distinct product category and becomes a serving option: the same family, with a parallelism dial on the inference side. That is a far more consequential claim than any single tokens-per-second record, and it is the reason to learn the mechanism now rather than when a provider flips a flag on a model you already use.
documents.s: Diffusion is a decoding mode you can retrofit, not a separate species

documents.t: Speed is the headline and the weakest part of the case, because speed is contested — specialised AR hardware is also delivering hundreds of tokens per second (see Token Speed). The durable advantages are the ones that follow from the shape of the algorithm. Any-order generation and native infilling. Because you choose which slot to commit, you can leave a hole in the middle of a sequence and have the model fill it with full context on both sides. Dream exposes this as the alg parameter — origin (random order), maskgit_plus (top-1 confidence), topk_margin (top1 − top2 margin), entropy — plus alg_temp to add randomness to those strategies. For code edits, template completion, or filling fields in a fixed JSON skeleton, that is a structurally better fit than asking an AR model to re-emit a whole file to change line 40. Latency-bound interaction. Inception's Mercury Voice advertises time-to-first-token under 170 ms on a 128K context, priced at $0.20/$1.50 per million input/output tokens at the time of writing. Voice is the clearest case where latency is the product; our full-duplex voice AI page covers why that threshold matters. End-to-end reasoning turnaround. Mercury 2's reported 1.7 s for a complete reasoning answer is a different claim from throughput — it is the number an agent loop actually feels, turn after turn. Bounded answers instead of prose. Inception's Mercury Decide returns a choice, a score, or a yes/no with a calibrated probability read off the model rather than written out as text — reported at up to 14 decisions per second, which makes "run it on every case and escalate the unsure ones" affordable. The category and its caveats are covered in depth on System One decision models; the diffusion backbone is an implementation detail there, not the point. Price pressure. Mercury 2.5 currently lists a 260K context at $0.04/$0.15 per million input/output tokens (promotional, off $0.20/$0.75) with cached input at $0.004 per million. Treat promo pricing as temporary and model your bill at list.
documents.s: What a diffusion LLM is actually better at

documents.t: Watch out Tokens/sec is measured at the vendor's chosen parallelism. Your quality bar may require more steps, which costs you the speedup. Benchmark on your own prompts at your own accuracy threshold. Output is not final left-to-right. Only block boundaries are monotonic; inside a block, slots can still be masked or revised. Any UI or parser that assumes 'token N will never change' is wrong. A pure masked dLLM bills and computes a length you chose in advance. Block diffusion reduces that to per-block granularity — it does not remove it. The third one deserves more than a bullet, because it is a security property and it has no autoregressive analogue. An AR model's alignment has a structural advantage: the refusal happens first. If the model decides to decline, every subsequent token is conditioned on "I can't help with that." A diffusion LLM has no such moment. There is no left-to-right point at which a refusal takes over the rest of the generation — masked slots get filled to be consistent with whatever is already on the canvas. DIJA ("The Devil behind the mask", ICLR 2026, arXiv:2507.11097, ZichenWen1/DIJA) turns that into an attack. The adversarial prompt puts the harmful intent in unmasked tokens and leaves masked spans for the model to complete in a contextually consistent way. The reported results: up to 100% keyword-based attack success rate on Dream-Instruct, surpassing the strongest prior baseline by up to 78.5% in evaluator-based ASR on JailbreakBench and by 37.7 points in StrongREJECT score — while requiring no rewriting or obfuscation of the harmful content. The authors' conclusion is that existing alignment mechanisms do not protect dLLMs against context-aware masked-input prompts, because the model cannot filter an unsafe generation mid-inference the way a sequential one can. A follow-up (arXiv:2602.00388) argues the picture is two-sided — diffusion confers a safety blessing in some settings that then breaks under context — which is a reason to measure rather than to assume either way. Practical takeaway: if you expose an open-weight dLLM, do not treat its instruction tuning as a guardrail. Filter and classify at the boundary, on both the request and the response, exactly as you would for a base model. Our securing local and hybrid agents page covers the boundary pattern.
documents.s: Three gotchas before you ship one

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Hosted, zero setup⌄ Inception serves Mercury through an OpenAI-compatible API, and the models are listed on OpenRouter (for example openrouter.ai/inception/mercury-2). Point an existing OpenAI-SDK script at it and change the model string — nothing about the request shape is diffusion-specific. ←PreviousNext→ 2Open weights, local⌄ LLaDA-8B-Instruct (MIT) and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B (Apache-2.0) both ship inference code on Hugging Face. DiffusionGemma's weights are CC-BY-4.0. Note that a pure masked dLLM has no KV cache, so plan VRAM for recomputing the full sequence every step. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run the steps sweep⌄ The single most informative experiment: hold the prompt fixed, vary steps, and plot wall-clock against a task metric you care about. You will find your own quality cliff, and it will not be where a benchmark table put it. ←PreviousNext→ 4Then test the seams⌄ Use prompts whose answers contain multi-token units — proper nouns, numbers with units, identifiers, JSON keys. Those are where conditional-independence errors show up first, and where a confidence threshold earns its cost. ←PreviousNext→ Call a hosted diffusion LLM with the OpenAI SDK (nothing changes but the model string) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Inception serves an OpenAI-compatible API; OpenRouter also lists the models. # Check the provider's model list for the current slug before you hard-code one. curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "inception/mercury-2", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Rewrite this function to stream its output, and explain the two failure modes you introduced."} ], "stream": true }' # What to watch for, beyond the content: # - time to first token vs time to last token (the diffusion win is usually in the gap) # - whether the stream arrives in chunks that look like BLOCKS rather than words The steps sweep on Dream 7B — find your own quality cliff CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import time, torch from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer NAME = "Dream-org/Dream-v0-Instruct-7B" tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(NAME, trust_remote_code=True) model = AutoModel.from_pretrained( NAME, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, trust_remote_code=True ).to("cuda").eval() PROMPT = "List the five largest cities in Germany with their populations." MAX_NEW = 256 # steps == MAX_NEW is the authors' best-quality setting: one token per # forward pass. Each halving doubles tokens-per-pass and doubles the # number of independence assumptions you are making. for steps in [256, 128, 64, 32, 16]: inputs = tok.apply_chat_template( [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT}], return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True, add_generation_prompt=True, ).to("cuda") t0 = time.perf_counter() out = model.diffusion_generate( inputs.input_ids, attention_mask=inputs.attention_mask, max_new_tokens=MAX_NEW, steps=steps, temperature=0.0, alg="entropy", # commit the lowest-entropy slots first alg_temp=0.0, ) dt = time.perf_counter() - t0 text = tok.decode(out[0][len(inputs.input_ids[0]):], skip_special_tokens=True) print(f"--- steps={steps} tokens/pass={MAX_NEW/steps:.0f} {dt:.2f}s ---") print(text.strip()[:400]) # Read the OUTPUTS, not just the timings. The numbers and the city names are # the multi-token units that break first when too many slots are committed # from one pass. That corruption is the conditional-independence bug, visible.

Key takeaways A diffusion LLM's speed comes from one ratio — generation length divided by denoising steps, i.e. tokens committed per forward pass. An AR model is fixed at 1. Everything else is a consequence of that dial. Over-parallel decoding is wrong, not just coarse: committing correlated slots from one pass samples the product of marginals instead of the joint. Confidence-threshold decoding is the fix, and Fast-dLLM reports up to 27.6x throughput with minimal accuracy loss. Pure masked diffusion has no KV cache and a fixed output length. Block diffusion (AR between blocks, diffusion inside) is what restored caching, variable length and streaming — it is why every callable dLLM today is a block model. DiffusionGemma converted an autoregressive Gemma 4 MoE into a diffusion model for under 10% of its original training token budget while keeping thinking mode, multimodality and AR generation. Diffusion is looking more like a decoding mode than a separate species of model. Pick it for infilling and any-order edits, sub-200 ms voice turns, fast bounded decisions and end-to-end turn latency — and assume its alignment does not hold, because masked-infill prompts reach up to 100% ASR on an aligned open dLLM. Check yourself 0/5 New to the underlying machinery? What is an LLM and Tokens and context cover the autoregressive baseline this page departs from, and Token Speed covers the hardware and software multipliers that attack the same latency problem from the other side.

复制为 Markdown 高级 What you'll learn Understand what an "overfit" inference engine is, why a narrow runtime can roughly double a general one on identical hardware, and why that stopped being an expensive bet in 2026 Learn the three mechanisms ds4 uses that a general GGUF runner will not give you — asymmetric routed-expert quantization, a bounded expert cache streamed from SSD, and KV snapshots that survive a restart Read ds4's own published numbers correctly: which figure is a single Mac, which is eight GPUs sharing 16 sessions, and which is a 178 GB model running on a 128 GB machine Price the real cost of the bet: model support that is designed to be withdrawn, a main branch you should check the date on, and a security posture that assumes you read C Decide when narrow beats llama.cpp for your job — and the three cases where it clearly does not On 2 October 2026 a link titled "From the creator of Redis; run LLM locally with ds4" reached the Hacker News front page and settled at 362 points and 104 comments. The surprising part is not the project. It is that the project was already five months old — antirez/ds4 was created on 6 May 2026 — and had quietly accumulated 23,582 stars, 2,268 forks and 761 open issues before the wider audience noticed. What it got noticed for matters more than the engine itself. ds4 is the most-starred member of a category that barely existed a year ago and now has at least six entries: the overfit inference engine. A runtime built for one model on one class of hardware, that will not run your other models, and whose author intends for it to be thrown away. If you have read Colibrì or Strata here, you have met two points on this map already. This page is about the third point and the map.
documents.s: DwarfStar (ds4) and the Rise of Overfit Inference Engines

documents.t: ds4 picks a short list of mixture-of-experts models, writes Metal, CUDA and ROCm kernels for those specific architectures, crushes only the routed experts to roughly two bits while keeping the per-token path at higher precision, and ships its own CLI, coding agent and HTTP server around them — buying speed and polish on six models at the price of running nothing else.

The category name comes from a deliberate analogy to overfitting a model: the runtime is tuned so tightly to one target that it generalises badly on purpose. The published roster, as of early October 2026: Engine Hardware target Model target DwarfStar (ds4) Metal 96 GB+, CUDA (DGX Spark, Ada/L40S), ROCm (Strix Halo) DeepSeek V4 / V4.1 Flash, V4 PRO, GLM 5.2/5.3, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Strata Consumer NVIDIA, 12 GB+ Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ninfer RTX 5090 Qwen checkpoints Splash Apple Silicon M3+ Qwen family llamAmpere RTX 3090 / 3090 Ti Qwen3.8-27B gufo AMD Strix Halo a curated set The one measurement in public that compares a narrow engine against a tuned general one, on the same box, is a developer's RTX 4070 (12 GB, 64 GB DDR5) running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 27 tok/s on best-tuned llama.cpp against 53 tok/s on Strata at 60K context. Roughly 2x. Take that number with the caveat its own author attaches: the quantizations and settings differed, so it is not a controlled experiment. It is a real-world delta, not a benchmark. That distinction is exactly the kind of thing this whole category is bad at printing, and it is worth internalising before you read any engine's README — the same discipline reading an AI benchmark asks for.

Three arguments, and the third is the non-obvious one: Generality costs throughput. Supporting many models and backends forces defensive branches and shared allocators that constrain how aggressively any single path can be scheduled. Coding agents collapsed the cost of writing kernels. A single competent systems programmer with an agent can now write, benchmark and fix GPU kernels at a pace that used to require a team. ds4's own author has described the project as built with heavy model assistance, with humans leading the ideas, testing and debugging. Inference optimisation has an unusually crisp objective function. Fixed inputs, a reference output to match, and one number to maximise. That is a loop an agent can be pointed at and left to run — which is why argument 2 bites here and not everywhere.

The headline that sounds impossible — a 284B-parameter model on a laptop — is not uniform compression. An MoE model touches only a small slice of its weights per token, and those slices are not equally fragile. ds4 exploits that asymmetry per tensor type. The Qwen3.8-Flash-Next configuration is the one the repo documents in exact terms, and it is worth reading closely: Component Treatment Size Main + MTP weights imatrix IQ2_XXS gate/up experts, padded Q2_K down projections 41.73 GiB Original BF16 n-grams read directly from disk, never resident 95.37 GiB Two things to take from that table. First, the quantization is chosen per tensor role — gate and up projections get a different scheme from down projections, because they tolerate different damage. Second, the single largest artifact on disk is not multiplied per token at all: an n-gram embedding is a lookup, so it stays on the SSD and never competes for RAM. Strata exploits the same property on the same model; the file size and the memory requirement are simply not the same number. The repo states which models survive this treatment: DeepSeek V4 Flash and PRO, and GLM 5.2, "tolerate aggressive routed-expert quantization." That is a per-architecture empirical claim, not a general law — which is precisely why the engine's model list is short.
documents.s: 1. Asymmetric quantization: crush the experts, keep the path

documents.t: The flag is --ssd-streaming, and what it actually does is narrower than the phrase suggests. From the project's own SSD_STREAMING.md: SSD streaming keeps a bounded cache of routed experts and reads missing experts from the GGUF. So: non-routed weights stay in RAM. Only routed experts page in and out of a bounded cache. The documentation is explicit that this does not remove the memory needed for other weights, activations, scratch and the context — a caveat worth noting, because the natural reading of "streaming" is that RAM stops mattering. The headline result here is the genuinely surprising number on this page. On an M5 Max with GLM 5.3 Flash Q4 — a 177.77 GiB model on a 128 GB machine: Phase Measured Prefill (initial / continued) 121 t/s / 104 t/s Generation 11.9–14.9 t/s Read it with the warning the docs attach: "Generation is usually more sensitive to cache misses than prefill. A large model that starts successfully can still be too slow for interactive work." Twelve tokens a second is fine for a batch summarisation job and painful for a coding agent you sit and watch. There is a counter-intuitive tuning trap too: making the expert cache bigger can make decoding slower, because an oversized cache displaces the non-routed weights that are touched every single token. More cache is not monotonically better. For the deeper treatment of expert streaming as an architecture — NVMe bandwidth as the real ceiling, SSD wear, O_DIRECT — see Colibrì, which is built entirely around that idea.
documents.s: 2. SSD streaming that streams experts, not everything

documents.t: This is the mechanism most likely to change how your day feels, and the one almost nobody writes about. ds4 stores session KV state and conversation history under ~/.ds4/kvcache, and the documented promise is that "compatible local KV snapshots avoid rebuilding the prompt." The session verbs: Command Effect /save Persist the current session /list List saved sessions /switch <sha> Resume a specific session with its KV state /strip <sha> Drop the KV payload, keep the text /del <sha> Delete the session Why it matters: a long-running agent re-sends a growing prefix on every turn. If the engine rebuilds that prefix from scratch each time, prefill dominates your wall clock on exactly the workload you care about. Commenters on the HN thread singled this out — append-only message history that preserves KV reusability — as the kind of detail a general runtime typically leaves to the caller. It is the local-engine analogue of prompt caching across providers: same economics, different layer. One documented limit: sessions containing images cannot yet be saved.
documents.s: 3. KV snapshots: the detail that makes agent loops cheap

documents.t: Four binaries ship, and the division of labour is the point: Binary What it is for ds4 Interactive multi-turn CLI with conversation history ds4-agent A native coding agent that calls inference directly — no HTTP hop ds4-server HTTP server on http://127.0.0.1:8000, for external clients ds4-eval Embedded capability regression tests against a real GGUF ds4-server is the integration surface, and the repo names its intended clients directly: Pi, OpenCode, Codex CLI, or Claude Code. That makes ds4 a plausible local backend for the hybrid setups described in Claude plus local models and local coding agents. Note what the repo says about ds4-eval, because it is unusually honest: these are "DwarfStar integration checks, not official leaderboard scores." It answers "did this build regress?", not "is this model good."
documents.s: It is a stack, not just a runtime

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Pick your build target⌄ Metal on Apple Silicon is the primary path and the default. CUDA has two targets — one tuned for DGX Spark, one generic for Ada/L40S-class cards. ROCm targets Strix Halo systems such as the Framework Desktop. You are choosing a compile-time target, not a runtime flag. ←PreviousNext→ 2Check the RAM floor before you download anything⌄ The Metal path wants 96 GB and up for the Flash-class models; the PRO variant is a 256 GB-plus machine. SSD streaming lowers the floor but, as the numbers above show, buys you single-digit-to-low-teens generation speed on the biggest models. Decide which side of 'interactive' you need to be on first. ←PreviousNext→ 3Build⌄ A plain make for Metal; make cuda-spark, make cuda-generic or make strix-halo otherwise. Pure C with platform kernels — the repository is roughly 8.7 MB of C, 4.5 MB of CUDA, 2.3 MB of Objective-C and 1.4 MB of Metal, with no runtime dependency on another inference library. ←PreviousNext→ 4Download a model by tag, not by URL⌄ The helper script takes short tags such as ds4f-q2, qwen38-q2, qwen38-q4k and qwen38-vision. These are project-specific GGUF builds — this is the step where 'not a general GGUF runner' becomes concrete. A checkpoint you already have on disk for Ollama or llama.cpp is not expected to work. ←PreviousNext→ 5Run the CLI first, the server second⌄ Verify quality and speed interactively with ds4 before wiring anything to it. Then start ds4-server and point your client at port 8000. Check the server and client guides in docs/ for the current API shape — the README defers it, and this is the surface most likely to have moved since this page was written. ←PreviousNext→ 6Save a session once you have a prompt you like⌄ Run /save, then /list. This is the step that turns a slow prefill into a one-time cost, and it is the single highest-leverage habit on this engine. ←PreviousNext→ Build, fetch and run — Apple Silicon CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ git clone https://github.com/antirez/ds4.git cd ds4 make ./download_model.sh ds4f-q2 ./ds4 The other three build targets CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ make cuda-spark # DGX Spark make cuda-generic # Ada Lovelace / L40S-class, multi-GPU make strix-halo # ROCm on Strix Halo (e.g. Framework Desktop) Serve it to Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode or Pi CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ ./ds4-server # listens on http://127.0.0.1:8000 by default # see docs/SERVER.md for the API surface and multi-session handling, # and docs/CLIENTS.md for per-client setup Flags worth knowing on day one CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ --ctx 32768 # context window size --prefill-chunk 1024 # prefill batch size --ssd-streaming # bounded routed-expert cache, rest read from GGUF --mtp # speculative decoding (GLM, Qwen) --nothink / --think # reasoning off/on; V4.1 uses --think-level 1-100 --temp 0 # greedy --vision FILE # load a vision encoder --prefix-file FILE # preload conversation pairs --power 100 # throughput/GPU-load trade (V4.1 and GLM require 100)

The repo reports "about 126 t/s aggregate generation with 16 sessions" on an eight-L40S deployment. That is aggregate throughput across sixteen concurrent sessions on eight datacentre GPUs — roughly 8 t/s per session if you divide it out. It is a serving-capacity number. It tells you nothing about how fast a single reply streams on your laptop, and it is the figure most likely to be quoted at you out of context. The general version of this trap is covered in fast inference and token speed.
documents.s: 1. The 126 t/s figure is not your Mac

documents.t: The repo's stated philosophy: "Model support is intentionally opportunistic." Models are added and removed based on relevance to 128 GB laptops and 256/512 GB workstations. The project describes itself as "a working template for the biggest use cases" rather than universal coverage, and encourages users to modify the codebase with coding agents for their own hardware. Read that as a dependency warning. If you build a workflow on ds4 plus DeepSeek V4 Flash, the supported combination is explicitly not a commitment. Pin a commit.
documents.s: 2. Model support is designed to be withdrawn

documents.t: As of 6 October 2026, the most recent commit on main is dated 20 September 2026, about two weeks earlier, against 761 open issues. The commits themselves look like careful engineering work rather than abandonment — test-suite guards for ROCm and Metal, QA preflight documentation. But the category's own chronicler predicts that by April 2027, at least four of the six engines listed above will have gone 60 days without a commit, as model architectures move underneath them. That is a forecast, not a fact. The reason it belongs on this page is that it is a checkable one, and checking it takes ten seconds before you adopt any engine in this class. The commit date is the maintenance column that none of these READMEs print.
documents.s: 3. Check the commit date yourself — and know what the category predicts

documents.t: A commenter on the Hacker News thread reported that the ROCm builds are "absolutely untested". The repository's own commit log from 19 September 2026 says the opposite in specific terms — a commit message describes verifying warning-free ROCm application and test builds on Strix Halo, with placement, memory, session, server and agent tests passing. Both are reported here rather than resolved, because they may both be true of different moments or different Strix Halo configurations. If you are on AMD, treat ROCm as the least-trodden of the three backends and verify on your own box before committing to it.
documents.s: 4. A contradiction worth knowing about on ROCm

documents.t: ds4 is "deliberately narrow, not a general GGUF runner" and requires its own GGUF builds. Separately: the project site at dwarfstar.sh was criticised in the HN thread as marketing-heavy — one commenter called it "pure slop" — with the technical substance living in the repository's docs/ directory instead. Read the repo, not the landing page.
documents.s: 5. Custom GGUFs, and a website the thread disliked

documents.t: These are young, largely single-maintainer projects with native GPU access and few external reviewers, and the whole category shares that shape. The standing advice from people tracking it: build from source, pin commits, and run them on hardware you would not mind losing. If a local engine is going to sit behind an agent with tool access, the threat model in securing local and hybrid agents applies to the runtime as much as to the model.
documents.s: 6. The security posture assumes you read C

documents.t: Choose an overfit engine when your model is on its list and will stay there for the duration of the project; your hardware is on its list; the workload is long-running with a reusable prefix, so KV snapshots pay for themselves; and you are able to build from source and read a diff. Stay on llama.cpp or Ollama when you switch models often, you want one runtime across machines you do not control, you need a model nobody has overfitted for yet, or the thing you are optimising is your own time rather than tokens per second. The general runtime is also your reference baseline: measure it first, or you will never know what the narrow engine actually bought you. Run models locally with Ollama is the right starting point if you have not set that baseline. Use a hosted API when the job needs frontier capability rather than locality. This came up in the HN thread directly: a commenter noted that frontier cloud models remain faster for actual coding work. Local inference buys privacy, cost control and offline operation — not parity. Local or Claude agent? walks that decision properly. The emerging consensus in the local-AI community is a two-tier ecosystem rather than a winner: general runtimes for breadth and portability, disposable overfit runtimes for maximum performance on the model you are actually running this quarter. You are expected to have both installed. 复制为 Markdown 进阶 On September 23, 2026 Fireworks published Ember-1: not a new architecture, not a new pre-train — Kimi K3 with its reasoning habit re-trained. Same 2.8-trillion-parameter body, same 1M context, same price per token. It just stops thinking so much. Fireworks reports 35–50% fewer reasoning tokens with no loss of accuracy, and on two of five published benchmarks Ember-1 outscores K3 running at its maximum effort setting while costing less. Four days later it was the top AI story on Hacker News. The interesting part is not the model — it is the claim underneath it: the cheapest way to run a reasoning model is no longer to tell it to think less. This page takes that claim apart, shows you the arithmetic the launch table implies but never prints, and gives you a way to test it on your own traffic in an afternoon. What you'll learn Separate the two things that make an agent expensive: price per token, and number of tokens — Ember-1 changes only the second Read the launch table honestly, including the benchmark where effort buys literally nothing and the one where every model scores under 22% Derive the cost per task the blog does not print (and discover a single benchmark run costs $5–$535) Understand why a 71% cut in reasoning tokens produced only a 39% cut in total tokens — and what that ratio tells you about your own bill Measure reasoning-token share on your workload with one field most SDK wrappers throw away Know the fine print before you migrate: research-preview status, no released weights, a lost input modality, and the revenue-tiered Kimi K3 licence underneath it all 最后验证时间：2026-09-28。 Benchmark table, training description, token-reduction figures and pricing are Fireworks' own announcement of September 23, 2026 — vendor-run, on vendor-chosen benchmarks, with no independent replication published yet. Context window (1,048,576), model id and rates were cross-checked against the Fireworks model page and the OpenRouter model API on 2026-09-28. Ember-1 shipped as a Research Preview with two weeks of serverless access, kept permanently "based on community demand" — availability is the most perishable fact here; check before you build on it. Licence clauses are quoted from the Kimi K3 LICENSE on Hugging Face. 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: Ember-1: Kimi K3's Answers for 40% Fewer Tokens (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Kimi K3, like every reasoning model, spends most of its generated tokens on internal reasoning — Fireworks puts it at sometimes more than 90%. In a multi-turn agent that reasoning is replayed into every later call, so context grows roughly quadratically with turn count and early thinking gets re-billed for the rest of the run. Fireworks' customers asked for K3's coding quality at lower cost; turning reasoning_effort down gave up too much quality, so Fireworks trained the behaviour instead — over 50 training runs and 200+ evaluations — teaching the model to keep the self-reflection that recovers from mistakes and drop the rest. The result is served as accounts/fireworks/models/ember-1 at exactly K3's rates: $3 / M uncached input, $0.30 / M cached input, $15 / M output.

This is the part that reframes how you should think about model cost. Ember-1's rate card is identical to Kimi K3's, on Fireworks and on OpenRouter alike ($3 input / $15 output per million, 1,048,576-token context on both). There is no discount. Every dollar saved comes from tokens that are never generated in the first place — and, in an agent loop, from those same tokens never being replayed as input on the next nineteen turns. That has a practical consequence: $/token is the wrong number on your dashboard. Two models at the same list price can differ 2× on the same task, and the model with the higher list price is regularly the cheaper one per finished task. AILmanac's What AI costs across providers makes the same point from the pricing side; Ember-1 is the cleanest natural experiment for it yet, because the price variable is pinned and only the token count moves.
documents.s: 1. Nothing got cheaper. The model just buys less.

documents.t: K3 exposes reasoning_effort at low, high and max. Fireworks ran all three as separate arms, which is what makes their table more useful than most launch tables: Benchmark N K3 low K3 high K3 max Ember-1 Ember-1 vs K3 max Terminal Bench 2.1 89 76.4% 77.6% 80.9% 82.0% −51.9% / −23.1 USD SWE-bench Verified 500 80.4% 86.0% 93.2% 92.2% −15.5% / −68.1 USD SWE-Interact 75 6.7% 13.3% 21.3% 20.0% −32.5% / −60.8 USD DeepSWE 1.1 113 55.8% 62.8% 66.4% 75.2% −23.7% / −126.9 USD τ-2 Bench Airline 50 64% 64% 64% 66% −5.9% / −0.3 USD Read down the K3 columns before you read the Ember column. On SWE-bench Verified, dropping from max to low costs you 12.8 points — that is the "give up too much quality" Fireworks is talking about, and it is why an effort dial alone could not solve their customers' problem. Ember-1 lands above K3 high on every row and above K3 max on two of five, at a lower cost than max on all five. Against K3 low it is strictly better on both axes. Two rows deserve separate attention: τ-2 Bench Airline: 64% / 64% / 64%. Three effort levels, one score. On this benchmark every extra thinking token K3 generates is pure waste — you pay max prices for low results. If your production workload looks like τ²-bench (a scripted customer-service policy, short turns, tool calls against a fixed API), the effort dial is a cost setting with no quality meaning, and you should have measured that rather than defaulted to it. The general habit — sweep effort on your eval before trusting a default — is in Effort tuning and Reasoning models compared. SWE-Interact: nobody breaks 22%. The same models that resolve 92–93% of SWE-bench Verified resolve one task in five when the benchmark requires interacting with a user mid-task. SWE-bench Verified is close to saturated and tells you almost nothing about a frontier model any more; the interactive variant is where the actual capability gap lives. Keep both in mind whenever a launch post leads with a 90-something SWE-bench number. This is the capability–reliability gap showing up as two columns in one table.
documents.s: 2. Turning effort down is not the same thing, and the table proves it

documents.t: Fireworks never labels the two figures in that last column. Read as relative cost reduction and absolute dollars saved over the whole run, they are internally consistent — and dividing one by the other recovers a number nobody publishes: what it costs to run these benchmarks once. The arithmetic below is ours, not Fireworks' — it is inference from their two published figures, so treat it as an order of magnitude, not a quote: Benchmark N Implied K3-max run cost Implied cost per task Terminal Bench 2.1 89 ~$44 ~$0.50 SWE-bench Verified 500 ~$439 ~$0.88 SWE-Interact 75 ~$187 ~$2.49 DeepSWE 1.1 113 ~$535 ~$4.74 τ-2 Bench Airline 50 ~$5 ~$0.10 A single DeepSWE 1.1 sweep on K3 at max effort runs to roughly half a thousand dollars — for 113 tasks. That is the real reason "just run your own evals on every model" is advice people nod at and do not follow, and it is worth knowing before you promise a stakeholder a five-model bake-off. It is also the number that makes a 24% saving matter: repeated nightly, that one benchmark is a $46,000-a-year line item.
documents.s: 3. The "−51.9% / −23.1 USD" column tells you what a benchmark run costs

documents.t: Fireworks' internal validation reports 71.3% fewer reasoning tokens and 39% fewer total tokens on the same traffic. The gap between those two numbers is the most useful thing in the announcement, and it generalises to any efficiency claim you are ever pitched. Reasoning tokens are a share of generated tokens. The rest of your bill is made of things an efficiency post-train cannot touch: System prompt and tool definitions, re-sent every turn (often the largest single block in an agent). Tool results — file contents, search results, HTTP responses — which arrive from the outside world at their own size. The final answer, which you actually wanted. Prior turns, replayed as input. So the ceiling on any "fewer thinking tokens" saving is your reasoning-token share, not the vendor's. An agent whose turns are 80% tool output will see a fraction of the advertised win; a chat workload with a short prompt and long deliberation will see most of it. Before you migrate anything, measure the share — the next section shows how. Why agents burn tokens covers the other three lines in that list. Watch out A vendor's token-reduction percentage is measured on the vendor's traffic mix. Your saving is bounded by your own reasoning-token share — measure it before you estimate anything.
documents.s: Why 71% off reasoning was only 39% off the bill

documents.t: Fireworks returns the model's thinking in a reasoning_content field (the content that would otherwise sit inside think tags) rather than in content. Many OpenAI-compatible wrappers drop unknown fields, which is how teams end up unable to answer "what share of our output is thinking?" — and, worse, how they silently break multi-turn quality. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Capture reasoning_content, do not discard it⌄ Log the length of reasoning_content next to the length of content for every assistant message, for a day of real traffic. The ratio is your reasoning-token share and the ceiling on any efficiency saving anyone can sell you. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pass reasoning_content back on the next turn⌄ Fireworks is explicit: if you build the assistant message yourself as a dict and omit reasoning_content, the model loses access to its own previous reasoning. Passing message objects through unchanged handles this for you. A harness that strips the field will look like a quality regression that has nothing to do with the model. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run the same 20 real tasks on K3 max and on Ember-1⌄ Not a benchmark — your tasks, your tools, your system prompt. Record pass rate, total tokens, wall-clock, and dollars. Twenty tasks is enough to see a 35% token difference; it is not enough to see a 1-point quality difference, so treat quality as a gate, not a ranking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Add K3 at low effort as a third arm⌄ This is the arm most teams skip, and it is the one that tells you whether you need an efficiency-trained model at all. If K3-low already passes your gate, you were never going to pay for max in the first place. ←PreviousNext→ 5Compare on cost per completed task, never on $/M tokens⌄ Divide total dollars by tasks that passed your gate. A model that fails 10% more often is more expensive than its token count suggests, because failures are re-run by a human or by the agent. ←PreviousNext→ One call against Ember-1 on the OpenAI-compatible endpoint CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ curl https://api.fireworks.ai/inference/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $FIREWORKS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "accounts/fireworks/models/ember-1", "max_tokens": 8192, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior engineer. Reply with a unified diff and one paragraph of rationale."}, {"role": "user", "content": "The test suite in ./tests fails on macOS only. Log and module attached: ..."} ] }' | jq '{ reasoning_chars: (.choices[0].message.reasoning_content // "" | length), answer_chars: (.choices[0].message.content // "" | length), usage: .usage }' The A/B you actually want: same task, three arms, one table CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Arm 1 — the incumbent at full effort MODEL="accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k3" EFFORT="max" ./run-evals.sh > k3-max.jsonl # Arm 2 — the cheap way people try first MODEL="accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k3" EFFORT="low" ./run-evals.sh > k3-low.jsonl # Arm 3 — the efficiency post-train (no effort setting to choose) MODEL="accounts/fireworks/models/ember-1" ./run-evals.sh > ember.jsonl # Then the only comparison that matters: # dollars spent / tasks that passed the gate jq -s 'group_by(.arm)[] | {arm: .[0].arm, passed: (map(select(.passed)) | length), usd: (map(.usd) | add), cost_per_pass: ((map(.usd) | add) / (map(select(.passed)) | length))}' *.jsonl
documents.s: Measure it on your own traffic in an afternoon

documents.t: It is a Research Preview. Fireworks ships new research models with two weeks of serverless access and makes them permanent "based on community demand". Do not put an unbudgeted migration behind that. Build the A/B, keep K3 as the fallback path, and re-check availability before you cut over — this is exactly the case server-side fallbacks and model routing patterns exist for. The weights are not released, and that is legal. The most-upvoted confusion in the Hacker News thread was some version of "they trained on open weights and are not releasing theirs — can they do that?" They can. The Kimi K3 licence grants the right to "use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell copies of the Software; to run, deploy, fine-tune, or otherwise modify the Software and create derivative works from it" — with no copyleft obligation to publish what you build. What it does attach are two revenue-tiered conditions, and they are worth knowing whether or not you care about Ember-1: Model-as-a-Service above $20M. If you (and affiliates) run a MaaS business — giving third parties access to model inference or fine-tuning, e.g. via API, with meaningful control over inputs, parameters or training data — whose combined revenue exceeds $20 million over any consecutive 12 months, you must enter a separate agreement with Moonshot AI before commercial use of the Software or its derivative works. Attribution above 100M MAU or $20M/month. A product or service built on it that passes 100 million monthly active users or $20 million in monthly revenue must display "Kimi K3" prominently in its user interface. Internal use that does not expose the model or its capabilities to third parties is exempt from the MaaS clause. The practical reading: an open-weight licence can be MIT-shaped at the top and still gate the two situations a serious business ends up in. Read the licence before the benchmarks — the same advice applies to every "open" frontier release on DeepSeek, Qwen and the open-weight wave. Check your input modalities. OpenRouter lists Kimi K3 as text+image+video and Ember-1 as text+image. Fireworks' own model page advertises image input for Ember-1 and says nothing about video. If any part of your pipeline sends video frames to K3, verify that path explicitly before switching — a modality that silently disappears is a much worse failure than a quality dip, because it usually surfaces as a malformed request in production rather than a lower score in an eval. Check your sampling parameters too. OpenRouter's parameter list for Ember-1 omits seed and min_p, both of which it lists for K3. If your eval harness pins a seed for reproducibility, confirm the behaviour on the endpoint you will actually call rather than assuming the parent model's surface carried over. Porting prompts across models has the broader checklist.
documents.s: The fine print before you migrate

documents.t: Ember-1's other headline — "sets a new Pareto frontier on Bedside Bench across open and closed models including GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5" — comes from the Specialized Intelligence Index, which Fireworks launched on September 22, 2026, one day before Ember-1. Same company runs the index and ships the model. That is not automatically disqualifying, but it changes how you read it. What the SII does better than the usual leaderboard: Benchmarks come from practitioners, not academia — Doximity's BedsideBench (500 physician-validated clinical cases) for healthcare, Harvey's legal agent benchmarks for law, Sierra's τ-Banking and τ-Voice and Decagon's DuetBench for support, Rogo for finance, Novee's PWNBench and depthfirst's dfbench for security, and a software cluster including Datacurve's DeepSWE and Proximal's FrontierSWE V2. It reports cost per task and wall-clock duration next to score, from provider rate cards — the axes this whole page argues for. It labels every result by who can reproduce it: anyone, Fireworks-with-partner, or partner-only. That single label is the most useful piece of leaderboard metadata published this year; treat a partner-only row as a vendor claim with a nicer table around it. It refuses a composite score. No rollup across domains, no single "intelligence" number — which is the right call, and rare. What to hold in mind anyway: the benchmark suite, the arms chosen, the effort settings, and the model that wins are all selected by the same party. Compare its rows against an index run by someone with no model to sell before you quote them in a design doc. The general discipline is in The verification bottleneck.

Agentic coding on K3 at max effort, at volume: run the A/B this week. This is the exact workload Ember-1 was trained on, the reported savings are 15–52% of cost, and DeepSWE 1.1 suggests you may gain accuracy rather than trade it. Already running K3 at low or high because max was too expensive: strong candidate. Ember-1 beats K3 high on all five published rows and dominates low outright. Workloads shaped like τ²-bench (short turns, scripted policy, heavy tool output): expect modest savings — the effort dial was already doing nothing for you, and your reasoning-token share is small. Anything needing video input, a pinned seed, or a guaranteed 12-month endpoint: stay on K3 for now and re-evaluate when the preview converts. Not on Kimi K3 at all: the transferable lesson is the measurement, not the model. Find your reasoning-token share, sweep the effort dial on your own eval, and start reporting cost per completed task instead of $/M tokens. Every provider's version of this question is the same question. Check yourself 0/6

Kimi K3: the open-weight frontier — the parent model Ember-1 is built on: the MoE arithmetic, KDA attention, and where K3 sits against Claude Effort tuning — how to sweep a reasoning dial on your own eval instead of inheriting a default Why agents burn tokens — the other lines on the bill that no efficiency post-train will shrink

Introducing Ember-1 — Fireworks AI blog — the announcement: benchmark table, training description, token-reduction figures, pricing basis Ember-1 model page — Fireworks — model id, 1M context, function calling, serverless rates fireworks/ember-1 on OpenRouter — independent listing used to cross-check price, context length and supported parameters against moonshotai/kimi-k3 Introducing the Specialized Intelligence Index — Fireworks AI — domains, partner benchmarks, reproducibility labelling, no-composite-score methodology Reasoning — Fireworks AI Docs — the reasoning_content field, reasoning_effort, and why multi-turn agents must pass reasoning back Kimi K3 LICENSE — Hugging Face — the grant, the $20M MaaS clause, the attribution threshold Kimi K3's full weights are here, but they're "open" with a caveat — VentureBeat — enterprise reading of the licence definitions, July 27, 2026 Ember-1 discussion — Hacker News — 500+ points, 200+ comments; the weights-release and latency questions Related: What AI costs across providers · Reasoning models compared · Model routing patterns 分享此页面 X LinkedIn Reddit Hacker News 复制链接

复制为 Markdown 进阶 2026 年 9 月 1 日，Anthropic 发布了 Claude Fable 5.1（claude-fable-5-1）及其需要通过验证才能使用的孪生模型 Claude Mythos 5.1（claude-mythos-5-1）。如果只是扫一眼发布信息，你会把它归为"更好的 Fable"然后继续往下走。别这样。这是第一个仅替换模型 ID 就可能在生产环境返回 400 的 Claude 小版本：强制 tool_choice 被移除，thinking 块现在与产生它们的模型和对话绑定，而修改对话历史在新账户上会被强制作为错误处理。这也是第一个价格表上最便宜的那一行最值得关注的版本：缓存读取从 $1 降到 每 MTok $0.25，这就是为什么 Anthropic 能在标价 $10 / $50 不变的情况下，宣称典型工作负载成本下降约 25%，高度智能体化的工作负载最多下降 45%。 本页是迁移指南：改了什么、哪里会出问题、你能得到什么，以及一份半天就能跑完的清单。 What you'll learn 了解让 claude-fable-5 → claude-fable-5-1 的替换变成 400 的三项破坏性变更，以及各自的修复方法 使用五项新增功能：按消息设置 effort、限定在单轮的系统消息、进度更新、更便宜的缓存读取、内容溯源 识别无需改代码就会出现的七种行为变化（并行工具调用减少、旁白减少、行文更密集、整文件重写） 对照 Fable 5、Opus 5 和 GPT-5.6 Sol 阅读发布时的基准测试，而不被营销话术带着走 为你的工作负载在 Fable 5.1、Opus 5 和 Fable 5 之间做出选择，然后执行迁移清单 最后验证时间：2026-09-14。 模型 ID、定价、破坏性变更、beta 请求头和行为说明均来自 Anthropic 官方的 "What's new in Claude Fable 5.1"、模型概览、迁移指南和定价页面，全部于 2026 年 9 月 14 日读取。基准测试数字是 Anthropic 在发布公告中自行给出的。这里提到的三个 beta 可能会改变形态；上线前请重新核对请求头。下文发布时期的对比是以 Opus 5 为对象，因为那是 2026 年 9 月 1 日需要超越的模型；而“从这里开始”的模型现在是 Opus 5.5，依据是 2026 年 10 月 25 日重新读取的模型概览。最新的模型表见当前模型与定价。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: Claude Fable 5.1：有哪些变化，以及如何迁移

documents.t: Fable 5.1 是 Fable 5 的继任者：同样是高于 Opus 的 Mythos 级别，同样是 1M token 上下文、128K 最大输出、$10 输入 / $50 输出，同样的分词器，同样始终开启的自适应 thinking，同样是在响应体内返回 stop_reason: "refusal"，同样要求 30 天数据保留（不支持 ZDR）。Anthropic 自己的建议在精神上没有变：大多数工作先用当前的 Opus，把 Fable 5.1 留给"高难度推理和长周期智能体工作，或者在更高 effort 下 Claude Opus 5.5 的评测仍不够用的时候"。发布时这句话点名的是 Opus 5；自 2026 年 9 月 22 日起，模型概览点名的是 Opus 5.5，它才是今天该对比的模型——Opus 5 现已进入旧版（legacy）。新增的内容是：三项破坏性变更、五项新增功能、便宜了 75% 的缓存读取，以及一组你最好在评测套件告诉你之前就了解的行为变化。
这是你不能直接换个 ID 就完事的原因。每一项都是 400，而不是悄无声息的性能下降。

tool_choice: {"type": "any"} 和 {"type": "tool", "name": "..."} 现在会返回 400 invalid_request_error： tool_choice: type "tool" and "any" are not supported for this model. 原因很能说明问题：thinking 始终开启，而强制工具调用会跳过它，于是模型会把推演过程放到工具参数里，参数质量随之下降。该检查适用于 Messages API、Message Batches API 和 token 计数端点。auto（默认）和 none 不变。 修复方法只需改两行：保持 tool_choice 为 auto，在工具上设置 strict: true，并在 schema 中加入 additionalProperties: false，同时在提示词里写明该工具何时适用。Anthropic 的说明是，Fable 5.1"能可靠地遵循明确的工具指令"。如果你真正想要的是符合 schema 的 JSON 而不是工具调用，请改用结构化输出。 强制工具调用 → strict 工具 + 明确指令 CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Before (Fable 5) — now a 400 on Fable 5.1 "tool_choice": {"type": "tool", "name": "record_summary"} # After (Fable 5.1) "tools": [{ "name": "record_summary", "description": "Record the structured summary of the document.", "strict": true, "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": {"summary": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["summary"], "additionalProperties": false } }], "tool_choice": {"type": "auto"}, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize: The meeting moved to Thursday. Call the record_summary tool with your result."}]
documents.s: 1. 强制使用工具会返回错误

documents.t: 现在每个 thinking 块都会记录是哪个模型产生的，而且保留是单向的：Fable 5.1 可以读取来自 Opus 5、Fable 5、Mythos 5 以及所有更早 Claude 的 thinking 块；它们都无法读取 Fable 5.1 的。 迁移到 Fable 5.1 的对话会保留其推理。迁移离开它的对话（路由器、回退到 Opus 5、会话中途为省钱而降级）会丢失 Fable 5.1 各轮的推理。 API 的处理方式是：在目标模型看到之前，丢弃它读不了的块。被丢弃的块不计费，也不计入 input_tokens。没有 thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01 beta 请求头时，丢弃是静默的；带上该请求头后，丢弃会在顶层的 input_transformations 数组中报告。如果你在模型之间做路由，请发送该请求头并记录这个数组。静默丢失推理，正是那种在 bug 报告里表现为"模型在第 12 步之后变笨了"的问题。

这一条值得读两遍。修改 Fable 5.1 thinking 块之前的任何内容，包括 system 提示词、tools 数组或任何更早的消息，都会使之后的所有 thinking 块失效。在强制执行检查的地方，下一次请求会被拒绝，返回 400，消息内容为 The block is bound to a different conversation。 截至目前的执行规则： 2026 年 8 月 31 日及之后创建的账户： 强制执行。 更早的账户： API 会记录不匹配，但只有在你自己设置了 thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior 时才会采取行动。 Mythos 5.1 完全不做这项检查。 Claude Code、claude.ai、Managed Agents 和 Agent SDK 会替你保持前缀完整。只有手工构建的 messages 数组有风险。 Anthropic 自己列出的会使块失效的情形，转述出来其实是一份常见智能体框架习惯的清单： 使之后所有 thinking 块失效 仍保持有效 编辑、重排或删除较早的轮次，同时保留之后的轮次 移除开头的一段 thinking 块，从最旧的开始 在较早的轮次中注入每次请求的提醒或状态行，然后在下一次请求时移除 服务端压缩，或裁剪历史的上下文编辑 在同一对话的多次请求之间重新构建顶层的 system 或 tools 移动 cache_control 标记 之后返回不同字节的图片或文档 URL（检查按字节进行，所以同一文件的轮换签名 URL 没问题） 在请求之间更改 effort 所有修复都归结为一条规则：把对话当作仅追加的。 每轮提醒改用限定在单轮的系统消息（见下文）。工具和指令的变更改用对话中途的系统消息与工具变更。裁剪改用服务端压缩。若想继续而不是报错，请发送 thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01 请求头并设置 prefix_mismatch_behavior: "drop_block"；之后丢弃会在 input_transformations 中报告，reason 为 prefix_binding_mismatch。 Anthropic 部分地把这视为一项反蒸馏措施：发布文章称，新的 API 账户不能再在保留对话记录的同时手动编辑先前的上下文，这堵住了一种公开记录过的蒸馏手法。对你的实际好处是，同样的纪律也能让提示词缓存保持热状态。
documents.s: 3. 修改更早的轮次会使 thinking 块失效
documents.h: #3-修改更早的轮次会使-thinking-块失效

documents.t: 现在可以在对话中途更改 effort，而不会使提示词缓存失效。难的一步调高，例行的步骤调低。发送 mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01 beta 请求头，并插入一条只包含 effort 的系统消息；新的级别从下一个用户轮次开始生效。在 Claude API 和 Google Cloud 上，Fable 5.1、Mythos 5.1 和 Opus 5 均支持。 在总结轮次降低 effort，同时不破坏缓存 CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ { "model": "claude-fable-5-1", "max_tokens": 4096, "output_config": {"effort": "high"}, "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Plan a migration from SQLite to PostgreSQL in three short steps."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "1. Export the SQLite data. 2. Create the PostgreSQL schema. 3. Import the data and verify row counts."}, {"role": "system", "content": [], "output_config": {"effort": "low"}}, {"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the plan in one sentence."} ] } # header: anthropic-beta: mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01 这与 Thinking 与 Effort 以及 Effort 调优中的 effort 指导相配合：默认值是 high，而"整个会话使用同一级别"现在只是偷懒的选择，不再是唯一的选择。

在 role: "system" 的消息上设置 clear_at: "next_user_message"，它就只在当前轮次拥有系统提示词的权威，一旦后面出现 user 消息便不再渲染。你需要继续原样回传它，因此之前的内容都不变，缓存保持命中，之后的 thinking 块依然有效，而且已清除的消息不消耗输入 token。请求头：mid-conversation-system-clear-at-2026-08-21。 { "role": "system", "clear_at": "next_user_message", "content": "Results have landed in your inbox. Check it before running more code." } 这是对"注入提醒、下次请求再删除"这一模式的官方替代方案，而破坏性变更 3 现在会惩罚这种模式。
documents.s: 限定在单轮的系统消息（beta）

documents.t: 与 Fable 5 一样，Fable 5.1 会在工具调用之间写简短的进度说明，每条都是紧挨在调用之前的一个独立 thinking 块。在默认的 thinking.display: "omitted" 下，这些内容返回时是空的，因此一个很长的智能体轮次在用户看来是静默的。新增：display: "updates"（请求头 thinking-display-updates-2026-08-18）会以文本形式返回进度说明，而推理保持隐藏。此时任何文本非空的 thinking 块都是一条可以渲染的状态行。"summarized" 也会返回它们，并与摘要后的推理混在一起。原始思维链依然不会返回。
documents.s: 工具调用之间的进度更新（beta）

documents.t: 基础输入 5 分钟缓存写入 1 小时缓存写入 缓存读取 输出 Fable 5 $10 $12.50 $20 $1.00 $50 Fable 5.1 $10 $12.50 $20 $0.25 $50 在 Fable 5.1 和 Mythos 5.1 上，缓存读取是基础输入的 0.025 倍，而其他所有 Claude 模型是 0.1 倍。写入价格和 512 token 的最小可缓存提示词不变；批处理仍是 5 折（$5 / $25）。对于每轮都要重新读取一大段缓存前缀的长智能体循环，发布文章里"最多便宜 45%"就来自这里。横向说明：三天后发布、标价同为 $10 / $50 的 OpenAI GPT-6 Astra，缓存读取收费 $1.00，是 Fable 5.1 的四倍；参见 Astra 指南。

所有 Fable 5.1 和 Mythos 5.1 的文本在所有平台上都带有 Anthropic 的统计型文本水印。Claude 生成的文件（例如通过代码执行）在经由 Files API 获取时，会带有已签名的 C2PA Content Credentials。Anthropic 表示，水印不会增加 token 或隐藏字符，不携带任何关于你或你所在组织的信息，也不需要更改请求。背景：Anthropic 于 2026 年 7 月签署了欧盟 AI 法案（EU AI Act）关于 AI 生成内容透明度的行为准则，并面向监管机构、事实核查人员、研究人员以及需要验证的企业，提供处于私有预览阶段的检测 API。
Anthropic 公开记录了这些变化，每一项在官方的 Prompting Claude Fable 5.1 指南中都有提示词层面的修复办法。请在用户发现之前，先在评测里留意它们。

documents.t: 如果你已经正确接入了 Fable 5，以下内容都会原样沿用： 自适应 thinking 始终开启。带 budget_tokens 的 thinking: {"type": "enabled"} 和 {"type": "disabled"} 都会返回 400。请省略 thinking，或发送 {"type": "adaptive"}。 thinking.display 默认为 "omitted"；原始思维链永远不会返回。 交错 thinking 是自动的，无需 beta 请求头。 预填充（prefill）返回 400。非默认的 temperature、top_p、top_k 返回 400。 拒绝以 HTTP 200 和 stop_reason: "refusal" 加 stop_details.category 的形式到达；在任何输出之前就到达的拒绝不会计费。允许的回退目标是 Opus 5 和 Opus 4.8，而回退抵扣会退还切换时的提示词缓存成本。完整模式见拒绝与安全。 30 天保留是强制的；来自没有它的组织或工作区的请求会返回 400。两个模型都属于 Covered Models。 一处值得知道的差异：Fable 5.1 和 Mythos 5.1 都不支持 Priority Tier。 Fable 5 支持。如果你购买了优先容量，这是暂时留在 Fable 5 的一个理由。

documents.t: 数字是 Anthropic 的，测试框架也是 Anthropic 的。与 GPT-5.6 Sol 的对比是 OpenAI 最先会提出异议的，而 OpenAI 自己的 GPT-6 Astra 三天后就发布了，所以请把它当作 9 月 1 日的状况，而不是 9 月 14 日的。 基准测试 Fable 5.1 Fable 5 Opus 5 GPT-5.6 Sol Terminal-Bench 4.0 55.8%（Mythos 5.1：60.9%） 42.0% 52.3% 37.3% Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 52.6% 24.7% 29.0% 22.4% GDPval-AA v2（Elo） 1853 1723 1824 1711 OSWorld 2.0，partial / strict 77.9% / 41.7% 72.9% / 36.1% 75.4% / 39.6% — Humanity's Last Exam，无工具 / 有工具 60.9% / 65.0% 57.8% / 63.8% 56.6% / 63.6% — AutomationBench 31.4% 17.1% 26.9% 19.6% CursorBench 3.2.0 73.4% 70.5% 70.0% 67.2% 三点解读，比任何单独一行都更重要： 从 Fable 5 到 5.1 的提升在长周期智能体工作上最大（Terminal-Bench-Science 翻了一番，AutomationBench 几乎翻了一番）。这与 Anthropic 自己"当更高 effort 的 Opus 5 仍然不够用时再用它"的定位一致：收益在持续数小时的运行上，而不是聊天。 Opus 5 比标题所暗示的更接近，在好几行上都是如此（Terminal-Bench 4.0：52.3 对 55.8；GDPval：1824 对 1853），而标价只有一半。Anthropic 一再让你先用 Opus 5，是有原因的。 客户引言谈的是 token，而不仅是准确率。 Cognition、Rogo、Browserbase 和 Block 都提到，在结果相同或更好的情况下 token 更少。结合 $0.25 的缓存读取，"同样的工作 Fable 5.1 比 Fable 5 更便宜"比"Fable 5.1 更聪明"这个说法更站得住脚。 发布文章中的科学案例（在 12 个靶点上命中率约 50% 的蛋白质结合剂，而典型水平为 10–15%；利用 30 年前的 Magellan 雷达数据绘制的 2–3 公里分辨率金星高程图；七个开源基因组学模型上 2.5 倍的提速）是 Anthropic 报告的研究成果，不是基准测试。对研究类工作负载是有趣的信号，但不能作为采购依据。

documents.t: 你的情况 选择 原因 大多数生产工作，对成本敏感 Opus 5.5 Anthropic 自己自 2026 年 9 月 22 日起的默认推荐（在这一位置取代了 Opus 5）；价格只是标价的一小部分；参见当前模型与定价 持续数小时的自主编码、研究，或文档/电子表格/幻灯片制作，且 high effort 的 Opus 5 仍然达不到 Fable 5.1 最大的提升正出现在这里；缓存读取让长循环比 Fable 5 更便宜 你依赖 Priority Tier Fable 5（暂时） Fable 5.1 和 Mythos 5.1 不在 Priority Tier 上 你强制使用 tool_choice，且本迭代无法修改框架 Fable 5 Fable 5.1 会返回 400；先迁移框架，再迁移模型 你在对话中途于模型之间路由或回退 任意，但要发送 thinking-binding 请求头 否则从 Fable 5.1 降级时会静默丢弃它的推理 合同规定必须零数据保留 Opus 5.5，或任意 Opus Fable 5.x 和 Mythos 5.x 要求 30 天保留，且不符合 ZDR 资格 需要更少分类器干预的防御性网络安全或生命科学研究 Mythos 5.1，如果你的组织已通过验证 同一模型，不同的安全防护配置；请申请 Cyber Verification Program（三个层级），而不是等待邀请

documents.t: Anthropic 提供了一个内置技能，能在 Claude Code 中完成其中大部分工作。先运行它，再核实它看不到的项目。 自动完成 ID 替换和参数修复 CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ /claude-api migrate this project to claude-fable-5-1 Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1替换 ID 并 grep 强制的 tool_choice⌄ claude-fable-5 → claude-fable-5-1（Bedrock：anthropic.claude-fable-5-1）。然后 grep 类型为 any 或 tool 的 tool_choice。每个命中项都改为 strict: true + additionalProperties: false + 明确的'调用 X 工具'指令，或改用结构化输出。别忘了 token 计数调用：它们同样会校验。 ←PreviousNext→ 2运行历史编辑检查⌄ 如果你的代码自己构建 messages 数组，请带着 thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01 请求头和 prefix_mismatch_behavior: "drop_block" 跑一次真实会话，并记录 input_transformations。每一条 prefix_binding_mismatch 记录都对应一个你在编辑历史的地方。从源头修复：每轮提醒 → 限定在单轮的系统消息；system/tools 变更 → 对话中途的系统消息；裁剪 → 服务端压缩。然后有意识地选定生产环境的 prefix_mismatch_behavior。 ←PreviousNext→ 3审计路由和回退路径⌄ 对话可能从 Fable 5.1 转到 Opus 5、Fable 5 或更早模型的每个位置，都要判断丢失 Fable 5.1 的推理是否可以接受。发送 binding 请求头，让丢弃至少能被报告出来。确认你的回退目标是 Opus 5 或 Opus 4.8（仅有的两个允许项）。 ←PreviousNext→ 4重新调整 effort，并考虑按消息设置 effort⌄ 默认是 high。对于长循环，添加 mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01 beta，在例行轮次降低 effort；在需要最新检索的轮次提高它，因为 low effort 更常凭记忆作答。 ←PreviousNext→ 5加入智能体循环的提示词行⌄ 一行要求批量发出相互独立的工具调用；一行要求开头一句话、定期更新和结尾回顾（如果你的 UI 展示进度，就把 thinking.display 设为 updates）；一行要求优先做有针对性的编辑而不是整文件重写。放宽任何为 Opus 4.x 编写的反格式规则。 ←PreviousNext→ 6重新运行评测并重新检查成本⌄ 拒绝、回退、回退抵扣和分词器都没有变化，所以你看到的差异是真实的行为差异。比较前后的缓存读取开销：如果没有下降，说明你的前缀不稳定，第 2 步还没有做完。 ←PreviousNext→

Anthropic 表示 Fable 5.1 和 Mythos 5.1 是同一个底层模型，只是安全防护配置不同，规格和定价相同。Mythos 5.1 只提供给通过 Anthropic 验证计划验证的组织：面向防御性安全工作的 Cyber Verification Program，以及面向生物工作的 Life Sciences Verification Program。在安全防护方面，有两处变化对所有人生效：Fable 5.1 现在被允许为防御目的识别软件漏洞（Anthropic 报告每个会话的网络安全防护干预减少约 60%），而渗透测试、漏洞利用生成和二进制漏洞扫描等双重用途任务仍会被重定向到 Opus 模型；并且对于无害的基础生物学和医学问题，生物安全防护的触发减少约 85%。Mythos 5.1 还会跳过 thinking 块的对话绑定检查。如果你没有通过验证，Anthropic 的指示很简单：使用 Fable 5.1。 最后验证时间：2026-10-21。 获得验证是一次申请，而不是邀请：这在 2026 年 10 月 6 日发生了变化，当天 Project Glasswing 被重组为 Cyber Verification Program 的三个层级：Defense Access（组织，以及付费套餐的个人）、Red Team Access（仅限组织）和 Specialized Access（仅限组织，与美国政府合作审核，现有 Glasswing 成员被归入此层级）。每个层级都提供 Opus 5.5、Sonnet 5.5 和 Mythos 5.1。请通过 portal.anthropic.com/programs 的 Verification Portal 申请；决定通常在七个工作日内送达。资格取决于防御是否是你的实际业务："Organizations whose main business falls outside that scope may not be eligible." 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源. 注意命名：Fable 5 指南把 Mythos 5 解释为"没有安全分类器的 Fable 5"。对于 5.1，Anthropic 的措辞是"不同的安全防护配置"，而且 Mythos 5.1 仍在为 Anthropic 自己的 Claude Security 产品提供支持。把它当作配置不同的部署，而不是不受过滤的版本。

documents.t: Check yourself 0/4

Key takeaways 只有在你从不强制 tool_choice、从不编辑对话历史、也从不把 thinking 块路由给更旧模型的情况下，Fable 5.1 才能直接替代 Fable 5。替换 ID 之前，先 grep 这三种情况。 把对话当作仅追加：每轮提醒用限定在单轮的系统消息，指令和工具变更用对话中途的消息，裁剪用服务端压缩。这样既能保持 thinking 块有效，又能让缓存保持热状态。 定价的重点是便宜的缓存读取，而不是标价：长智能体循环会变便宜，短对话不会。当前的 Opus——自 2026 年 9 月 22 日起是 Opus 5.5——仍然是 Anthropic 自己说的'从这里开始'，价格只是 Fable 5.1 的一小部分。当前数字见：/docs/whats-new/models-and-pricing。 预期会看到并行工具调用减少、旁白减少、行文更密集和整文件重写；每一项都有一行提示词的修复办法，而 thinking.display: "updates" 能恢复可见的进度。 Priority Tier 和 ZDR 是留在 Fable 5，或者改用 Opus 模型的两个合同层面的理由。
