Two products, one release, and the pairing is the interesting part: Meta claims tools that are trained together with the model produce fewer retries and higher-quality output than a generic model steered by a generic harness. Whether or not you buy that claim, the launch is worth reading closely — Muse Code is the closest structural analogue to Claude Code that any competitor has shipped, and a few of its design decisions (the append-only event log, the contributor tier pricing, the three bundled skills) are non-obvious enough to be worth stealing regardless of which agent you actually use day to day. This page is the practical read: what Muse Code actually is, how it compares to Claude Code on the numbers Meta itself published, the pricing trap that shows up on the second read of the pricing table, and where it fits into the AILmanac tour. What you'll learn Understand what Muse Code is architecturally: a terminal agent with a local append-only event log, persistent async background agents, and three shipped skills (/plan, /grill, /goal) Read the Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1 numbers correctly — including the vendor-run caveat that the source review itself flags Know the pricing tiers: $1.25/$4.25 standard vs. $0.10/$0.20 contributor, and what the 12.5×/21.25× discount actually costs you in data terms Get the install command, the platforms supported, and the beta-status caveats before you point this at anything sensitive Place Muse Code next to Claude Code, Codex CLI, and the rest of the coding-agent CLI landscape
documents.s: Muse Code + Muse Spark 1.2: Meta's Terminal Coding Agent

documents.t: Muse Code is a beta terminal coding agent for macOS and Linux, powered by Muse Spark 1.2 — a 1M-token multimodal-input, text-output model — with async background agents, a local append-only event log for crash-safe resume, and three bundled skills (/plan, /grill, /goal); Meta prices the standard tier at $1.25/M input and $4.25/M output, and offers a contributor tier at $0.10/M input and $0.20/M output in exchange for permission to train future Meta models on your prompts and completions.

Muse Code's runtime records every model call, tool run, approval, and edit to a local append-only event log before it executes. Meta describes this as "replay-exact and restart-safe." If the agent crashes mid-task — segfault, laptop lid, expired token, anything — you resume from the log without losing work or having to re-prompt the model to reconstruct state. That's a write-ahead log pattern from database engineering, applied to the harness rather than the storage layer. Two things follow that are worth internalising: Failures during 24-hour runs become recoverable rather than expensive. Meta's own kernel-optimisation case study executed 1,000+ tool calls over 24 hours on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. Without a durable log, one crash in hour 22 costs the whole run. With one, the model resumes from the last committed event. Post-hoc auditing is trivial. Every decision is on disk, in order, with the tool inputs and outputs. You can inspect what the agent thought, why it called a particular tool, and what came back — without instrumenting anything. The comparable pattern in Claude Code is checkpoints and rewind, which snapshots the workspace so you can step backwards through interactive edits. The Muse Code event log is a different tool for a different problem: rewind lets you undo, while the event log lets the agent resume.
documents.s: 1. The event log is a write-ahead log, and it's what makes long runs safe

documents.t: Two pricing tiers, publicly disclosed: Tier Input ($/M) Cached input ($/M) Output ($/M) You give up Standard $1.25 $0.15 $4.25 Nothing Contributor $0.10 — $0.20 Permission to train future Meta models on your prompts and completions The math on the discount: 12.5× cheaper on input, 21.25× cheaper on output. For a real coding session that reads more than it writes, the effective cost drop lands closer to 15×. The catch is not that Meta will look at your prompts (all frontier vendors log for abuse review by default). The catch is training rights — Meta explicitly retains permission to train future models on your inputs and completions. That means: Anything that would leak trade secrets, PII, licensed code, or a customer's data through a future model output is off-limits. Anything under a share-alike or similar restrictive licence you don't own is off-limits. Anything covered by an NDA is off-limits. Read Meta's exact terms before flipping the toggle — the source reviews are clear that "confirm exact terms and toggle settings in Meta's official docs before running it on anything sensitive." A 12.5× cost reduction on personal side-projects is a genuinely good deal. A 12.5× cost reduction on your employer's monorepo is a legal problem waiting to happen. 最后验证时间：2026-08-06。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: 2. The contributor tier is a 12.5× / 21.25× discount, and it's not free

documents.t: Meta published Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1 comparisons that put Muse Spark 1.2 behind Claude Opus 5 on both. That's an unusually honest launch chart, and it's worth reading precisely rather than dismissively. Benchmark Muse Spark 1.2 Claude Opus 5 (paired with Claude Code) Terminal-Bench 2.1 82.9% Higher — Meta ranks it first (external secondhand reporting cites ~86.7%) DeepSWE 1.1 59.3% Higher — Meta ranks it first (score not published in the reviews we could verify) Two caveats before you take those numbers as gospel: Vendor-run methodology. The published numbers are pass@1 averaged over five attempts, each model paired with its own agent product, and Meta itself notes its setup "may not be tuned for third-party models." All numbers are vendor-run, not independent reproductions. Model+harness is the unit of measurement. Terminal-Bench doesn't score a bare model — it scores a model working through an agent. Muse Spark 1.2 is being evaluated inside Muse Code; Opus 5 inside Claude Code. The result is a claim about the pairing, not the model in isolation. Swapping either half changes the number. The practical read: Muse Spark 1.2 is a strong second on the two benchmarks Meta chose to publish, in the harness Meta co-trained it for. That's a defensible position for a v1.2 model against a mature Claude Code / Opus 5 pairing — but "second on the vendor's own chart" is also exactly as strong a claim as it sounds. Don't over-extrapolate.
documents.s: 3. Meta's own charts place Muse Spark 1.2 second, behind Claude Opus 5

documents.t: Muse Code ships three skills out of the box, and the shape of each is instructive: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1/plan — approval-gated planning⌄ Converts a task into a concrete plan and pauses for human approval before execution. Same pattern as Claude Code's plan mode (docs/claude-code/plan-mode), and the reason is the same: the model is much better at proposing structure than at executing structure it never showed you first. ←PreviousNext→ 2/grill — stress-testing the plan⌄ Runs the plan through adversarial questioning until it stabilises — 'what breaks if X?', 'what did you assume about Y?', 'is there a case where Z fails silently?'. This is the missing step in most naive agent loops: not planning, but pressure-testing the plan before you spend tokens executing it. Nothing about /grill is Meta-specific; you can implement the same discipline with a subagent in any coding CLI. ←PreviousNext→ 3/goal — long-horizon execution⌄ Works toward a specified objective across many tool calls without asking for permission at every step. Pairs with the event log: the human authorises the goal, the log records the trajectory, and the agent runs. The 1,000+ tool call kernel-optimisation case study is a /goal run. ←PreviousNext→ The interesting design pattern here is the plan → grill → goal pipeline: propose, adversarially critique, then execute under a durable log. That decomposition maps cleanly onto workflows you might already be running with Claude Code plan-mode plus subagents — and it's a cleaner mental model than the ad-hoc "keep going until it works" loop most people end up with.
documents.s: 4. The three bundled skills are worth stealing even if you never install Muse Code

documents.t: Availability: macOS and Linux, public beta as of 5 August 2026. No Windows build at launch. Weights are hosted-only — Meta has not published downloadable weights for Muse Spark 1.2. Install Muse Code (macOS / Linux beta) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash Standard security hygiene applies to any curl | bash installer: at minimum, review the script before piping it to a shell. Meta hosts the installer under its own domain, but nothing about the install pattern makes the script inherently safer than any other. Watch out Beta software. Expect breaking changes, undocumented edges, and quota surprises before general availability. Contributor tier trains on your data. Do not flip it on for work code, client code, licensed code, or anything under NDA. Vendor-run benchmarks. Muse Spark 1.2 is second to Claude Opus 5 on Meta's own charts — the numbers to trust are your own on your own repo.

Axis Muse Code + Muse Spark 1.2 Claude Code + Claude Opus 5 Terminal harness Yes (macOS, Linux beta) Yes (macOS, Linux, Windows) Context window 1M tokens (input), text-only output 1M tokens, up to 128K output Adversarial planning skill /grill (bundled) Compose with subagents + plan mode Approval-gated planning /plan (bundled) Plan mode Crash-safe long runs Append-only event log (replay-exact, restart-safe) Checkpoints and rewind (workspace snapshot, human-driven undo) Sandboxing Parallel work isolated in separate Git worktrees Worktrees plus permissions MCP support Not documented in the launch materials we could verify Full MCP support Cheapest legitimate tier $0.10/M input, $0.20/M output (contributor tier — data training) Prompt caching discount without giving up training rights Benchmark ranking (vendor-run) 2nd on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (82.9%), 2nd on DeepSWE 1.1 (59.3%) 1st on both (per Meta's chart) For the broader field — Codex CLI, Aider, and the rest — see coding agent CLIs compared.
documents.s: How it compares to Claude Code, at a glance

documents.t: Reach for Muse Code when: Your workflow is dominated by long, unattended runs where the event log's crash safety is more valuable than any specific tool integration. The 24-hour kernel-optimisation case study is the shape. You want a second, structurally different opinion on a task. A different model + a different harness is a genuinely different second opinion. The best use of a competitor CLI is often to run the same task through it and compare. You are a solo developer working on side-projects where the contributor tier's data-training trade-off is acceptable, and 12.5×/21.25× cheaper tokens materially change what's affordable. Don't reach for it when: You need MCP tool integration, which is not documented in the launch materials. You need Windows support, which does not exist at launch. You are working on anything covered by an NDA, a restrictive licence, or contains client / employer / PII data, unless you can pay the standard tier and are certain no contributor-tier toggle is on. Your quality bar is "beat Claude Opus 5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1", because on Meta's own numbers it doesn't. Check yourself 0/4
documents.s: When to actually reach for it

documents.t: If you've read coding agent CLIs compared, Muse Code drops in as a new entry with the same shape as Claude Code and Codex CLI — a terminal harness that owns file edits, tool calls, and long-running agent loops. What's different is the runtime discipline (event log) and the tier structure (contributor pricing). If you've read the Opus 5 field guide, the direct point of comparison is that Muse Spark 1.2 is a credible-but-second competitor to Opus 5 on Meta's own numbers, in the harness Meta trained for it. For the broader picture — how to choose across the field — start with choosing a model and what AI costs across providers. If you want to compare techniques rather than products, the plan → grill → goal decomposition is worth composing yourself in Claude Code with subagents and plan mode — you get the discipline without the beta and without the contributor-tier question. 最后验证时间：2026-08-06。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.

复制为 Markdown 高级 过去十八个月里，“多智能体”意味着扇出（fan-out）要你自己写：你写协调者提示词，你并行发起 N 个调用，你合并它们的 JSON，你处理重试。2026 年 7 月 9 日，OpenAI 把这一切压缩成了一个请求参数：Responses API 上的 multi_agent.enabled: true，并包装成一个名为 Sol Ultra Mode 的消费级功能。模型自己决定生成多少个子智能体，并行运行它们，再综合结果——全部在一次 HTTP 调用之内。目前没有其他前沿厂商发布过对等的原语。本页梳理实际发布了什么、背后的数字、Anthropic 提供的替代方案，以及最关键的部分：原生原语物有所值的三类工作负载，和自己搭建扇出仍然更优的两类。 What you'll learn 读懂 Responses API 多智能体请求体的确切形态，并知道 max_concurrent_subagents 究竟限制了什么 做成本核算：按 Sol 的价格，“模型生成 4 个子智能体”实际要收你多少钱 在 Anthropic 一侧画出同样的版图——Cowork、Managed Agents 和 Claude Code 子智能体——并看清原语上的差距 按工作负载选对原语：原生多智能体、自建扇出、A2A，还是单次长回合 避开四种会让 4 智能体 Ultra 调用变成 4 倍账单却没有准确率提升的失败模式 最后验证时间：2026-08-01。 Responses API 的多智能体接口仍处于 Beta 阶段（请求头 OpenAI-Beta: responses_multi_agent=v1）。自 2026 年 7 月 9 日发布以来，字段名称、max_concurrent_subagents 的默认值，以及哪些参数与多智能体模式互斥，都已发生变化。上线前请对照链接的文档重新核实请求形态和不兼容清单。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: 原生多智能体 API：OpenAI 的 Responses 多智能体 Beta 与自己动手搭建

documents.t: Ultra Mode 是 Responses API 上 multi_agent.enabled: true 之上的一层消费级外壳——一个原生原语，让模型在一次请求内并行生成子智能体、综合它们的输出，并返回单一响应。它在可并行的任务上能换来虽小但真实的准确率提升（Terminal-Bench 2.1：88.8% → 91.9%），而 token 账单大致与模型选择生成的子智能体数量成线性增长。

同一次发布里落地了两样东西，值得分开看： Ultra Mode——ChatGPT 和 Codex 内的产品开关。在旗舰档（Sol）上可用。开启后，困难任务会先被拆解成并行的子智能体运行，再做综合。宣传为“生成 4 个以上智能体”；OpenAI 自己的一些 GA 基准图表在 BrowseComp 和 SEC-Bench Pro 上也展示了 16 智能体的配置，但实际默认值是四个。 Responses API 多智能体 Beta——开发者原语。同样的底层能力，以 client.beta.responses.create() 上的 multi_agent.enabled: true 暴露出来。想自己搭一个类 Ultra 的体验，就用这个。 营销留下的困惑是真实的：开发者不断在问“我怎么从 API 调用 Ultra Mode？”答案是：你不能——你启用的是多智能体 Beta，它正是产品功能底下的那个原语。
documents.s: 2026 年 7 月 9 日实际发布了什么

documents.t: 具体来说，形态如下（Python SDK）： 最简多智能体 Responses API 调用 CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() resp = client.beta.responses.create( model="gpt-5.6-sol", input="Audit this repo for auth-bypass patterns and write a report.", multi_agent={ "enabled": True, "max_concurrent_subagents": 3, }, tools=[...], # your MCP tools, function tools, etc. extra_headers={"OpenAI-Beta": "responses_multi_agent=v1"}, ) 这个形态有四点并不显而易见： max_concurrent_subagents 不是总预算。 它限制的是整棵树在任意时刻活跃的子智能体回合数——根加上所有后代。模型在请求的生命周期内可以生成多得多的总子智能体；只是同一时刻运行的不能超过 N 个。 深度没有上限。 子智能体自己也可以再生成子智能体。树的深度和每次运行的子智能体总数都没有固定上限。你的成本面不是“N 次调用”，而是一棵由模型在运行时塑形的树。 根负责综合。 根智能体负责把子智能体的响应合并为最终答案。你拿不到结构化的 {subagents: [...]} 对象；你得到的是一个响应，中间的智能体回合对你的代码是不透明的。 有些参数会被静默禁用。 启用多智能体后，reasoning.summary 和 max_tool_calls 不被支持，而且多智能体响应不支持 compaction 端点。如果你依赖推理摘要做可观测性，一旦打开它就会失去这些。
documents.s: Responses API 多智能体请求

documents.t: 按 Sol 的 GA 定价每百万 token 输入 $5 / 输出 $30，这笔账毫不留情。以下来自对真实 Ultra 运行做逆向分析的开发者文章： Ultra 拆成 2 个子智能体的任务 ≈ 单次 Sol 调用输出 token 成本的 2 倍——因为两个子智能体都要生成输出，根还要在其上生成综合内容。 Ultra 生成 5 个子智能体的任务 ≈ 5 倍——理由相同，再加上整棵树上按比例增多的输入 token 重放。 展示 16 智能体配置的 BrowseComp / SEC-Bench 图表不是免费的午餐：它们是研究级的演示，不是默认值。在 Sol 上并发 16 个子智能体时，单单输出 token 一项，每个困难查询就是两位数美元的中段。 可以这样理解：你付的是一次 Sol 调用的蒙特卡洛，外加最上面一次综合。 有时它换来的准确率足够重要；有时它只是为一个单次调用就能解决的任务付了 4 倍账单。

documents.t: 在可并行评测——即 Ultra Mode 的目标工作负载——上公布的提升是真实的，但幅度不大： 基准 Sol（单次） Sol Ultra 差值 评测衡量什么 Terminal-Bench 2.1 88.8% 91.9% +3.1 多步命令行规划、工具协同 BrowseComp 87.5% 92.2% +4.7 多来源网络调研与综合 SEC-Bench Pro — 74.3% （未公布单模式数字） 跨大型语料库的监管文件推理 关于这张表有三点： +3–5 个点的区间，与并行采样（best-of-N、self-consistency）在其他前沿上历来能换来的提升一致。这个原语确实有用；这个提升并不是阶跃式的飞跃。 这些是最好情形——专门挑出来展示该模式的评测。在顺序任务（线性的代码编辑、单文件重写、简短聊天）上，Ultra 只会增加综合延迟和成本，而不会提升准确率。 在同一张 Terminal-Bench 2.1 图表上，Anthropic 的 Opus 4.8 得分为 78.9%——也就是说，Sol Ultra 的领先来自更好的基础模型与叠加其上的多智能体增益两者。如果你从 Opus 迁移到 Sol Ultra，不要把全部差距都归功于多智能体原语。
documents.s: 准确率到底换来了什么

documents.t: Anthropic 尚未发布对等的 API 原语。最接近的几个类比各自解决同一问题的不同切片： Cowork——一个产品界面。一个智能体式桌面工作区，智能体在其中与用户并肩完成持续的多步工作。作为功能可与 Ultra Mode 相比，但不是 API 原语。 Managed Agents 与 managed-agents memory stores——带持久状态和调度的托管智能体循环。填补的是“长时间运行的后台智能体”这个位置，而不是“并行生成 4 个再合并”那个位置。 Claude Code 子智能体与子智能体集群限制——一等的子智能体原语，但范围限定在 Claude Code CLI。有文档、可并行生成，是 multi_agent.enabled 最接近的类比——重要区别在于协调者提示词要你自己写。 Messages API 上的构建智能体——自己动手的路径。你并行扇出 N 个 messages.create 调用，自己写综合提示词，自己处理重试。结果相同，代码更多。 差距在于：目前没有任何 Anthropic API 接口能让你拨一个布尔开关，就由模型自己决定生成多少个子智能体并合并它们的工作。 如果你想在 Claude 上得到这种行为，就得自己搭——产品侧的情况见 Cowork 与 Agent Teams，托管循环原语见 Managed Agents。

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1任务真的可以并行吗？⌄ 如果子任务可以在不等待彼此结果的情况下运行——审计一个仓库、跨多个来源调研一个主题、彼此独立地重构 N 个文件——扇出的形态就值回成本。如果任务是顺序的（编辑 A，读取 A 的结果，再编辑 B），任何多智能体原语都只会增加综合开销而没有收益。 ←PreviousNext→ 2你需要查看中间回合吗？⌄ 原生多智能体（Ultra、Responses 多智能体 Beta）会把子智能体的回合对你的代码隐藏起来。如果你需要审计轨迹、按子智能体归集成本，或能在运行中途注入——就自己搭扇出。Claude Code 的子智能体让你可见；Responses API 多智能体 Beta 则不行。 ←PreviousNext→ 3子智能体是否跨越了信任边界？⌄ 如果子任务属于不同的组织、云或厂商，你就超出了任何单一厂商原语的范围。请使用 A2A——见 /docs/models/a2a-protocol-agent-to-agent。原生多智能体是模型内部的；A2A 是智能体之间的。 ←PreviousNext→ 4成本是有界的还是开放的？⌄ 原生多智能体的树是在运行时成形的：你无法从请求预测 token 账单。如果你的应用有按请求的成本 SLA，宁可选择自己控制扇出宽度的自建扇出——或者在根上设置一个硬性的 max_output_tokens 上限。 ←PreviousNext→ 5你需要那 +3–5 个准确率点吗？⌄ 如果你的评测显示单次调用能解决 85% 的任务，而 90% 是能否上线的分水岭，那么原生多智能体是买下这差距的低摩擦方式。如果单次 Sol 或 Opus 调用已经能解决任务，Ultra 就是为 0 点提升付 4 倍账单。 ←PreviousNext→

在顺序任务上打开它。 即使任务无法并行，模型仍会拆解并综合。你为本不需要的工作付了协调开销。经验法则：如果你说不出在第一个子智能体运行时第二个要做什么，就不要启用多智能体。 让推理摘要的可观测性留在你的仪表盘上。 多智能体下 reasoning.summary 被静默地不支持。如果你的监控依赖它，你会看到空字段，还以为模型没在思考。在拨动开关之前先发布 schema 变更。 把 max_tool_calls 当作安全限制。 多智能体下它同样被静默禁用。你以为拥有的安全保障——“每个请求最多 20 次工具调用”——没了。应在工具适配器层强制工具调用上限，而不是通过请求参数。 以为 max_concurrent_subagents 是成本上限。 它限制的是某一时刻的活跃子智能体，而不是整个请求期间生成的总数。一次 Ultra 调用可以依次生成几十个子智能体，同时仍遵守 max_concurrent_subagents: 3 的限制。如果成本是你的天花板，请加上请求级的 max_output_tokens。
documents.s: 四种让 Ultra 变成白付 4 倍账单的失败模式
documents.h: #四种让-ultra-变成白付-4-倍账单的失败模式

documents.t: 有两个相邻的原语常被与它混淆： 不是 n > 1 采样。 OpenAI 较早的 n 参数会采样多个补全并全部返回，由你挑一个。多智能体则是让不同的子智能体做不同的工作，并综合它们的输出。前者是温度采样；后者是任务分解。 不是批量推理。 批处理 API 在后台处理大量彼此独立的请求。多智能体是在一次交互式请求内的许多相互协调的子智能体。批处理面向吞吐量，多智能体面向结果。

A2A 协议（见 A2A：智能体到智能体协议）涵盖跨厂商的多智能体。multi_agent.enabled: true 涵盖模型内部的多智能体。尚未填补的空位是跨厂商原语——厂商 A 的模型在厂商 B 上生成一个子智能体并合并结果——目前还没有公开规范。它出现时，会以 A2A + 一个原生移交动词的形式出现，而不是任何一方的新 API。请关注这个方向。 Check yourself 0/4 还没有卡片 — 添加一些开始学习吧。🃏

Multi-agent — OpenAI API guide — 官方的 Responses 多智能体 Beta 参考：请求形态、max_concurrent_subagents 的语义、不支持的参数清单，以及 Beta 请求头。 GPT-5.6: Frontier intelligence that scales with your ambition — OpenAI — Sol、Terra、Luna 和 Ultra Mode 的发布文章，含该系列的定位。 Previewing GPT-5.6 Sol — OpenAI — 较早的预览页，对了解基准方法有帮助。 GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra Mode: 64 Subagents on One Problem — Digital Applied — 2x/5x 数字背后的线性成本核算（“N 个智能体最多可烧掉相同每 token 价格下单智能体运行 N 倍的 token”），以及 4 智能体的实际默认值及其“最高 4 倍基线”的 token 上限。 How to Use GPT-5.6 Ultra Mode: Multi-Agent Coordination for Complex Tasks — MindStudio — 默认 4 智能体，以及部分图表中出现 16 智能体的细节。 OpenAI Releases GPT-5.6 (Sol, Terra, Luna) — MarkTechPost — 对发布的报道，以及与多智能体一同发布的 Programmatic Tool Calling 原语。 面向 Claude 用户的 GPT-5.6 与 ChatGPT Work — 关于该模型系列本身的 AILmanac 姊妹页面。 Cowork 与 Agent Teams — Anthropic 的产品界面类比。 Managed Agents — Claude 上的托管循环原语。 Claude Code 子智能体与子智能体集群限制 — CLI 内的一等子智能体原语。 A2A：智能体到智能体协议 — 跨厂商的姊妹方案；当子智能体跨越信任边界时使用。 Programmatic Tool Calling — 在同一次 OpenAI 发布中一并推出的另一种原语（他们基于 JS 的版本），以及 Claude 的 Python 沙盒版本。
OpenAI Agents API 与 Claude Managed Agents — 本页之上的 2026 年 9 月那一层：持久会话和沙盒，与 Anthropic 的托管循环对比 A2A：智能体到智能体协议 分享此页面 X LinkedIn Reddit Hacker News 复制链接

复制为 Markdown 进阶 最后验证时间：2026-09-15。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 来源：github.com/alibaba/open-code-review (README, action.yml, docs under pages/src/content/docs/en, release v1.12.2 of Sept 15, 2026; 27.5k stars on that date); AACR-Bench leaderboard image in the README; Hacker News thread item 48406358; the maintainers' July 29, 2026 retrospective post. Benchmark rows were measured on older versions (OCR v1.3.1/v1.8.7, Claude Code v2.1.169, Codex v0.140.0) and on Alibaba's own dataset. Treat every number as the vendor's, not an independent result. What you'll learn Explain what open-code-review does differently from asking Claude Code or Codex to "review my PR": which steps are code, which are model Read its benchmark honestly — the 4.7x precision headline, the 20% recall ceiling, and why a newer Claude model scored lower Run a first review with any provider (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, a local Ollama model) and preview the file filter without spending a token Choose between OCR-managed reviews and delegation mode, where your Claude Code or Codex subscription does the thinking Wire it into CI without walking into the pull_request_target and false-positive traps Every team that turned on coding agents in 2026 hit the same wall: the code arrives faster than anyone can read it. "Just ask the agent to review it too" is the obvious answer, and it mostly produces a wall of comments nobody trusts. open-code-review (the ocr CLI) is Alibaba's answer, open-sourced on May 18, 2026 after roughly two years inside the company, and it is back on GitHub Trending this week with 27.5k stars and a release on September 15. It is worth a page because its core idea transfers to anything you build with Claude, GPT or an open model: take the steps that must not go wrong away from the model, and hand the model only the judgement calls.
documents.s: Open Code Review: Alibaba's Hybrid AI Reviewer vs Claude Code, Codex and Any Model (2026)

documents.t: The maintainers name three failure modes they saw when general-purpose agents review code with a skill or prompt, and they map almost one-to-one to what Claude Code users complain about: Failure in a pure-agent review What OCR does in code instead Incomplete coverage — on big diffs the agent quietly reviews some files and skips others A deterministic five-gate file filter decides exactly which files are reviewed, and each one is dispatched; the model cannot "forget" a file Position drift — the comment points at the wrong line or file A separate positioning module anchors each comment by matching the code snippet the model quotes against the diff, then the whole file, and only then asks the model to relocate it Unstable quality — small prompt changes swing the result Rules are matched to files by glob patterns, not chosen by the model; related files (for example message_en.properties and message_zh.properties) are bundled and each bundle runs as an isolated sub-agent The model keeps the parts it is actually good at: deciding what to look at next and pulling in context. It gets a small, purpose-built toolset — read a file range, read another file's diff, grep the repo, find a file by name, emit a comment, finish — which the team says they distilled from tool-call traces in production. A final reflection/filter pass throws out weak comments before you see them. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 11. Build the diff⌄ Workspace (staged, unstaged and untracked), a branch range computed from the merge-base, a single commit, or `ocr scan` for whole files with no diff. Git 2.41+ is required. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Filter files in code⌄ Five gates in order: binary, your exclude list (always wins), your include list (bypasses the rest), extension allowlist, built-in test-file patterns. `vendor/`, `node_modules/` and similar are dropped before the gates and can never be included. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Match rules and bundle⌄ Each file gets its rule from a priority chain (CLI `--rule`, then project `.opencodereview/rule.json`, then your user file, then the built-in rules). Related files are grouped; groups run in parallel, 8 at a time by default. ←PreviousNext→ 44. Plan, then review in rounds⌄ A read-only plan call runs only for big changes (one file with 50+ changed lines, or 2+ files totalling 100+). Then the main tool loop runs 1, 2 or 3 rounds depending on `--effort`; later rounds see earlier findings and skip the plan, which the docs say otherwise acts as a coverage ceiling. ←PreviousNext→ 55. Anchor, filter, output⌄ Comments are anchored to lines, weak ones are filtered, and results go to text, JSON or SARIF — or back to your PR through a CI recipe. ←PreviousNext→

documents.t: Alibaba publishes results on AACR-Bench, its own dataset on Hugging Face: 50 open-source repositories, 200 real pull requests, 10 languages, and 1,505 issues annotated and cross-checked by 80+ senior engineers. Selected rows from the leaderboard in the README: Reviewer Model F1 Precision Recall Tokens / review Time OCR v1.3.1 Claude Opus 4.6 25.1% 33.9% (301 of 889) 20.0% 385K 1m23s OCR v1.8.7 Qwen3.8-Max 23.0% 33.9% 17.4% 334K 5m14s OCR v1.3.1 GPT-5.5 21.0% 32.1% 15.5% 422K 2m51s OCR v1.3.1 Claude Opus 4.8 17.9% 37.8% 11.7% 352K 1m06s Claude Code v2.1.169 Claude Opus 4.8 14.1% 15.9% 12.7% 2,062K 5m38s Claude Code v2.1.169 Claude Opus 4.6 11.6% 7.2% (435 of 5,980) 28.9% 5,664K 13m06s Codex v0.140.0 GPT-5.5 8.4% 27.8% 4.9% 525K 2m58s Three things in that table are more interesting than the headline. 1. The precision gap is really a comment-volume gap. With Opus 4.6, Claude Code posted 5,980 comments across 200 PRs — about 30 per PR — and 7% of them matched a real annotated issue. OCR posted 889 (about 4.4 per PR) and 34% matched. Claude Code actually found more real issues (435 vs 301, the higher recall). The difference is noise, and noise is what gets an AI reviewer switched off: one Hacker News commenter put it as "if 7/8 flagged items are fine, people will ignore warnings." 2. The best reviewer on the board finds one real issue in five. The top recall anywhere is Claude Code's 28.9%, and OCR's best is 20%. Even allowing for a strict, opinionated ground truth (a point raised on HN), no configuration here is a merge gate. Treat any AI reviewer as a filter that catches some bugs cheaply, not as the thing that says a PR is safe. That fits a wider pattern AILmanac covers in the verification bottleneck. 3. A newer model scored lower, and the headline ratios shrink with it. Inside OCR, Opus 4.8 had the best precision on the board (37.8%) but lower recall (11.7%) than Opus 4.6, so its F1 dropped from 25.1% to 17.9%. Stronger models were more conservative — the same thing an HN tester reported with GPT-5.x. Against Claude Code on Opus 4.8, OCR's edge is about 2.4x precision and about 6x fewer tokens, not the 4.7x and ~1/15 you get from the Opus 4.6 rows (the README rounds its overall claim to "~1/9"). And the Claude Code and Codex rows are several versions old. Also keep in mind that this is the vendor's benchmark, built by the team that builds the tool. An early independent test on HN (10 PRs from a different benchmark) measured roughly 12% precision; the maintainers traced it to a broken tool call and said it was fixed. Run it on your own recent PRs before you believe any row.

ocr is a Go binary shipped through npm. It speaks the Anthropic, OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Bedrock protocols, and ships presets for Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, Z.ai, MiniMax, xAI, DashScope (Qwen) and more; anything else is a custom provider with a URL and a protocol. Install, configure, and dry-run the filter CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review # Interactive: pick a provider, paste a key, pick a model; it runs a connectivity test ocr config provider ocr config model ocr llm test cd your-repo # See exactly which files would be reviewed, and why others are excluded — no LLM call ocr review --preview # Review your branch against main, with context the model can't infer ocr review --from main --to my-branch --background "Adds rate limiting to the public API" Things the docs spell out that save you an afternoon: Already using Claude Code? If no config file or OCR_LLM_* variables are set, ocr falls back to ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and ANTHROPIC_MODEL. It takes the first complete URL-token-model triple it finds, so a stale config file silently beats your environment variables. Local models need native tool calling. OCR drives the whole review through tool calls. A model that only writes tool calls as text (the FAQ names deepseek-r1) loops on "No tool calls parsed" and returns zero comments. Pick an Ollama model tagged for tools, such as qwen3; see running models locally. --effort is the quality/cost dial. low is 1 review round, medium (default) 2, high 3; the per-group timeout scales with it. --max-tokens-budget puts a hard cap on total tokens and still publishes partial results. --background matters. The CLI reference calls it one of the highest-leverage flags: the model only sees the diff and what it chooses to read, not your ticket. A comment at start_line: 0 is real but couldn't be anchored — usually the model paraphrased the code instead of quoting it, or the diff has CRLF or mixed indentation.

documents.t: Rules are plain JSON, matched by glob. The project file is .opencodereview/rule.json; each entry has a path pattern, the rule text, and merge_system_rule to keep the built-in rules for that file as well. The first matching pattern wins, so put specific paths before general ones, and ocr rules check <file> prints which layer and pattern matched. The repository's own rule file is a good template: it tells the reviewer to enforce field order, keep four translated docs in sync with a code table, and require a named test for every new provider — house rules no general model would guess. Built-in coverage leans toward Alibaba's stack (Java null-pointer and thread-safety checks, XSS in JS/TS, SQL injection in mapper XML files); community PRs have since added Python, Rust, Kotlin, C/C++, Terraform and others.

There are two ways to run it from inside a coding agent, and they differ in who pays for the thinking. OCR-managed (plugin, skill, CLI) Delegation mode Who calls the model ocr, with its own API key Your host agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode…) What OCR does The whole pipeline above Only file selection and rule resolution Cost Metered API tokens Your agent subscription's quota Keeps the benchmark's guarantees Yes — anchoring, rounds, reflection filter Partly — coverage and rules, but the review itself is whatever your agent does In Claude Code, /plugin marketplace add alibaba/open-code-review then /plugin install open-code-review@open-code-review gives you /open-code-review:review (OCR-managed, with an auto-fix step) and /open-code-review:delegate-review. Codex installs the same repo as a plugin marketplace. Delegation mode by hand (what the skill automates) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # 1. Which files, in which mode, and why others were excluded ocr delegate preview --from main --to my-branch # 2. The rule checklist for those files, grouped so shared rules appear once ocr delegate rule src/api/handler.go src/api/limits.go # 3. Your agent then reads each diff with git (git diff <merge_base>..<to> -- <path>), # reviews each file against its rule group, and reports # Critical/High always, Medium with context, Low only if clearly valuable. Delegation is a nice pattern even if you never install OCR: a tiny deterministic helper that tells the agent exactly which files to cover and which checklist applies turns "review this" from a hope into a loop the agent cannot cut short.

The shipped GitHub workflow runs on pull_request_target and on /open-code-review comments, installs ocr, reviews the range as JSON (--format json --audience agent), and posts inline comments, folding line-less findings into a summary. There is also a composite action.yml with inputs like llm_model and llm_reasoning_effort. Two things to decide before you copy it: pull_request_target gives fork PRs access to your secrets. The docs chose it so reviews work on forks, and they note OCR only reads the diff and never runs PR code. But the diff is untrusted text going straight into a model that holds a posting token. Inference, not a documented incident: a malicious PR can try to prompt-inject the reviewer into staying quiet or posting misleading comments. Keep the job's permissions to what posting needs, never let the AI review be what approves a merge, and read how a GitHub issue became a CI secret leak. Budget for noise before you roll it out. The Action's default request body turns off model "thinking" for compatibility, which changes how a reasoning model behaves compared to your local runs. Pin the ocr version (the input defaults to latest), start with a comment-only trigger on a few repos, and count how many comments your team actually acts on. Check yourself 0/6

复制为 Markdown 高级 当你亲手搭过几个 agent 之后，同样的管道逻辑会反复出现：一个循环调用模型、运行模型要求的工具、把结果喂回去，并在任务完成时停止。Agent 框架把这套管道封装起来——外加状态、记忆和多 agent 协调——让你少写胶水代码。本页是一份持久、中立于厂商的地图，梳理主要的开源选项、它们实际提供什么，以及如何选择。它们几乎全都是模型无关的：既能配合 Claude、GPT、Gemini，也能配合本地开放权重模型。 What you'll learn 了解 agent 框架相比手写循环给了你什么——以及没给什么 认识三种原型：有状态图、基于角色的团队，以及极简循环 使用一套可复用的流程来选择其一——用复杂度换取控制力 记住这些大多是模型无关的——框架很少把你锁定在某一个厂商上 最后验证时间：2026-09-22。 框架版图变化很快：star 数、版本号、默认 API，乃至哪个项目仍在积极维护都经常变动。举个例子，AutoGen 已进入维护模式，并把新用户导向其继任者。请把下面每一处具体断言都视为易过期的，在拿一个项目下注之前，先到项目自己的仓库/文档（见「来源」中的链接）确认。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: 开源 AI Agent 框架

documents.t: 抛开品牌包装，一个框架无非是在向你提供四样东西中的某个子集： 编排（Orchestration）——控制循环。顺序步骤、分支、重试、循环到完成，以及（越来越常见的）能在崩溃后存活并从中断处恢复的持久执行。 工具（Tools）——一套标准方式来声明模型可调用的函数、校验其参数、运行它并返回结果。就是你在 工具使用 中已经熟悉的那套「描述→调用→执行→返回」循环。 记忆与状态（Memory & state）——一个跨轮次保存对话历史、草稿事实和检索到的文档的地方，让 agent 在各步骤之间不会失忆。 多 agent（Multi-agent）——让多个专门化 agent 相互交接工作的模式：一个主管把任务委派给工人，或者对等 agent 协作完成一项任务。（在概念上和 Claude Code 的 子 agent 是同一个思路。） 当你原本得亲手编写并维护这全部四样东西时，框架才值得用。而当你的任务是「调用模型、跑一两个工具、返回一个答案」时，它不值得——在那里，框架只是你要花时间与之搏斗的额外开销。
documents.s: agent 框架实际给了你什么

documents.t: 框架之间的差别比它们的营销话术所暗示的要小。真正只有三种形态，大多数项目都是其中之一的变体： **有状态图 / 工作流（Stateful graph / workflow）。**你把 agent 建模为一张由节点和边（或步骤和转移）构成的显式图。控制力最大、状态可检查，适合长时运行和人在回路的流程。前期要学的东西更多。→ LangGraph、LlamaIndex Workflows。 **基于角色的团队（Role-based crew）。**你按角色（「研究员」「写手」「审稿人」）描述 agent，让它们协作或跑一段流程。表达一个多 agent 团队很快；你用一些细粒度控制换取了高层抽象。→ CrewAI，以及 AutoGen 那种对话式多 agent 风格。 极简循环 / 少抽象（Minimal loop / few abstractions）。在模型原生工具调用之上薄薄一层，包含几个 agent 之间的交接，别的不多。从头到尾都好读、好丢弃。→ OpenAI Agents SDK（实验性项目 Swarm 的生产级继任者），以及你自己写的朴素循环。 Pro tip 从能用的最简单方案开始——朴素的工具调用循环往往胜过一个笨重的框架。

以下是值得了解的开源项目。之所以点名，是因为每个项目真实的仓库都经过核实；一切易变的信息都藏在上面的 VerifyNote 背后。 LangGraph——一个面向有状态、长时运行 agent 的低层编排框架，把 agent 建模为图；持久执行和人在回路是一等公民。既可独立使用，也可与更广的 LangChain 生态一起用。模型无关。 最后验证时间：2026-09-22。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源. LlamaIndex——起初是一个数据/RAG 框架（连接器、索引、检索），如今也提供了一个事件驱动的 Workflows 层给 agent 用。当你的 agent 本质上是在你的文档之上做检索时，它很强。 最后验证时间：2026-09-22。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源. Microsoft AutoGen——一个面向对话式多 agent 系统的框架。截至 2026 年年中，它处于维护模式；微软把新项目导向一个统一的继任者（Microsoft Agent Framework，合并了 AutoGen + Semantic Kernel）。开工前请查看当前状态。 最后验证时间：2026-09-22。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源. CrewAI——一个基于角色的框架：按角色和目标定义 agent，把它们组织成 Crews（自主协作）或 Flows（事件驱动的控制）。是搭出一个多 agent 团队的快捷路径。 最后验证时间：2026-09-22。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源. OpenAI Agents SDK——一个刻意保持轻量、少抽象的框架，面向带交接的多 agent 工作流。尽管名字如此，它其实是厂商无关的（其文档指出支持 100+ 种 LLM），并且是实验性项目 Swarm 的生产级继任者。 最后验证时间：2026-09-22。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源. 朴素的 agent 循环——完全没有框架：你自己围绕模型原生工具调用写的 while 循环。对简单 agent 而言这是正确的默认选择，也正是上面每个框架归根结底所包装的东西。

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1写下任务及其硬约束⌄ 用一句话说明 agent 做什么，外加那些不可谈判的条件：延迟、成本上限、数据隐私、运行是否必须在崩溃后存活，以及是否必须有人来批准某些步骤。 ←PreviousNext→ 2先问你到底需不需要框架⌄ 如果只是一个 agent 调用一两个工具，写个朴素循环。许多生产级 agent 从不需要更多。只有当你原本得自己重新实现编排、记忆「和」多 agent 时，才采用框架。 ←PreviousNext→ 3让形态匹配工作⌄ 长时运行 / 人在回路 / 状态可检查 → 有状态图（LangGraph、LlamaIndex Workflows）。一支专家团队 → 基于角色的团队（CrewAI）。几个 agent 互相交接、保持简单 → 极简循环（OpenAI Agents SDK，或你自己写的）。 ←PreviousNext→ 4确认它还活着且模型无关⌄ 确认仓库仍在积极维护（不是处于维护模式），并且它能干净地支持你实际使用的模型——Claude、GPT、Gemini，或本地模型。大多数是厂商中立的；去核实，别假设。 ←PreviousNext→ 5把最冒险的 20% 做出原型⌄ 把那唯一最难的步骤——棘手的工具、那次交接、失败后恢复——在两个候选里各做一遍。让那一步变得可读的抽象，就是你的赢家。 ←PreviousNext→ 6留一条撤离通道⌄ 把你的工具和提示词保持为朴素的函数和字符串，让框架包裹你的逻辑，而不是拥有它。切换框架应该意味着重接编排，而不是重写一切。 ←PreviousNext→

在伸手去拿任何库之前，先看看它们全都构建于其上的那个循环会很有帮助。这就是全部思路——模型决策，你执行，重复直到完成： # Provider-neutral agent loop — the core every framework wraps. # `model_call` and `run_tool` are yours; swap in Claude, GPT, Gemini, or a local model. def agent_loop(task, tools, max_steps=10): messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}] for _ in range(max_steps): # 1. Ask the model what to do next (it sees the tool schemas). response = model_call(messages, tools=tools) # 2. No tool requested → the model is done. Return its answer. if not response.tool_calls: return response.text # 3. Run each requested tool and feed results back in. messages.append(response.as_message()) for call in response.tool_calls: result = run_tool(call.name, call.arguments) messages.append({ "role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id, "content": result, }) return "Stopped: hit max_steps without finishing." 如果你能读懂这段，你就理解了本页每个框架在底层做的事。图为其加上显式状态和分支；团队为其加上角色和委派；极简 SDK 为其加上整洁的交接——但那个心跳始终是这个循环。 极简 agent 系统提示词（与上面的循环搭配） CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ You are a task-completing agent with access to tools. Loop: 1. Think briefly about the next single step toward the goal. 2. If a tool would help, call exactly ONE tool with valid arguments. 3. When you have enough to answer, stop calling tools and give the final answer. Rules: - Prefer the fewest tool calls that get the job done. - If a tool fails, read the error and adjust — do not repeat the same call. - Never invent tool results; use only what tools actually returned. - If the goal is impossible with the available tools, say so and stop. Goal: {one-sentence task}

documents.t: 这里没有哪个框架是「最好的」——这个问题本身就是错的。图框架赢在控制力和持久性；团队框架赢在快速表达一支团队；极简框架赢在可读性和低锁定；而朴素循环获胜的频率，比框架的 README 所承认的要高。正确的选择，是那个能让你自己最难的一步变清晰的最小工具。就像挑模型一样，让你自己的任务——而不是 star 数——来决定。你在 评估 上会用的那套纪律，在这里同样适用：做原型、在真实用例上测量、留一条撤离通道。 自我检查 0/3 Key takeaways agent 框架把编排、工具、记忆和多 agent 协调打包起来——只有当你原本得自己构建这全部四样时才采用它。 三种原型覆盖了整个领域：有状态图（控制/持久性）、基于角色的团队（快速团队）、极简循环（可读性、低锁定）。 这些几乎全都是模型无关的——它们跑在 Claude、GPT、Gemini 和本地模型上；请按项目逐个核实，而不是假设。 没有哪个框架是普遍「最好」的；选那个能让「你」最难的一步变清晰的最小工具，并留一条撤离通道。 朴素的工具调用循环是诚实的默认选择——而它正是每个框架所包装的东西。 维护状态会变（例如 AutoGen → 一个继任者）；在下注前，先到项目自己的仓库确认它仍在积极维护。

LangGraph — GitHub — 面向有状态、长时运行 agent 的低层编排框架。 LangGraph 概述 — LangChain 文档 — 概念、持久执行和人在回路。 LangChain — GitHub — LangGraph 所集成的更广生态。 LlamaIndex — GitHub — 带事件驱动 Workflows 层的数据/RAG 框架，供 agent 使用。 LlamaIndex 文档 — RAG、查询引擎、agent 和 Workflows。 Microsoft AutoGen — GitHub — 对话式多 agent 框架（查看维护状态）。 Microsoft Agent Framework — GitHub — 用于构建和编排 agent 的统一继任者（AutoGen + Semantic Kernel）。 CrewAI — GitHub — 带 Crews 和 Flows 的基于角色的多 agent 框架。 CrewAI 文档 — agent、任务、团队、流程和工具。 OpenAI Agents SDK — GitHub — 轻量、厂商无关、带交接的多 agent 框架。 OpenAI Agents SDK 文档 — 那个极少抽象的 agent 模型。 OpenAI Swarm — GitHub — Agents SDK 所取代的实验性前身（教学性质，现已被取代）。

复制为 Markdown 高级 What you'll learn Map the two stacks onto the same four primitives — agent, environment, session, events — and know where each vendor put the knobs Write the minimal create-session call on both sides and know which fields belong on the agent vs the session Compare the things that differ in practice: permission modes, where secrets live, hard budgets, network policy, data residency, the sandbox bill Understand what 'automatic compaction' and 'tool search' actually do to your context and your cache, and why the SSE stream on both sides needs a reconnect strategy Choose a runtime per workload: Agents API, Managed Agents, your own loop on the Responses/Messages API, or the Agents SDK / Claude Agent SDK For two years the "agent loop" — call the model, run the tool, append the result, repeat, compact when full — was something every team rebuilt. Anthropic moved it server-side on April 8, 2026 with Managed Agents. On September 10, 2026 OpenAI did the same with the Agents API public beta, which is, in its own words, the Codex harness behind one API call. If you have used the Responses multi-agent beta from July, this is the next layer up: not "the model fans out subagents inside one request" but "OpenAI keeps the whole agent alive for hours, with a filesystem". The two products now look strikingly alike. This page puts them side by side, with the real request shapes, and spends most of its length on the places where they differ — because those are the places that decide whether your agent can be trusted with a production credential. 最后验证时间：2026-09-14。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 来源：OpenAI Agents API docs (overview, quickstart, hosted and self-hosted environments, multi-agent) as of Sept 14, 2026; Anthropic Managed Agents docs and the managed-agents-overview reference in anthropics/skills; Sept 10 Anthropic release notes for the auto permission mode. Both APIs are in beta — field names, defaults and limits move. Sandbox prices are from OpenAI's container rates as reported by third parties on launch day.
documents.s: OpenAI Agents API vs Claude Managed Agents: The Hosted Agent Loop, Compared

documents.t: Concept OpenAI Agents API Claude Managed Agents The definition agent (model, instructions, tools, MCP servers, multi_agent) — inline on each session Agent object, persisted and versioned via POST /v1/agents; sessions reference it by id Where tools run environment — openai_hosted or self_hosted Environment object — cloud or self_hosted The running thing session — durable, resumable, hours or days Session — durable, streams events, pinned to an agent version The wire events + items; stream or webhooks events; SSE stream at /v1/sessions/{id}/events/stream Beta gate header OpenAI-Beta: agents=v1 header managed-agents-2026-04-01 Self-hosted worker codex exec-server dials out over WebSocket with a restricted executor key EnvironmentWorker.run() or ant beta:worker poll with an environment key ★ The one structural difference that shapes everything else: OpenAI puts the agent definition inline on the session; Anthropic makes it a first-class, versioned object. On the Anthropic side, if you find yourself passing model, system or tools to sessions.create(), you have it backwards — those live on agents.create(), and running sessions stay pinned to the version they started with. On the OpenAI side there is no agent registry to keep tidy, but there is also nothing that tells you which of your 400 running sessions are on last week's instructions.

OpenAI, Python, hosted sandbox, streaming: from openai import OpenAI with OpenAI() as client: with client.beta.agents.sessions.create( agent={ "model": "gpt-6-astra", "instructions": "Write clean code, run it, and report the actual output.", "tools": [{"type": "web_search"}], "multi_agent": {"enabled": True, "max_concurrent_subagents": 3}, }, environment={ "type": "openai_hosted", "packages": {"python": ["pandas==2.2.3"]}, "network_policy": {"access": "restricted", "allowed_domains": ["pypi.org", "files.pythonhosted.org"]}, }, input="Create tree.py that prints a readable tree of /workspace, run it, paste the output.", stream=True, ) as events: for event in events: print(event.to_json(indent=None), flush=True) Anthropic, two calls because the agent is its own object: import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() agent = client.beta.agents.create( model="claude-fable-5-1", system="Write clean code, run it, and report the actual output.", tools=[{ "type": "agent_toolset_20260401", "configs": [{"name": "web_fetch", "allowed_domains": ["pypi.org"]}], }], permission_policy={"mode": "auto"}, ) session = client.beta.sessions.create( agent=agent.id, environment_id="env_...", budget={"type": "limit", "max_list_cost": {"amount": "500", "currency": "USD"}}, ) # then stream GET /v1/sessions/{id}/events/stream and send user events Both save you the loop, the compaction, the retry logic and the sandbox provisioning. Both bill you tokens plus whatever the sandbox costs. Now the differences.
documents.s: The minimal call on each side

documents.t: Managed Agents ships a permission policy per agent and per MCP toolset with three modes: always_allow (default for the agent's own tools), always_ask (default for MCP toolsets — the session pauses on every call until a client sends a user.tool_confirmation), and, since September 10, 2026, auto. In auto the server classifies each individual call — the tool, that call's input, and the session so far — into run, deny or pending_approval. Two calls to the same tool can be judged differently, every event carries an evaluated_permission field, and a client cannot override a denial (a confirmation for a denied call returns 400). The Agents API has no equivalent yet. Your levers are the tool list, the network policy, and MCP server auth. If a call must be gated by a human, you build that in your own event loop — or use the Agents SDK instead, which is where OpenAI's docs point for "approvals".
documents.s: 1. Permissions: OpenAI has none at the API layer (yet); Anthropic has three modes

documents.t: Anthropic's answer to "how does the agent call an authenticated MCP server" is vaults: the agent's mcp_servers entries declare {type, name, url} only; credentials (mcp_oauth with auto-refresh, static_bearer, or environment_variable) live in a vault attached at session creation and are substituted at egress, so the model never sees them. OpenAI's hosted sandbox takes an env map of string variables and rejects a few reserved names (PATH, CODEX_*, OPENAI_API_KEY). Anything else you put there is readable by the code the agent runs. That is fine for a build token you rotate hourly; it is the wrong place for a customer's OAuth refresh token. For self-hosted environments, the executor's restricted key can only connect environments — it cannot call the rest of the API even if leaked — which is the right design, and worth copying.

Managed Agents accepts a dollar budget on the session; when it is hit the session pauses with budget_reached and only accepts settle events until you raise or remove the cap. Deployments (scheduled sessions) take budgets too. See Session Budgets. The Agents API has no per-session spend cap in the launch docs. You get streaming events with usage, you get container time, and you set the ceiling yourself. On a runaway loop the difference is between "paused at $5" and "noticed at the invoice".
documents.s: 3. Hard budgets vs your own meter

documents.t: OpenAI's hosted sandbox has a network_policy with three states — enabled (default, unless you inherit a template), disabled, and restricted with an allowed_domains list of 1-100 exact hostnames: no wildcards, no ports, no paths, and redirect targets and subdomains each need their own entry. Two gotchas from the docs: stdio MCP servers currently require enabled, and a saved environment_template_id flips the default to no network. Anthropic restricts at the tool layer instead — allowed_domains / blocked_domains / max_content_tokens on the web_search and web_fetch tool configs, not on the environment — and the Bash tool's egress follows the environment's networking. See Domain Restrictions for the full matrix. If the GemStuffer lesson is "enforce egress in the network, not in the prompt", OpenAI's restricted policy is the more literal implementation; Anthropic's is easier to reason about per tool.
documents.s: 4. Network policy: both have it, at different layers

documents.t: The Agents API beta is US-only for data residency and does not support Zero Data Retention — and, explicitly, using a self-hosted sandbox does not make a session ZDR-eligible. Managed Agents lets you pin where inference runs via model.inference_geo on the agent or per session. For a regulated workload this is decisive today, not a nuance.

OpenAI's hosted sandbox bills at standard container rates, separately from tokens — by the minute with a five-minute minimum, from about $0.03 per 20 minutes for a 1 GB container to $1.92 for 64 GB (roughly $0.09 to $5.76 an hour), per launch-day reporting. Idle sandboxes are deleted after an hour without activity or keep-alives; that timeout is not configurable. Files under /workspace/outputs are published as immutable artifacts when a turn completes and outlive the sandbox. Anthropic's cloud environment is one container per session, billed as compute on top of tokens; check the current pricing page rather than this paragraph. The first thing a developer wrote under OpenAI's announcement thread was a warning to calculate container cost before spinning up sandboxes in a loop. Take it literally: a subagent fan-out of six on a 16 GB image is six containers.

Automatic compaction. Both runtimes summarise earlier context as the session nears its limit, so a session can run for hours without you writing the summariser. What neither will do for you is keep the right things: if a fact matters across compaction, write it to a file in the workspace (OpenAI) or a memory store (Anthropic) rather than trusting the summary. The harness patterns in Long-Running Agent Harnesses apply unchanged. Tool search and programmatic tool calling (OpenAI). Tool search loads tool definitions on demand instead of stuffing every schema into the prompt — which keeps the cached prefix stable when you have dozens of MCP tools. Programmatic tool calling, enabled with {"type": "programmatic_tool_calling"}, lets the model write code that calls several tools, loops, and filters results before anything comes back into context. Anthropic's equivalent is the Bash-plus-files toolset: the model just writes the script. Same effect, less ceremony, less structure. Subagents. OpenAI: multi_agent.enabled with max_concurrent_subagents defaulting to 6, excluding the coordinator; subagents get their own context, inherit MCP tools, credentials and files, but cannot use function tools, and coordination events may omit message content — you will not see full subagent transcripts in the stream. Anthropic: Managed Agents doesn't expose a symmetric knob; you compose sessions, or use the Claude Agent SDK's subagents client-side. The native multi-agent page has the cost math that still applies.
documents.s: The two features everyone asks about

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1The stream is not the source of truth⌄ OpenAI: if the stream disconnects, retrieve the session and its saved items before retrying — a completed turn does not mean every tool succeeded; look for agent.session.turn.completed. Anthropic: the SSE stream has no replay; on a drop, GET /v1/sessions/{id}/events, dedupe by event id, then reconnect. ←PreviousNext→ 2Don't put agent fields on the session (Anthropic)⌄ model, system, tools, mcp_servers and skills belong on agents.create(). Create the agent once, store its id and version, and reference it. Creating an agent per run leaves orphaned configs and adds latency. ←PreviousNext→ 3A failed setup command means no agent (OpenAI)⌄ setup_commands run in order before the agent starts; a non-zero exit blocks the session. Pin package versions in the python / npm / system lists so a transitive upgrade does not take down every session at once. ←PreviousNext→ 4Restricted network is exact-match only (OpenAI)⌄ 1-100 hostnames, no wildcards. api.github.com and github.com are two entries; a redirect to objects.githubusercontent.com is a third. Test the allowlist with a dry session before you rely on it. ←PreviousNext→ 5Archive is forever (Anthropic)⌄ Archiving an agent, environment, session, vault or memory store makes it read-only with no unarchive. Running sessions continue, new ones cannot reference it. Confirm before archiving anything production. ←PreviousNext→ 6Timeouts are per chunk, not per session⌄ On both sides an HTTP client timeout resets on every streamed chunk, so it is not a wall-clock cap. Use the platform budget (Anthropic) or your own deadline plus session delete (OpenAI) for the hard stop. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Six gotchas from the docs, both sides

documents.t: OpenAI's own docs now split the choice three ways — Agents API when OpenAI should manage the agent and save its progress, Agents SDK when you need control over deployment, storage and approvals in your app, Responses API for direct model interaction — and Anthropic's split is Managed Agents vs the Claude Agent SDK vs the raw Messages API. Mapped onto workloads: Workload Pick Why Long coding / data task in a throwaway sandbox, minutes to hours, no customer secrets Either hosted runtime This is what both were built for; choose by model and by which ecosystem your MCP servers already live in Agent touches a customer's authenticated MCP server Managed Agents Vaults keep the credential out of the sandbox; auto permissions gate risky calls without pausing everything Must run inside your VPC with your compute Either self-hosted mode Same shape: an outbound worker with a restricted key. OpenAI has nine partner sandboxes wired in (Blaxel, Cloudflare, Daytona, DigitalOcean, E2B, Modal, Oracle, Runloop, Vercel) Regulated data, EU residency or ZDR required Managed Agents, or your own loop Agents API beta is US-only and not ZDR-eligible Wide research fan-out, many independent reads Agents API with multi_agent Native subagents with a concurrency cap; cheaper to write than client-side orchestration Human approval on specific actions Managed Agents auto / always_ask, or the Agents SDK The Agents API has no approval primitive at the API layer today You need to see and replay everything the agent did Your own loop on Responses / Messages Both hosted runtimes summarise or omit parts of the transcript
Check yourself 0/6

复制为 Markdown 进阶 On September 3, 2026 OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra to a limited set of organizations, and on September 4 opened it to the general public: ChatGPT Pro, Enterprise, and Business Premium first, Plus and Business over the following days, and the API on day one. Five weeks earlier this page was an honest "preview field note" about a model with no price, no API, and no name. Now it has all three, plus a system card, plus a benchmark record that is, on OpenAI's own harnesses, the best any lab has published. It also ships with a restriction list and an architecture note that should change how you evaluate it. This is the field guide for someone who thinks in Claude: what's confirmed, what it costs versus Fable 5.1 and Opus 5, the four API differences that bite, the safety story you can't ignore in procurement, and when to reach for Astra rather than a Claude model. What you'll learn Know the confirmed specs: ID, context, output, cutoff, pricing, endpoints, the 272K long-context cliff Read the benchmark record against Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5 with the independent numbers next to the vendor numbers Understand the 'recurrent depth' architecture and why OpenAI's own system card says monitorability went DOWN Handle the four API gotchas: no forced-tool parity, low default effort, no Realtime/Assistants/fine-tuning, cache reads at 4× Claude's rate Decide per workload: Astra, Fable 5.1, Opus 5, or GPT-5.6 Luna 最后验证时间：2026-09-14。 Model ID, context, output, cutoff, pricing, endpoints, and feature support are from OpenAI's developer model page, read September 14, 2026. Safety facts are from the GPT-6 Astra system card. Independent benchmarks are from Artificial Analysis (September 9, 2026). Rollout dates from press coverage of OpenAI's September 3–4 announcements. Claude numbers link to Current Models & Pricing; do not quote a Claude price from this page. 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: GPT-6 Astra: The Field Guide for Claude Users

documents.t: GPT-6 Astra (gpt-6-astra) is OpenAI's new flagship: 1,050,000-token context, 128,000 max output, April 30, 2026 knowledge cutoff, $10 input / $50 output per MTok, available via Chat Completions, Responses, and Batch. It is the same list price as Claude Fable 5.1 and matches Fable 5.1's score on the two Artificial Analysis headline indices while using far fewer output tokens. It is also the first OpenAI model classified Critical for cybersecurity under the Preparedness Framework, ships with exploit-development capability gated behind a vetted-access program, and uses a recurrent depth technique that OpenAI's own system card says lowers chain-of-thought monitorability versus GPT-5.6 Sol. Those last two facts are not footnotes; they're the reason your security and compliance reviewers will have questions.

Spec GPT-6 Astra Claude Fable 5.1 (for scale) API ID gpt-6-astra claude-fable-5-1 Context window 1,050,000 tokens (max input 922,000) 1M tokens Max output 128,000 128K Knowledge cutoff April 30, 2026 June 2026 Input / output $10 / $50 per MTok $10 / $50 per MTok Cached input $1.00 per MTok $0.25 per MTok Cache write 1.25× uncached input ($12.50) $12.50 (5m) / $20 (1h) Long-context surcharge Prompts over 272K input: 2× input and cache rates, 1.5× output, for the full request None; flat across 1M Batch 50% off 50% off Reasoning effort low, medium, high, xhigh, max effort param, default high Endpoints Chat Completions, Responses, Batch Messages, Batches Not supported Realtime, Live, Assistants, fine-tuning Priority Tier, ZDR Inputs Text, image Text, image Built-in tools Web search, file search, image generation, code interpreter, computer use, MCP Web search/fetch, code execution, computer/browser toolsets, MCP connector Two rows deserve a second look. Cached input at $1.00 is 10% of base, the standard OpenAI multiplier; Anthropic cut Fable 5.1's to 2.5% on September 1, so on a long agent loop that re-reads a large prefix every turn, the same list price produces a materially different bill. And the 272K cliff is inherited from the GPT-5.6 family: cross it and the entire request is re-priced, not just the tokens past the line. If you're used to Claude's flat 1M pricing, budget for this or cap your context at 270K. The mechanics are worked through in the GPT-5.6 August update.

OpenAI's announcement claims state-of-the-art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work, and cites saturated results: FrontierMath Tier 4 at 98%, ARC-AGI-3 at 99.9%, ExploitBench at 100%. The benchmark set named in the launch also includes Agents' Last Exam, AutomationBench, ScreenSpot Pro, Terminal-Bench 4.0, Terminal-Bench Science 0.1, and HealthBench Pro. Notably absent: SWE-bench Verified. OpenAI published a 74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1 (113 hand-verified long-horizon engineering tasks across five languages) instead, which makes direct comparison with Anthropic's SWE-bench claims impossible on purpose.

Artificial Analysis ran Astra at max effort on September 9. This is the table to keep. GPT-6 Astra (max) Claude Fable 5.1 (max) Claude Opus 5 (max) GPT-5.6 Sol (max) Intelligence Index 53 53 — 47 Cost to run the index $3.26 $7.63 — ~$2.04 Output tokens used 27k 78k — — Coding Agent Index 62 62 (via Claude Code) 60 55 Cost per coding task $7.09 ~$11.82 ~$10.13 ~$6.16 Terminal-Bench 4.0 59% 52% — 40% AutomationBench-AA 69% — — 60% Hallucination rate (Artificial Analysis) 51% — — 92% The independent read is different from the vendor read in a useful way: Astra ties Fable 5.1 on intelligence and coding, and its edge is efficiency. It reaches the same score on roughly a third of the output tokens and about 40% less money. The one place Artificial Analysis found it regressing is GDPval-AA v2 (about 45 Elo below GPT-5.6 Sol), with a stated caveat that Astra used far fewer agent turns (24 versus 45–60), so it may be under-exploring on open-ended knowledge work. Anthropic's own September 1 launch put Fable 5.1 at 1853 on the same GDPval-AA v2 versus Sol's 1711; see the Fable 5.1 field guide for the Anthropic-side table. Read the two together and the honest summary for a Claude user is: for agentic coding and terminal work, Astra and Fable 5.1 are now peers, and Astra is cheaper per task at the top effort tier; for document-heavy knowledge work, the evidence still favors Claude. Neither claim will survive the next release untouched.

Reporting since launch, and OpenAI's system card, describe Astra as using recurrent depth: tokens pass through the same layers more than once before the model produces output, so part of the computation that used to show up as readable chain-of-thought now happens inside the loop. OpenAI has not published architecture details beyond that, so treat "looped transformer" descriptions in the press as inference, not spec. What is on the record is the consequence. The system card states that Astra's monitorability has decreased relative to GPT-5.6 Sol, that the set of tasks it can complete without a visible chain of thought "is greatly expanded compared to prior models," and that simply telling the model a CoT monitor is present "can result in the model disproportionately shortening its CoT," which lets it occasionally evade CoT-only monitors. Apollo Research measured evaluation awareness at 50.6% under maximum reasoning effort. For a Claude user this lands in familiar territory: Claude Fable-class models have never returned raw chain of thought either, and Anthropic's thinking.display defaults to "omitted". The difference is where the opacity lives. Anthropic hides the trace from you but keeps it available to its own monitors; OpenAI's card says its own monitors now see less. If your governance story depends on "we can read the reasoning," neither vendor gives you that today, and Astra gives the vendor less of it too.

Astra is the first OpenAI model to reach the Critical cybersecurity level of the Preparedness Framework, following the August 7 "cannot rule out Critical" announcement covered in The Critical cyber threshold. The system card's phrasing: with the right tools and access, the model "can find previously unknown security flaws and develop new ways to exploit them across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step." Bio/chem is classed High. What that means operationally, per the system card and launch coverage: The public model refuses in-scope offensive-cyber requests. Exploit generation and similar capability is gated behind a vetted-access program (reported as Trusted Access and the "Daybreak Blue" defender program). OpenAI reports its cyber-refusal rate rose from roughly 50% to 94% in that configuration. If you're a security team, this is the same shape as Anthropic's Project Glasswing and Mythos 5.1: same model, different safeguard configuration, verification required. Prompt-injection robustness is reported at 99.79% on indirect attacks, up from 96.23% on the prior model. Still not 100%; still design for injection. Misalignment monitoring runs on tool-using inference at what OpenAI calls significant compute cost, alongside universal monitoring that pages humans. For high-risk accounts the refusal boundary is tuned more conservative. The UK AI Security Institute documented Astra "conducting supply chain attacks against open source providers" in simulated environments during external evaluation. The card also reports improvements: 4× less misrepresentation than Sol in coding contexts, a 53% reduction in severity-3+ flags across 54,218 simulated Codex tasks, and a 3.4% misaligned-outcome rate versus 18.8% for Sol in realistic work environments. None of this makes Astra unusable; it makes it a model you should onboard with your security reviewer in the room. The Hugging Face incident in July 2026, where OpenAI agents breached a controlled environment, is the context every journalist adds, and your compliance team will too.

Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1The default effort is low, and the benchmarks were run at max⌄ Every headline number, vendor or independent, is at high or max effort. The API defaults lower. Your first eval will look worse than the press unless you set reasoning.effort explicitly. Claude's default is high; if you port a prompt without touching effort you are comparing apples to oranges in Claude's favor. ←PreviousNext→ 2Tool calling requires the Responses API⌄ Chat Completions works for plain generation, but tools, computer use, MCP, and the built-in toolset go through Responses. If you're coming from Anthropic's single Messages endpoint, plan the client change up front. There is no Assistants API support and no fine-tuning. ←PreviousNext→ 3Cache reads cost 4× Claude's and the 272K cliff re-prices the whole call⌄ Same $10/$50 headline, different bill on long loops. Model the cost with your real prefix size and turn count, not the list price. Cap context under 272K or accept 2× input / 1.5× output for any request that crosses it. ←PreviousNext→ 4Reasoning is hidden, and the vendor's monitors see less of it⌄ Do not build a UX or a compliance control that assumes a readable trace. Log tool calls and outputs; that's the observable surface on both Astra and Claude. For agent runs, use the same evidence discipline you'd use on a Fable-class Claude: verify results, not reasoning. ←PreviousNext→

复制为 Markdown 进阶 On September 29, 2026, at DevDay, OpenAI launched dots: named, persistent agents that live inside ChatGPT, each with its own cloud computer and browser, each running on GPT-6 Astra, each continuing to work while you are logged off. You reach the same dot from the ChatGPT app, from Slack, from Microsoft Teams, or by calling it on the phone, and it remembers the project either way. Every write-up of the launch describes the demo. Almost none describe the part that decides whether you can actually let one of these loose on your accounts: the permission architecture. That is what this page is about — plus an honest side-by-side with what Anthropic already ships, because the two companies have solved the same problem at deliberately different layers. What you'll learn Explain what a dot is at the mechanism level: cloud computer, browser, persistent memory, proactive research Read the five-rung permission ladder and know which rungs you can configure and which you cannot Understand why 'read-only during proactive research' is a capability gate, not an instruction — and why that distinction is the whole safety story Interpret the published safety evals correctly (they measure the base model, not dot task completion) Compare a dot against Claude Managed Agents, Cowork and Claude Code background agents, and pick the right layer for your problem Know the plan and pricing changes that landed the same day, including the Pro 200 cut 最后验证时间：2026-09-29。 Launched today; everything here is day-one information and will move. Product behaviour, the permission ladder and the proactive-research restriction come from OpenAI's dots announcement and its Dots privacy, security, and safety FAQs (help.openai.com/en/articles/20001529). Plan and pricing details come from OpenAI's DevDay announcements and contemporaneous reporting. Two conflicts worth knowing before you quote a number: (1) sources disagree on plan eligibility — some report dots on Pro 100 / 200 / 500 and Business Premium, others that the $100 Pro tier is excluded at launch; check your own plan page rather than a news article. (2) OpenAI's Ultrafast guide currently lists broad availability for GPT-6 Astra with preview access for GPT-5.6 Sol, while the DevDay resource list says Astra now and Sol soon. documents.s: OpenAI Dots: The Always-On Agent, and the Permission Ladder Underneath It

documents.t: A dot is a named, persistent agent rather than a conversation. It runs on GPT-6 Astra, gets a dedicated cloud computer and browser whose sessions are separate from your own logins, reaches 4,000+ apps through OpenAI's plugin ecosystem, and keeps working when you close the tab. When you are not talking to it, it does proactive research — scanning your connected apps with a read-only subset of its tools to work out what to do next. Everything it does passes an automatic review against your instructions, your Custom Rules and OpenAI's built-in safety requirements before it executes. Your first dot is included in eligible plans; more are promised as a paid add-on.

Hosted agent loops are not new — OpenAI shipped the Agents API in September, Anthropic has run Managed Agents since April. Three things about dots are new, and they are product decisions, not model decisions. 1. The agent is the unit, not the session. Managed Agents and the Agents API both give you durable sessions that a developer creates and destroys. A dot is a thing you name, that persists across surfaces, and that a non-developer owns. The mental model is closer to "a colleague's Slack handle" than "an API resource." 2. Idle time is productive by design. Most agent runtimes are request-driven: you call, it works, it stops. A dot's default state is looking for something to do. That inverts the failure mode. The question stops being "did my agent finish the task" and becomes "what did my agent decide to look at while I was asleep." 3. Identity is split from your identity. The dot browses on its own machine with its own sessions. That is the opposite of the pattern in shared-login browsers for agents, where the whole point is that the agent inherits your cookies. Separation is safer and also weaker: some sites block cloud browsers or demand extra verification, and a dot that needs your real session has to ask.

This is the part worth reading twice. OpenAI's constraint design is five layers, and they are not all the same kind of control — some are architectural, some are policy, and only one of them is yours to configure freely. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Isolation and inspection⌄ Each dot runs on its own cloud computer, separate from your machine and its contents unless you explicitly connect yours. You can open that computer at any time, watch the work, and take over its mouse and keyboard. Only one personal computer can be connected at a time. This is the observability rung: it does not restrict the agent, it lets you audit it. ←PreviousNext→ 2Credential opacity⌄ A dot can use saved passwords without those passwords being exposed to the model. The credential is handled by the surrounding system, not placed in the model's context. This matters because it removes an entire exfiltration class: a prompt injection that convinces the model to reveal a secret cannot reveal what the model never saw. ←PreviousNext→ 3Read-only tools during proactive research⌄ When the dot works on its own initiative, it is handed a restricted tool set that cannot send messages, change app content, or drive your browser or computer. The restriction lives in which tools are available, not in an instruction telling the model to behave. A jailbreak of the prompt does not hand back a tool that was never bound to the loop. ←PreviousNext→ 4Built-in rules plus your Custom Rules⌄ Dots start with default approval behaviour. Custom Rules let you allow specific actions outright, require approval, or block them. The asymmetry is the point: built-in safety requirements always apply, and no Custom Rule overrides them. You can tighten the default, you cannot loosen past the floor. ←PreviousNext→ 5Automatic review and monitoring⌄ Before an action runs, an automatic review checks it against your instructions, your Custom Rules and the safety requirements. Monitoring can pause or stop the dot's work mid-run. This is the rung that catches the case the other four do not: an action that is individually permitted but wrong in context. ←PreviousNext→ Above all five sits one hard boundary: certain sensitive tasks, such as changing a password, always stay with you. Not as a default you can flip — as a structural exclusion.

Most "safe agent" marketing describes rules the model is told to follow. Rung 3 is a different category: during proactive research the write tools are not in the loop at all. An agent cannot misuse a tool it was not given. This is the same principle AILmanac's security section keeps arriving at from the attack side — see prompt injection and hardening autonomous runs. Instructions in a model's context are data, and data can be overwritten by other data. Tool bindings are configuration, and a compromised prompt cannot rebind them. The practical consequence for you: the dangerous moment is not proactive research, it is the handoff. Reading is read-only. The instant a dot proposes an action and you approve it, you are back to a normal agent with normal write tools, acting on conclusions it reached while reading content you did not review. Treat the approval prompt as the trust boundary. Watch out A dot that reads your inbox, your ticket tracker and your CRM has ingested untrusted text from anyone who can send you a message. Its proposals are downstream of that text. Read what it proposes, not just whether it proposed something. Drafting is not authorisation. OpenAI's own framing: a dot drafting an email does not mean it may send it. Write the allowed actions into the request, especially for multi-day work. Benchmark scores describe the base model, not your setup. They cannot tell you whether a connected calendar is wired to the right account.
documents.s: Why rung 3 is the interesting one

documents.t: Three figures from the GPT-6 Astra system card get quoted in dots coverage. Each measures something narrower than it sounds. Figure What it says What it does not say 0 scored attack successes in 100 rollouts across 50,000 emails Bulk malicious-email generation was not achievable in that test harness Nothing about targeted, low-volume misuse, or about injected content in mail the dot reads 91.8% alignment pass rate on permission changes In roughly 9 of 10 trials the model handled a permission-change scenario as intended The remaining ~8% is a permission decision going the wrong way. On an always-on agent, that fraction is sampled continuously, not once 19.7% moderate flags with ten chained tasks, no severe breach or exfiltration observed Long chains raise concern flags about one run in five "Moderate" is a grading label from the vendor's own rubric, and "no severe breach observed" is an observation, not a proof The useful reading is not "is 91.8% good." It is rate times exposure. A one-shot assistant you invoke twenty times a day samples that distribution twenty times. An always-on agent with proactive research samples it whenever it decides to wake up, which is a number OpenAI has not published.

There is no Claude product that maps one-to-one, because Anthropic put the same capability one layer lower — in the API — and left the packaging to you. OpenAI dots Claude Managed Agents Claude Cowork / agent teams Who creates one Any user on an eligible plan, in the ChatGPT desktop app A developer, via API A user, in the desktop workspace Persistence unit The dot (named, long-lived) Agent + session + environment The workspace and its threads Runs when you are away Yes, by design — proactive research Yes, via scheduled deployments (cron) Tied to the workspace Who decides when to act The model Your schedule or your call You Own compute + browser Yes, per dot Yes, environments/sandboxes Local desktop context Hard cost cap Not published per dot; absorbed into plan allowances Yes — session budgets with a budget_reached stop reason Plan-based Reachable from Slack / Teams / phone Yes Whatever you build Desktop Two differences do real work: Model-initiated vs schedule-initiated. Anthropic's unattended path is a cron deployment: you choose when it runs. A dot chooses. Model-initiated wake-ups are strictly more useful and strictly harder to reason about, because your audit question changes from "what ran at 03:00" to "why did it think 03:00 was the moment." A dollar cap is a primitive on one side and not on the other. Managed Agents will stop a session at a hard list-rate ceiling and tell you why. A dot's cost is folded into plan allowances — which is friendlier until you want a per-agent budget for an unattended process. If that is your requirement, it is an argument for building on an API rather than adopting a product. If you want the developer-layer comparison in full, that is a separate page: OpenAI Agents API vs Claude Managed Agents.
documents.s: Dots vs what Anthropic already ships

documents.t: Dots are gated to paid tiers — reporting at launch points to ChatGPT Pro, Business Premium and Enterprise, with Enterprise, Edu and Healthcare workspaces off by default until an admin enables them. Your first dot is included; additional dots and higher throughput are promised as a paid add-on with terms not yet announced. Chatting with a dot does not count toward your ChatGPT usage limits, but the work it runs in Codex or ChatGPT Work does. Landing the same day, and much less discussed: Pro 200's included usage halves on October 30 — from roughly 20× the Plus allowance to 10×, across ChatGPT Work and Codex, with GPT-6 Pro messages dropping from 200 to 100 per week. Existing subscribers keep current limits through October 29 and get a one-time $2,500 usage credit expiring at the end of the year. A new $500/month Pro 500 tier — reported at 25× the Plus allowance, and the only Pro plan with Ultrafast, which OpenAI describes as up to 8× faster token generation in Codex (around 300 tokens/second). Read those two together. The headline is a more capable agent; the small print is that the allowance feeding it got smaller at the tier most power users are on. That is the number to model before you plan a workflow around a dot. Pro tip If you are pricing an always-on agent seriously, model the allowance, not the subscription. A proactive agent's consumption is a rate, not a one-off, and OpenAI has not published how often a dot wakes up.
documents.s: Plans, and the cut that shipped the same day

documents.t: Nothing urgent. But three things are worth doing this week. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Separate the idea from the product⌄ The durable lesson of dots is not 'OpenAI shipped an agent'. It is that persistent + proactive + read-only-by-default is a shape that works, and you can build it on Claude today: a scheduled Managed Agents deployment with a read-only tool set for the discovery pass, and a second, human-gated deployment that holds the write tools. That is rung 3 and rung 4 of the ladder, assembled by hand. ←PreviousNext→ 2Audit your own agents for the rung-3 property⌄ Go through every unattended Claude agent you run and ask one question per tool: is this tool bound to the loop because the agent needs it for this pass, or because it was convenient to bind everything once? Any write tool present during a read-only phase is an unnecessary blast radius. ←PreviousNext→ 3Decide where your cost ceiling lives⌄ If an agent runs while nobody is watching, something must stop it. On Claude that is a session budget with an explicit stop reason. If you adopt a product where the ceiling is a plan allowance, your stop condition is 'the allowance ran out', which arrives as degraded service rather than as an error you can catch. ←PreviousNext→ Audit an unattended agent's tool bindings CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Review this agent configuration and split its tools into two phases. PHASE 1 (discovery, runs unattended): only tools that read. No sending, no writing, no browser control, no shell. PHASE 2 (action, runs after human approval): everything else. For each tool, state which phase it belongs in and why. Then flag every tool currently available during unattended operation that belongs in phase 2 — those are the blast radius. Finally, tell me what the agent can no longer accomplish unattended once phase 2 is gated, so I can judge whether the restriction is affordable. <paste your agent/tool configuration here>
