复制为 Markdown 高级 On 17 September 2026, PrismML published Ternary Bonsai 2 27B: a 27-billion-parameter model whose weights are only -1, 0 and +1, packed into a 5.95 GB file, released Apache 2.0. The Hugging Face GGUF repo passed 2.5 million downloads inside five days. The headline everywhere was the same — a 27B model that fits on a laptop. The headline is true. Almost everything people assume follows from it is not. Stock llama.cpp will load the file and produce fluent nonsense without raising an error. Ollama and LM Studio refuse it outright. The 5.95 GB file needs roughly 12 GB of VRAM at default settings. The larger 7.21 GB build is faster on a datacenter GPU and slower on a 4090. And the widely-quoted "98.2% of full precision" is an average across fourteen benchmarks that hides a 6-point collapse in multimodal reasoning and, in one independent test, complete failure on low-resource languages. This page is the practical layer: what ternary quantization actually buys you, how to run this model without silently corrupting your output, and how to read a compression retention number honestly. The technique outlives the model — the same reasoning applies to every low-bit release that follows. What you'll learn Understand why ternary weights are 1.75 bits in practice, not the 1.58 bits the theory promises Recognise the silent-garbage failure mode: stock loaders ignore the Hadamard rotation and never error Pick between PTQ1_0 and PQ2_0 using the bandwidth-vs-unpack crossover, not file size Budget real memory: 5.95 GB of weights, ~64 KiB per token of cache, and why defaults blow past 12 GB Read '98.2% retention' correctly — which capabilities survive compression and which quietly do not
documents.s: Ternary Quantization in Practice: Bonsai 2 27B in 5.95 GB

documents.t: A normal model stores each weight as a 16-bit float. A ternary model stores each weight as one of three values — -1, 0, +1 — with a single shared FP16 scale per group of weights. Reconstruction is w = scale_g * t, where t is the trit. Three states need log₂(3) ≈ 1.58 bits. That is the number the research literature uses, from Microsoft's BitNet b1.58 onward. It is not the number you get on disk. Bonsai 2 27B ships at 1.75 bits per weight for its densest build. The extra 0.17 bits per weight is the part nobody explains: Group scales. One FP16 scale per group of 128 weights is 16 bits amortised over 128 weights — 0.125 bits per weight before anything else. Packing waste. Trits do not divide neatly into bytes. Dense packing recovers most but not all of the theoretical density. Unquantized components. Embeddings, output projections and normalisation layers stay at higher precision. On a 27B model these are a small fraction of parameters but a noticeable fraction of bytes. So the real ratio is not 16/1.58 ≈ 10×. It is 53.8 GB → 5.95 GB, or about 9× — which is exactly what the model card reports. Why ternary is fast, and it is not the maths The intuition most people have is that ternary multiplication is cheap: multiplying by -1, 0 or +1 is a sign flip, a skip, or nothing. True, but that is not where the win comes from on real hardware. Token generation is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Every generated token requires streaming the entire weight matrix from memory. Cut the bytes by 9× and you cut the dominant cost by 9×. The arithmetic was never the bottleneck. This matters practically: a CPU or GPU without native ternary support must dequantize back to a normal format to use its existing multiply-accumulate units, which throws away the arithmetic saving while keeping the bandwidth one. Which is why the packing format you pick changes performance in a direction that looks backwards — see below.

This is the single most important thing on this page, and it appears in almost no coverage of the release. Bonsai 2's weights have a blockwise Hadamard rotation folded into storage. A matching inverse transform must be applied to the activations at runtime. The rotation is a standard trick for low-bit quantization — it spreads outlier magnitudes across a block so the ternary grid has less to lose — but it means the stored weights are not directly usable by a loader that does not know about it. A stock llama.cpp build does not know about it. Depending on version it will either reject the tensor types or, worse, load the file successfully and generate fluent, confident, completely wrong output. There is no error, no warning, no degraded-quality flag. The model card states this plainly: stock llama.cpp will not run these files, and standard builds produce garbage because the Hadamard activation transform is missing. Downstream tools inherit the problem in different ways: Runtime Behaviour with Bonsai 2 27B GGUF PrismML's llama.cpp fork (branch prism) Works — the only local GGUF path today Stock llama.cpp Rejects the tensor types, or loads and emits nonsense Ollama Import fails with a tensor size overflow error LM Studio Rejects ggml tensor types 142 and 143 MLX (Apple) Separate mlx-2bit build required; larger footprint The Ollama and LM Studio failures are the safe outcome. The stock-llama.cpp silent success is the dangerous one, because a benchmark script or an eval harness will happily record the nonsense as a result. If you are evaluating a low-bit model, verify the loader first Run one known-answer prompt before you run anything else. If a model that scores 95+ on HumanEval cannot answer "what is 2+2" coherently, you have a loader problem, not a model problem. This applies to every exotic quantization format, not just this one.
documents.s: The trap: stock llama.cpp loads it and lies

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Build PrismML's fork, not mainline⌄ git clone https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp, then cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build -j for NVIDIA. On Apple Silicon drop the CUDA flag — Metal is on by default. On AMD use -DGGML_HIP=ON. The default branch is prism; the README explicitly warns against building from prism-v6 and against mixing this fork's libraries with a stock llama.cpp install on the same machine. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick the right GGUF before downloading 7 GB⌄ PTQ1_0 is 5.95 GB at 1.75 bits per weight — dense trits. PQ2_0 is 7.21 GB at 2.13 bits per weight — each trit gets its own 2-bit slot. Same weights, same quality, different packing. The choice is a throughput decision, not a quality one. See the crossover table below. ←PreviousNext→ 3Download, and check the byte count⌄ hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --local-dir . — PTQ1_0 is 5,946,648,928 bytes and PQ2_0 is 7,206,168,928 bytes. A truncated download is another way to get plausible-looking garbage. Add the mmproj file (629 MB at Q8_0, 931 MB at BF16) only if you need vision. ←PreviousNext→ 4Serve it with an explicit context size⌄ ./build/bin/llama-server -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --alias bonsai-2-27b -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080. The -c flag is not optional in practice: -c 0 defaults to the full 262K window and will try to allocate roughly 16 GB of attention cache before it has generated a single token. ←PreviousNext→ 5Verify with a known-answer call, then wire up your tooling⌄ The server exposes an OpenAI-shaped /v1/chat/completions endpoint, so anything that speaks chat-completions can point at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1. Send one trivial prompt and read the answer with your own eyes before you point an eval harness or an agent loop at it. ←PreviousNext→ 6If PQ2_0 crashes on CPU, disable repacking⌄ PQ2_0 can crash during llama.cpp's CPU repack step. Pass --no-repack, or set LLAMA_ARG_REPACK=0 in the environment. ←PreviousNext→ Minimal end-to-end: build, fetch, serve, verify CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # 1. Fork only — stock llama.cpp will silently produce garbage git clone https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build -j # 2. Fetch (PQ2_0 = 7.21 GB, faster on big GPUs; PTQ1_0 = 5.95 GB, fits 8 GB cards) hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf \ Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --local-dir . # 3. Serve — always set -c explicitly, never leave it at 0 ./build/bin/llama-server -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf \ --alias bonsai-2-27b -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 # 4. Verify the loader BEFORE trusting any output curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"bonsai-2-27b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 2+2? Answer with one number."}]}' # Coherent "4" => loader is correct. Fluent nonsense => wrong build, stop here.

Two builds of the same weights. PTQ1_0 packs trits densely at 1.75 bits. PQ2_0 gives each trit its own 2-bit slot at 2.13 bits — 21% more disk, but the unpacking is far cheaper because slots are byte-aligned. Measured generation throughput, tokens per second: GPU PQ2_0 (7.21 GB) PTQ1_0 (5.95 GB) Winner RTX 5090 129.9 120.5 PQ2_0 RTX 4090 81.2 91.1 PTQ1_0 L4 (24 GB) 29.8 32.1 PTQ1_0 M5 Pro (Metal) 28.1 — — The pattern generalises: PTQ1_0 wins on Ada-generation and lower-end GPUs, PQ2_0 wins on H100, A100 and Blackwell. That is the opposite of the usual quantization rule of thumb, where smaller is always faster. The reason is the bandwidth-versus-unpack tradeoff from earlier. On a bandwidth-starved card, moving 21% fewer bytes dominates and the dense packing wins. On a card with enormous memory bandwidth, bandwidth stops being the constraint and the bit-shuffling cost of dense unpacking becomes the bottleneck instead — so the fatter, byte-aligned format runs faster. Prompt processing tells the same story more loudly: on an RTX 5090, PQ2_0 processes prompts at 3,893 tok/s against PTQ1_0's 1,805 — more than double, because prefill is compute-bound, where unpacking cost hits hardest. Rule of thumb: below 12 GB of VRAM you have no choice, take PTQ1_0. Above it, take PQ2_0 unless you are on a 4090 or an L4, where PTQ1_0 measurably wins.
documents.s: PTQ1_0 vs PQ2_0: the crossover that looks backwards

documents.t: Three different "size" numbers are circulating for this model — 5.9 GB, 7.2 GB and 8.6 GB — and all three are defensible, because they measure different things. Here is the actual budget: Weights: 5.95 GB (PTQ1_0) or 7.21 GB (PQ2_0). Vision projector: +629 MB (Q8_0) or +931 MB (BF16), if you need images. Attention cache: roughly 64 KiB per token. That is ~0.5 GB at 8K context, ~2 GB at 32K, and ~16 GB at the full 262K window. Parallel slots: llama.cpp allocates cache per slot. Defaults allocate several. One independent test measured just over 12 GB of VRAM at default settings, dropping to about 8 GB when the server was restricted to a single parallel slot. The disk footprint they measured — around 7 GB — corresponds to the PQ2_0 build, which is where part of the number confusion comes from. Practical context headroom by card, using PQ2_0 unless noted: VRAM Build Usable context 8 GB PTQ1_0 ~16K tokens (~6K with vision) 12 GB PQ2_0 ~56K tokens 16 GB PQ2_0 ~118K tokens 24 GB PQ2_0 ~240K tokens 32 GB+ PQ2_0 Full 262K window The "runs on a laptop" claim survives all of this — but "runs on a laptop with an 8 GB GPU and a 16K context" is the honest version, and that is a materially different product.
documents.s: File size is not memory requirement

documents.t: PrismML reports an aggregate of 84.78 against the full-precision base model's 86.32 across fourteen benchmarks — the 98.2% figure. Averages are where compression damage goes to hide. The per-benchmark spread: Benchmark Bonsai 2 27B FP16 base Delta AIME26 95.83 94.58 +1.25 MATH-500 98.80 99.80 −1.00 LiveCodeBench 90.07 90.05 +0.02 HumanEval+ 95.12 93.29 +1.83 MMLU-Redux 89.09 91.46 −2.37 MMMU-Pro 75.49 81.73 −6.24 Three things to take from this table. First, the damage is not uniform — it is structural. Maths and code are essentially untouched. Knowledge recall drops (composite knowledge-and-reasoning lands near 79.9 versus 85.6 for full precision). Multimodal reasoning takes the real hit: MMMU-Pro falls 6.24 points, and OCR Bench v2 drops from 60.99 to 56.88. Compression costs you breadth of stored fact, not procedural skill — which is exactly what you would expect when you crush the precision available to store long-tail associations. Second, be suspicious of the positives. The compressed model "beating" its own full-precision base by 1.83 points on HumanEval+ and 1.25 on AIME26 is not evidence that compression helps. It is evidence that these benchmarks have run-to-run variance of a couple of points. Which should also make you discount the small negatives. Third, the vendor's own numbers do not fully agree. The model card's benchmark table aggregates to 84.78, while PrismML's launch post reports an aggregate of 83.9. Both are described as the same 98.2% retention. The discrepancy is small and unexplained; we report it rather than pick one. The failure mode benchmarks did not catch One independent hands-on test found behaviour no benchmark row predicts: asked to translate into low-resource languages including Tamil, the model entered a repetitive loop and never completed the task — worse than the previous Bonsai generation. The same test found it identified a real timezone bug and then talked itself out of the correct conclusion, and failed to produce a working reset button in a small HTML task across three correction rounds. This is the characteristic signature of aggressive quantization: aggregate scores hold, while the long tail — rare languages, long-horizon self-correction — degrades in ways that only show up in use. Community reports also describe recall and coherence degradation past roughly 200K tokens of the advertised 262K window.

There is a parallel effort to get ternary Bonsai into upstream llama.cpp, and its current state is a useful lesson in how low-bit formats fragment. PrismML proposed group-128 ternary packing for the smaller Bonsai models. The llama.cpp maintainer pushed back in favour of group size 64, on the grounds that it costs under 6% extra memory while supporting more tensor shapes and giving better quality. Q2_0 with group-64 became the official format and has been merged into multiple backends including CUDA and Vulkan. PrismML kept their group-128 variants in the fork. So "does llama.cpp support ternary models" has two correct and opposite answers: Yes — Q2_0_g64 builds run on mainline across backends, and the fork's own README points at them as the portable path. No, not for this model — as of verification, the published Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf repo contains F16, PQ2_0, PTQ1_0 and the two mmproj files. There is no Q2_0_g64 build of the 27B. The fork is the only path. Two older ternary formats, TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, already exist in ggml but use group size 256, which is incompatible with how these models are natively packed. TQ2_0 is also the tightest faithful ternary layout in ggml at roughly 2.06 bits per weight — and in current mainline it implements a CPU-only dot product with no CUDA, Metal or Vulkan path. Seeing "ternary supported" in a changelog tells you very little about whether your GPU will use it. For the next low-bit model you evaluate, the question to ask is not is it quantized but which group size, which packing, which backends have kernels, and is there a portable build — because that determines whether you are running on mainline or maintaining someone else's fork.
documents.s: The mainline story, and why it matters for the next release

documents.t: Worth it when: You need a capable maths or coding model on hardware that cannot hold a 27B at higher precision. That is where retention is near-perfect and the value is highest. You are bandwidth-constrained — a laptop GPU, an edge box, a shared L4 — and 9× fewer bytes per token is the difference between usable and not. Energy matters. PrismML reports 0.714 mWh per token on an RTX 4090, which they put at 40% more efficient than a full-precision 8B model. The Apache 2.0 licence and fully local execution are requirements, not preferences. Not worth it when: The work is knowledge-heavy or multimodal. That is precisely where the compression bill lands. You need non-English long-tail language coverage. The independent evidence here is bad and benchmarks did not predict it. You cannot maintain a forked inference runtime. Ollama and LM Studio do not load it today, and a stock build fails silently rather than loudly. You were going to run it past ~200K tokens of context on the strength of the 262K spec.
documents.s: When this is the right tool

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 最后验证时间：2026-09-22。 本页引用了会随时间变化的事实——请把上面的日期视为它的时效性参考。 来源：PrismML launch post and the prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf model card and file listing on Hugging Face; PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp README (branch prism, 716 stars at check); ggml-org/llama.cpp discussion #22019; independent hands-on testing and benchmark tables published by MindStudio, DataCamp and Atomic Chat. 复制为 Markdown 高级 最后验证时间：2026-09-29。 Every accuracy, latency and training-time figure on this page is self-reported by the project that published it, on benchmarks that project chose. Nothing here has been independently replicated. Both repositories are days old and moving fast — star counts, model names, checkpoint ids and CLI flags are the most perishable facts here; read the current README before you copy a command. Neither project is affiliated with or endorsed by TypeSafe, the makers of Jev. 来源：README of firelex/jeff (created 2026-09-28, 895 stars at time of writing) and PostHog/jeeves (created 2026-09-29, 107 stars); denis-pplx/autojev README; Hacker News items 49883844 (Jeff, 536 points / 204 comments) and 49891290 (Jeeves, 105 points / 44 comments). What you'll learn Explain the actual training recipe behind an open decision model — cross-entropy over option letters, one epoch, and a temperature fitted afterwards — and why calibration is a separate step from accuracy Read the published benchmark tables honestly: the three rows where a 0.8B model beats the commercial API, and the two rows where it loses by 20–26 points Decide between four options — hosted API, zero-shot open weights, your own fine-tune, or a plain embeddings classifier — using the one baseline number that kills most of these projects Train and serve a Jev-compatible model yourself in an afternoon on a single GPU, including the checkpoint-selection rule that keeps the result honest Know when adding reasoning back to a decision model is worth 11x the latency, and how a confidence threshold buys most of the accuracy for a third of the wait System One decision models explained the category: you send program state plus typed questions, and you get calibrated probabilities back instead of text. That page ended where the open recreations were in mid-September — Kev, Nimble, a logprob shim. In the last week of September the story changed shape. The question stopped being "can we clone the API" and became "should you train your own?" On September 28 a project called Jeff shipped 0.8B and 2B fine-tunes that land within four points of Jev's overall benchmark score and run in ~22–28 ms on a laptop-class GPU, trained in about two hours on one workstation card. It was the top AI story on Hacker News that day. Twelve hours later PostHog published Jeeves, which does the opposite thing — bolts reasoning onto a decision model — and reports beating Jev on Jev's own hard tier. Both are MIT code with Apache-2.0 weights. Both are honest enough in their READMEs to publish the rows where they lose. This page is about what those rows mean for you.
documents.s: Train Your Own Decision Model: Jeff, Jeeves and the DIY System One Stack (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Date (2026) What shipped Why it matters Sep 15 Jev (TypeSafe AI), API-only Defined the category and the /v1/systemone request shape Sep 21 Kev, Nimble, openjev-sglang Proved the interface was reproducible on open weights — AutoJev (denis-pplx) The recipe: full-weight SFT of Qwen3.8-27B, 73,000 examples, one H200, 84.60% vs a 69.83% base Sep 28 Jeff (firelex) Shrank it — 0.8B/2B students, ~2 h on one workstation GPU, MLX serving, game evals Sep 29 Jeeves (PostHog) Reversed the premise — a thinking decision model, LoRA + RL on Qwen3.5-9B The through-line: in two weeks a category went from a closed API with undisclosed training to a recipe you can run overnight. AutoJev is the hinge — it published the loss function, and everything after it is a variation on that one idea.
Strip the marketing and a decision model is a startlingly small change to a normal LLM.

The model is not taught to "make decisions". It is taught to put probability mass on a single letter token — A, B, C — at one specific position. You lay the options out as a lettered panel, you train with plain cross-entropy on the correct letter, and at inference you read the logits for the letter tokens and renormalise them over just the options you offered. That one implementation detail explains the headline limitation. Jeff caps you at 26 options, and the README is blunt that positions past that are "effectively never selected" — because the alphabet ran out, not because of anything architectural. (Jev itself advertises up to 255 options, which tells you it encodes options differently.) Jeeves takes the other road: a pointer head that scores a projected hidden state against each option's embedding with a scaled dot product. No letters, no alphabet ceiling. It marks the structure with rare tokens borrowed from Qwen's tokenizer that real text essentially never uses — <|fim_prefix|> for state, <|fim_middle|> for questions, <|box_start|>/<|box_end|> around options, <|fim_suffix|> at the decision point. Reusing dead tokens as delimiters is the cheap trick that avoids growing the vocabulary or colliding with content.
documents.s: 1. The loss is cross-entropy over option letters

documents.t: This is the part people skip, and it is the part that makes the output trustworthy. Accuracy and calibration are different properties. A model can rank the right answer first almost every time and still say "91%" when it is right 75% of the time — the independent BANKING77 pilot on Jev found exactly that shape of over-confidence. So all three projects fit a single scalar temperature on a held-out development set after training, and ship it alongside the checkpoint. Divide the logits by it, softmax, done. AutoJev publishes what that buys, and it is the cleanest before/after in the whole stack: Metric Base Qwen3.8-27B AutoJev-27B Accuracy 69.83% 84.60% ECE (expected calibration error — lower is better) 0.06483 0.04282 Brier score (lower is better) 0.40834 0.22027 Note that all three moved, but by different amounts. Accuracy climbed ~15 points while ECE fell ~34% — training made the model both righter and more honest, and the honesty is measurable separately. If you train your own and only report accuracy, you have not finished.
documents.s: 2. The calibration is a separate, one-parameter stage

documents.t: One epoch. Batch 256. Full-weight (Jeff, AutoJev) or LoRA r=16 (Jeeves). Checkpoint selection on a development set, never on the benchmark panel — Jeff states this explicitly, and it is the single line that separates a credible small-model result from a leaked one. Jeff also keeps at least half of each training family in the same panel layout it will see at inference, which matters more than it should; see the wording section below. Train a 0.8B decision model (Jeff's own recipe) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # 1. Build the training mix from public datasets uv run autojev-mix ... # 2. One epoch, full-weight, lr 5e-6 scripts/train.sh RUN data/mix/public.jsonl data/mix 5e-6 40 Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B <revision> --epochs 1 # 3. Evaluate the SELECTED checkpoint against a held-out panel uv run autojev-evaluate --data data/panel.jsonl --local \ --checkpoint checkpoints/RUN/selected --output runs/eval/RUN.json Reported cost of step 2: ~2 hours for 0.8B, ~3.5 hours for 2B, on one RTX PRO 6000. That is the number that made this a front-page story.

Here is Jeff's published panel — 4,599 questions across five public datasets plus JevBench's hard tier — with the commercial API in the last column. Read it by row, not by the overall line. Benchmark Jeff-0.8B Jeff-2B Jeff-Gemma4-E2B Jev (API) Overall 79.1% 83.1% 81.6% 83.0% Financial PhraseBank 96.4% 96.3% 96.1% 77.0% RAGTruth 86.1% 88.9% 87.4% 77.3% WinoGrande 68.6% 79.0% 77.4% 90.7% JudgeBench 62.6% 64.6% 60.6% 78.6% BBH 64.0% 68.0% 66.4% 94.3% JevBench Hard 47.6% 53.3% 48.6% 73.3% The overall scores are nearly tied. The rows are not close at all: Where the tiny model wins, it wins big. Financial PhraseBank: 96.4% against 77.0% — a 0.8B model beating a commercial API by 19 points. RAGTruth (does this answer stay faithful to the retrieved passage?): 86.1% against 77.3%. Both are narrow, high-volume, pattern-shaped jobs — sentiment on a fixed vocabulary, groundedness on a supplied passage. If your agent's hot path is that shape, a local 0.8B is not a compromise, it is the better tool. Where it loses, it is not close. BBH is 30 points down. JevBench Hard is 26 points down. Those are the rows that need multi-step reasoning, and the README says so plainly: small decision models give you "fast, calibrated choices between the options you describe" and no reasoning chain. The overall number is the average of those two facts and therefore describes nothing. This is the most transferable lesson on this page, and it is not specific to decision models: any single headline score is a weighted average over a benchmark mix that is not your mix.

Jeff also evaluated zero-shot game play — 20 episodes each of Doom, Frogger and Pac-Man — and the result is uncomfortable enough that publishing it earns trust: Model Doom (kills) Frogger (crossings) Pac-Man (pellets / 98) Random −0.05 0 11.2 Hand-coded rule bot 6.55 10.25 94.1 Jeff-0.8B 6.55 10.3 57.0 Jeff-2B −0.9 6.0 41.2 The 2B is worse at all three games than the 0.8B it outscores on every benchmark row. The README's read is that the bigger model came out more risk-averse. Whatever the cause, the pairing of those two tables is the point: benchmark rank did not predict behaviour in a loop. And the hand-coded rule bot still wins Pac-Man by 37 points — the reminder that "can a model do it" and "should a model do it" are different questions.
documents.s: The games table is the honest one

documents.t: Median latency per decision, ~200-token questions: Model RTX PRO 6000 Apple M4 Max (MLX) CPU (32 threads) Jeff-0.8B 22 ms 28 ms 463 ms Jeff-2B 24 ms 60 ms 708 ms Jeff-Gemma4-E2B 29 ms — 1.0 s Two things to take from this: "Tiny model" does not mean "runs anywhere fast." The same 0.8B checkpoint is 22 ms on a GPU and 463 ms on 32 CPU threads — a 21x gap. A decision model is only a decision model at GPU latency; on CPU it is a slow API call you happen to host. If your plan was "sprinkle these calls everywhere in the request path", the CPU column is the plan's budget. 2.5x the parameters cost 2 ms on the big GPU. 22 → 24 ms. At this size a single forward pass over ~200 tokens is dominated by overhead and memory bandwidth, not by arithmetic, so on a fast card the 2B is nearly free relative to the 0.8B — while on the M4 Max the same step costs you 2.1x (28 → 60 ms). Pick your model per deployment target, not from the parameter count. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Serve one locally before you train anything⌄ Install with uv, pull a checkpoint from Hugging Face, start the server. You want the zero-shot number on YOUR data before you decide training is necessary — the most common outcome reported by practitioners is that zero-shot is not good enough, and that is much cheaper to discover in twenty minutes than after a training run. ←PreviousNext→ 2Build a labelled dev set of a few hundred real examples⌄ Real traffic, real label distribution, including the ambiguous ones you would normally throw out. This set does double duty: it selects your checkpoint and it fits your temperature. It must never overlap the panel you report numbers on. ←PreviousNext→ 3Measure the boring baseline first⌄ Embeddings plus a logistic-regression head, on the same dev set. On BANKING77 this approach was reported in the Jeff discussion at 93.0% with a model roughly 15x smaller. If it wins on your data, stop here — you have saved yourself a fine-tune and a GPU. ←PreviousNext→ 4Fine-tune only the gap you measured⌄ One epoch, batch 256, cross-entropy over the option letters, lr around 5e-6. Keep at least half your training examples in the exact panel layout you will use at inference. Select the checkpoint on the dev set. ←PreviousNext→ 5Fit the temperature, then report both numbers⌄ One scalar on the dev set, stored with the checkpoint. Then publish accuracy AND calibration error to yourself. An uncalibrated decision model is a classifier with a confidence field you are not allowed to trust — which defeats the entire purpose of the category. ←PreviousNext→ 6Set the threshold from the reliability curve, not from a round number⌄ Find the confidence at which observed accuracy is actually good enough to skip a human or a frontier model. Everything below it escalates. That number is a property of your data and will not be 0.9 just because 0.9 looks tidy. ←PreviousNext→ Serve a Jev-compatible model locally and send it a real request CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Apple silicon (MLX backend) uv sync --no-default-groups --extra mac uv run --no-default-groups hf download mstrasser/Jeff-Qwen3.5-0.8B --local-dir checkpoints/jeff-0.8b JEFF_BACKEND=mlx JEFF_CHECKPOINT=checkpoints/jeff-0.8b PORT=8765 \ uv run --no-default-groups --extra mac jeff-serve # Two independent questions, one request, one parallel pass curl -s localhost:8765/v1/systemone -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{ "model": "jeff-latest", "state": "Refund request: the customer says the parcel arrived crushed and wants their money back.", "questions": { "route": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": {"1": "Refunds and payments", "2": "Damaged or lost parcels", "3": "Account and login problems"}}, "angry": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer angry?"} } }'

The sharpest criticism in the Hacker News thread was not that Jeff performs badly. It was structural: if you have to fine-tune it on your own labelled data anyway, you have not bought a zero-shot classifier — you have bought a somewhat awkward way to train a classifier, and the field already has cheaper ones. The numbers in that thread support taking it seriously. A commenter reported testing the 0.8B zero-shot on job-ad classification and finding it unusable, with the 2B still missing categories. Another reported that plain embeddings plus a logistic-regression head reached 93.0% on BANKING77 using a model about 15x smaller than the decision models being compared — against the 87.4%-confidence/75.3%-accuracy shape the independent Jev pilot found on the same dataset. So the honest decision table: Situation Use Handful of fixed labels, plenty of examples, latency matters Embeddings + logistic regression. Smallest, fastest, trains in seconds. Beat this before considering anything else. Labels change often, or questions are written in prose per request Zero-shot decision model — the schema is the interface, which is the actual product One high-volume domain, you have labels, you have a GPU for an afternoon Fine-tune. Jeff's chess run went 15.5% → 55.8%; a voice-navigation fine-tune on ~11,000 examples went 31.7% → 95.8% in under 30 minutes Genuinely hard, multi-step judgements Reasoning — Jeeves, or a frontier model behind a cascade You need it working this afternoon and the volume is low Hosted API. Your own GPU is not free either The general rule underneath: a decision model earns its place when the schema is the valuable part — arbitrary typed questions, in prose, resolved in one pass. When your label set is fixed and known, you are paying model-shaped costs for classifier-shaped work.
documents.s: The uncomfortable question: do you need a model at all?

documents.t: Jev's founding pitch was that this class of model does not generate text. PostHog's Jeeves tests that premise directly by letting a decision model think first, then decide, on Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA r=16 and a pointer head. Training runs in three stages: SFT (19,126 questions from 12 public datasets plus synthetic policy data, half carrying reasoning chains, 2 epochs / 596 steps on 8 GPUs), then CISPO reinforcement learning (9,992 questions, 8 rollouts each at temperature 1, thinking capped at 2,560 tokens — a 624-step schedule deliberately stopped at step 402 because calibration was degrading past it), then the same scalar temperature fit. Reported results: Benchmark Jeeves Jev Kev-9B Test overall 0.889 0.857 0.822 JevBench overall (231 items) 0.935 0.866 0.715 JevBench hard (111 items) 0.865 0.730 0.451 And the ablation that matters more than any of those rows: 0.804 without reasoning, 0.840 with it. Thinking is worth about 3.6 points on this model. Now price it. On one H100, Jeeves answers in ~0.3 s with reasoning off and 3.3 s median with it on — 17.1 s at p90. That is roughly 11x the median latency and a tail an order of magnitude worse, for 3.6 points. The README's own mitigation is the interesting engineering: cap thinking at 2,560 tokens and add a 0.9 confidence threshold that stops early when the model is already sure, which brings the median to 2.0 s. Reasoning becomes something you spend only on the items that need it. Two caveats Jeeves publishes about itself: it is worse than Jev on knowledge-heavy tasks (MMLU 0.793 vs 0.900) — reasoning does not add facts — and its reasoning chains were never rewarded for language consistency, so they are not reliably readable. If you wanted the chain as an audit trail, check that it is legible before you promise anyone it is.

Wording consistency beats wording quality. Jeff reports Frogger crossings going from 15 to 23 purely by phrasing every option the same way as its siblings. Options are compared against each other in one pass — asymmetric phrasing is a thumb on the scale. Keep keys short and put the description in the text. Prompt formats do not port between decision models. Jev's bearing-number style did not transfer to Jeff; consequence-focused wording was needed instead. Treat a switch of decision model as a re-tuning job, exactly like porting prompts across models. The 26-option ceiling is silent. Nothing errors. Options 27+ simply never win. Chunk large label sets into a two-stage decision instead. English, text-only for Jeff. AutoJev accepts base64 images; Jeff does not. Zero-shot quality is workload-shaped and often disappointing. Multiple practitioners reported the small models being unusable on their own real classification tasks. Measure on your data on day one. Training-data leak filtering is your job. Jeff generates synthetic data locally with leak filtering precisely because a decision model trained near its eval panel produces a number that means nothing. Both repos are days old. Flags, checkpoint names and defaults are moving. Nothing here substitutes for the current README. Check yourself 0/5

复制为 Markdown 进阶 “AI 要花多少钱？”没有唯一答案——它取决于你买的是哪种定价原型，以及你实际用了多少。具体的美元数字每隔几个月就变；但成本的结构几乎不动。本页教你这个持久的形状：AI 的三种定价方式、在动手搭建之前如何估算一个工作负载、削减账单的杠杆，以及租用 API 与自建之间那个真正的岔路口。 What you'll learn 分清三种成本原型：按 token 计费的 API、固定订阅、开源/自建 在上线前，用 token × 单价 × 用量估算任何工作负载的成本 在不损害质量的前提下，拉动削减开支的大杠杆 知道开源/自建在成本上何时胜过 API，以及 API 何时更优 知道哪些数字很快就会过时——以及去哪里查今天的真相 最后验证时间：2026-06-28。 按 token 计费的单价、订阅档位、缓存与批量折扣，以及哪个模型最便宜，几乎每个月都在变——把每一个具体的美元数字都当成易腐品对待。本页教的是持久的模型（原型 + 如何估算 + 各种杠杆）；今天的数字请查看各服务商自己的定价页面（在“来源”中链接）、像 Artificial Analysis 这样的独立追踪器，并用我们的 成本计算器 亲自算一遍。 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.

documents.t: 几乎你能为 AI 付费的每一种方式，都归结为三种形状之一。学形状，别记价格。 按 token 计费的 API（用量计费）。 你通过 API 调用一个托管模型，按 token 付费——而且输入和输出分别定价，输出几乎总是两者中更贵的那个。更大/更聪明的模型每 token 更贵；更小的模型便宜得多。多数服务商还提供折扣：对你重复发送的缓存输入有一个更低的单价，对非紧急的异步任务有一个统一的批量折扣。当你在 Claude、GPT 或 Gemini 上构建产品时，就是这样付费的。成本随用量直接增长——小规模时是几分钱，大规模时则是最大的账单项。 固定的消费者/席位订阅。 为一个聊天应用或 IDE 助手支付固定的月费（Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini 的消费者套餐、Copilot 式的席位）。你看不到 token；你得到一个用量额度和速率限制。对坐在键盘前的人类来说可预测又便宜——但它无法扩展到程序化/高并发的工作，而且按席位的成本会随团队人数累加。 开源/本地（自建）。 你在自己的硬件或租来的 GPU 上运行一个开源权重模型（Llama、Mistral、Qwen、DeepSeek）。没有按次调用的价格——你为硬件（或按小时租的 GPU）+ 电费 + 运维付费，无论模型是忙是闲。再多一次调用的边际成本在规模化后实际上接近于零，但你要背负固定成本和运维负担。见 用 Ollama 在本地运行模型。 Pro tip 关键的分野：API 和订阅是边际成本（你按使用付费）；自建大多是固定成本（无论用不用，你都要维持容量）。 在 API 上，最大的意外是输出 token 通常比输入贵好几倍——啰嗦的回答会真的花钱。 固定订阅是人类聊天的合适工具；按 token 的 API 是应用在循环中调用模型的合适工具。

在写一行生产代码之前，你就能估算一笔 API 账单。整个模型就是一个公式： 成本 ≈ (输入 token × 输入单价) + (输出 token × 输出单价)，每次调用 × 调用次数 单价按每百万 token报价，而输入和输出有不同的单价——所以分别估算两半再相加。一个粗略的 token 经验法则：约 1 token ≈ 4 个英文字符，或约 0.75 个词。要精确计数，请使用 Token 估算器 区域并阅读 Token 与定价。token 到底藏在哪里的完整机制在 Token 经济学。 Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1算出单次调用的 token 量⌄ 把输入加起来：系统提示 + 工具 + 检索到的上下文 + 历史 + 用户这一轮。然后估算你要求的输出。输入和输出分开计——它们定价不同。 ←PreviousNext→ 2每一半各乘以自己的单价⌄ 输入 token × 输入单价，加上输出 token × 输出单价。用服务商定价页面上今天的每百万数字（别信你记住的某个数字——见 VerifyNote）。 ←PreviousNext→ 3按真实用量放大⌄ 把单次调用成本乘以每天调用次数 × 天数。一个单次微不足道（几分之一分钱）的成本，在数百万次调用时会变成你最大的账单项——按你的实际流量建模，而不是一次请求。 ←PreviousNext→ 4套用你真正会用到的折扣⌄ 如果每次调用都有一大块重复的输入，就按缓存单价定价，而不是完整输入价。如果任务是离线的，套用批量折扣。它们在规模化时会极大改变答案。 ←PreviousNext→ 5对照追踪器做合理性检查，然后削减⌄ 把你的按 token 假设与一个独立追踪器和我们的成本计算器对比，然后用下面的杠杆攻击账单。 ←PreviousNext→ 信封背面的估算（填入今天的单价） CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Per call: input_tokens = system + tools + context + history + user_turn output_tokens = the answer you ask for call_cost = (input_tokens * input_rate_per_million / 1e6) + (output_tokens * output_rate_per_million / 1e6) Per month: monthly_cost = call_cost * calls_per_day * 30 Then adjust: - cached repeated input -> use the (lower) cache-read rate for that slice - offline / non-urgent -> apply the batch discount to the whole job Rates change monthly — pull today's numbers from the provider's pricing page.
documents.s: 如何估算一个工作负载的成本
documents.h: #如何估算一个工作负载的成本

documents.t: 大多数真实工作负载都背着无用的重量。以下这些杠杆，大致按杠杆效应排序，能在不触及质量的前提下削减开支——先拉便宜的结构性杠杆。 给模型选对尺寸。 别为一个小/便宜模型就能做好的活儿付旗舰级单价。分类、抽取、路由和简单格式化，通常在最小档上就跑得很好，而每 token 的价格只是零头。把大模型留给真正困难的推理，并考虑路由：便宜模型处理简单的大多数，只在困难的情况才升级。见 选择模型。 精简你发送的上下文。 最便宜的 token 是你从不发送的那个。裁掉臃肿的系统提示，把长历史压缩成一份滚动摘要，只暴露任务需要的工具——每一个都是你每次调用都要重付的输入。 用 RAG 而非塞入巨大上下文。 为回答一个问题就粘贴一份 50 页的文档，意味着每次调用都为这 50 页付费。检索只取回那几段相关的内容——用远少的输入 token 得到同样（往往更好）的答案。只有当你确实需要一次性看到整个语料时，才动用超大上下文窗口。 提示缓存。 如果许多调用共享一段不变的大前缀（系统提示、工具目录、参考文档），缓存会处理它一次，并在之后每次调用时以大幅折扣重新提供。这是聊天和智能体工作负载中杠杆效应最高的单项结构性改动，因为它每一轮都在回本。 把非紧急的批量处理。 评测、批量打标、给一份存档做摘要——任何你不需要在几秒内拿到答案的活儿——都能走异步批量通道，在多数服务商那里享受统一折扣。用即时性换来实质性更低的账单。 缩短输出。 输出是更贵的一边。要求 JSON 或一个紧凑的 schema，而不是一段唠叨的话：更少的输出 token，而且没有下游解析的猜测。 用更小/开源模型处理简单的那部分。 对于高并发、低难度的大多数调用，一个开源或小模型每次调用可能便宜得多——如果你已经自建，有时几乎免费。把前沿模型留给真正需要它的情况。 Pro tip 这些是相乘叠加的：缓存输入 × 选对尺寸的模型 × 更简短的输出 × 批量折扣，在一个简单任务上会复合成一大笔总削减——而质量不变。 在微调措辞之前，先拉结构性杠杆（选对尺寸、缓存、RAG、批量）——它们对账单的影响大得多。 永远用真实账单来度量改动，而不是靠猜。深度打法在《Token 经济学》。

这是真正左右你 AI 预算的决策。它是一个固定成本与边际成本的交叉点，而用量是决定它的变量。 开源/自建在高、稳定的用量下胜出。 一旦你跑的调用足以让一块 GPU 大部分时间都忙碌，那么每次调用接近于零的边际成本就胜过永远按 token 付费。你把固定的硬件/租用成本摊到海量调用上，获得数据隐私和完全的定制能力——并接受运维负担（供给、扩缩容、可用性、MLOps）作为入场费。 API 在低或波动的用量下、或没有基础设施时胜出。 如果流量很小、突发或不可预测，按 token 付费意味着你只为用到的付费，闲时分文不花——没有凌晨 3 点还热着的 GPU。你也省掉了所有运维。对于大多数要发布产品、做原型、或流量呈尖峰的团队来说，API 既更便宜又省事得多。 Watch out 自建很少是“免费的”。模型权重也许免费，但 GPU、电费，以及让它持续运行的工程师工时都不免费——在宣称省钱之前，诚实地把它们算进去。 闲置的 GPU 是纯粹的损失：固定成本的基础设施只有在利用率高时才胜过按 token 定价。低或尖峰的流量每次都更利于 API。 每当 API 降价或硬件变便宜，交叉点就会移动——定期重算这笔账，别一次决定就忘。 自我检查 0/3 Key takeaways 三种原型：按 token 的 API（用量计费，输入与输出分别定价）、固定订阅（可预测，无法扩展到高并发）、开源/自建（固定成本，每次调用接近于零）。 在搭建前估算：(输入 × 输入单价) + (输出 × 输出单价)，每次调用 × 用量——然后套用缓存和批量折扣。 最大的杠杆：给模型选对尺寸、精简上下文、用 RAG 替代巨大上下文、提示缓存、把非紧急的批量处理、缩短输出。 自建在高且稳定的用量下胜出（摊薄固定成本）；API 在低/尖峰用量或无基础设施时胜出（只为用到的付费）。 每个美元数字都很快过时——在服务商定价页面和一个追踪器上核实，并在成本计算器里亲自算一遍。

复制为 Markdown 进阶 What you'll learn Understand what is actually inside 16.9 MB — and which part of the 9x size headline is architecture versus a quantization choice the comparison does not hold constant Read the vendor's own WER chart including the competitor bars it never labels: Whistle wins 5 of 8 head-to-heads and loses the three that look most like real life Know why 30 seconds is a wall in the encoder rather than a setting, and build the VAD segmentation it forces on you Find the streaming API the launch discussion concluded did not exist, and understand why its real latency is not the 11.1 ms time-to-first-token Use keyword biasing as the primary accuracy lever, not a nicety — it is the difference between 41% and 96% on a closed vocabulary Decide between Whistle, Whisper, Parakeet and a cloud API for your specific audio On 8 October 2026 a blog post titled "Whistle: Speech to Text in 16.9 MB" reached 768 points on Hacker News. The number in the title is the whole pitch, and it is true: the entire multilingual speech recognition model is a single 16.9 MB file that runs on a CPU with no GPU and no dependencies. The discussion that followed split cleanly in two. People who read the benchmark chart were impressed. People who pointed a microphone at it were not — one tester reported 70 correct out of 170 utterances. Both groups were right, and the reason they were both right is printed in the vendor's own chart. It is just in the bars that carry no number.
documents.s: Whistle: Speech-to-Text in 16.9 MB — and the Benchmark Bars Nobody Labelled

documents.t: Whistle buys its size by quantizing a small encoder–decoder ASR model to 2–4 bits and band-limiting its front end to 250–3500 Hz, which costs it almost nothing on close-microphone single-speaker speech — where it genuinely beats Whisper base — and costs it a great deal on far-field, overlapping or accented speech, where it is the worst of the three models in its own comparison.

Component Detail Front end 25 ms window, 10 ms hop, 80 log-mel bins, band-limited 250–3500 Hz Stem 128-channel convolutional, downsamples to one frame per 80 ms Encoder 8 Simple Attention blocks, Monarch Hadamard MLP Decoder 8 laddered Simple Attention blocks, width 512, 8 query heads to 2 KV heads Vocabulary 8,192 text pieces plus 7 language tokens Output ceiling 320 tokens per clip Input ceiling 480,000 samples — 30 s at 16 kHz mono Container .cact, Cactus Quants, 2–4 bit Licence Apache-2.0 Three of those rows do more work than the rest, and two of them are the ones people skip.
documents.s: What is actually in the 16.9 MB

documents.t: The comparison everyone quotes is 16.9 MB against Whisper base's 145.3 MB. That is one ninth the size — but the vendor's own footnote says Whistle is measured at 2 to 4 bit while Whisper is fp32 in memory on the CPU. Those are 8–16x apart in bits per weight before a single architectural decision is made. The honest apples-to-apples row in the same chart is Moonshine tiny v2 at 41.9 MB in int8. Whistle is 2.5x smaller than that, not 9x. The remaining 2.5x is real and is where the architecture earns its keep — but if you repeat the 9x number you are mostly repeating a quantization choice. This is the same trap covered in how to read an AI benchmark without getting fooled: the number is not wrong, the comparison is not held constant.
documents.s: The 9x size headline does not hold precision constant

documents.t: The front end keeps 250–3500 Hz and throws away everything else. That is roughly telephone band, and it is a sensible choice for a model meant to run on a wearable — most speech energy lives below it. Most, not all. The acoustic-phonetics literature is specific here: 3–4 kHz is enough bandwidth for intelligible vowels but not for most voiceless fricatives, whose spectra are concentrated above 4 kHz. English s has its greatest energy concentration in roughly the 5–10 kHz range, peaking near 8 kHz — more than twice Whistle's cutoff — and sh centres near 4 kHz with energy extending to 8. Cutting at 3500 Hz does not make those sounds inaudible. It removes the band that separates them from each other most cleanly. So before you run a single test you can predict the error class: confusions and dropped word-endings on fricatives, worst on speakers whose rhythm or accent gives those consonants less duration to compensate with. The field reports in the launch thread — Spanish output with "non-existent words and terrible typos", Mexican and Venezuelan accents not detected, heavy accents degrading sharply — are that prediction arriving on schedule.
documents.s: Band-limiting to 3500 Hz is a design decision with a predictable error class

documents.t: Here is the part worth the page. Whistle's chart plots word error rate across nine test sets for three models. It prints a number on every Whistle bar and on none of the others. The bars are still there, drawn to a linear scale. Whistle's printed labels calibrate that scale exactly — 6.867 pixels per WER point, consistent to ±0.01 across all nine — so the competitor values are recoverable from bar height. Doing that produces the table the chart stops just short of giving you. Test set What it is Whistle Whisper base ≈ Moonshine tiny v2 ≈ LibriSpeech test-clean Read audiobooks, clean 4.31 4.89 4.51 LibriSpeech test-other Read audiobooks, harder 10.49 11.00 11.71 SPGISpeech Financial calls 7.65 — 7.70 Earnings-22 Earnings calls, accented 19.01 — 21.25 AMI Meetings, far-field, overlapping 26.07 21.50 22.78 AMI cleaned Same, cleaned refs 22.87 — — TED-LIUM Conference talks 7.61 4.99 5.64 FLEURS Multilingual read speech 21.39 24.50 — MLS Multilingual audiobooks 24.90 23.10 — Lower is better; bold marks the winner of each row. Whistle's column is the vendor's printed figures. The other two columns are read off the chart's bars — the vendor states they are Whisper's and Moonshine's own published numbers, and declines to print them. Whistle wins five of the eight rows where a comparison exists. For a model 2.5x smaller than its nearest-precision rival that is a genuine result, and the FLEURS row — 3.1 points better than Whisper base on multilingual read speech — is the most impressive thing in the chart. Now look at what it loses: AMI, by 4.57 points to Whisper base. Far-field microphones, multiple speakers, overlap, interruption. Whistle is not merely behind here, it is the worst of the three, losing to a model 8.6x its size. TED-LIUM, by 2.62 points. Single speaker, but a large room, a stage mic and unscripted delivery. MLS, by 1.80 points. Multilingual long-form, averaged over six non-English languages. The pattern is not subtle once the numbers are side by side. Every row Whistle wins is close-microphone and effectively single-speaker. Every row it loses has either distance between the mouth and the microphone or more than one person in the room. Read-audiobook and dictation audio is exactly the profile a 16 kHz band-limited front end with a tiny encoder handles well. Reverberation and overlapping talkers are exactly what it cannot afford the capacity to disentangle. That single sentence reconciles the two halves of the launch thread. Everyone who tested dictation into a phone held near their face liked it. Everyone who pointed it at a film clip, a meeting or a room disliked it. Nobody was measuring wrong. The number to carry away 4.31 and 26.07 are the same model on the same weights. If you only remember one WER figure for Whistle, remember the spread, not the headline.

The most-quoted field result in the thread — 70 correct out of 170, against 168/170 for a much larger Qwen ASR model — is a real measurement, but it is a measurement of stock settings on a closed vocabulary. The same tester reported 164/170 after tuning. What changed is the subject of the next section, and it is the most under-sold feature on the model card.

Whistle decodes with five beams scored by length-normalised log probability, and it will accept a list of words you expect to hear and favour them during that search, matched with an Aho-Corasick automaton. In a general-purpose ASR model this is a convenience. In a 16.9 MB model with an 8,192-piece vocabulary it is closer to load-bearing. The model has very little capacity to spend on an implicit language model, so proper nouns, product names, place names and domain jargon are precisely what it gets wrong — and precisely what a keyword list fixes. Going from 70/170 to 164/170 is 41% to 96% on the same weights. Transcribe with the two arguments that matter CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import needle r = needle.transcribe( "clip.wav", keywords=["Kubernetes", "Grafana", "Prometheus", "Aoife", "Nguyen"], word_timestamps=True, language="en", # skip detection when you already know ) print(r["text"]) for w in r["words"]: print(w["word"], w["start"], w["end"], w["probability"]) Three things in that snippet are worth stating plainly: keywords is not a post-processing filter. It changes the beam search, so it can recover a word the decoder would otherwise never have placed. language="en" removes a failure mode, not just latency. Automatic detection across seven languages on a short or noisy clip is one more thing that can go wrong. If your app knows the language, say so. Every word carries its own probability. That is your confidence gate — see the handoff pattern below. Watch out A keyword list that is too long dilutes the bias and starts pulling the decoder toward words nobody said. Keep it to the vocabulary your users actually produce in this context — the current screen, the current contact list, the current document — not your entire product glossary.
documents.s: Keyword biasing is the primary accuracy lever

documents.t: 30 seconds at 16 kHz is 480,000 samples. After the convolutional stem that is one frame per 80 ms, so 375 encoder frames, and the decoder tops out at 320 output tokens. Those are fixed shapes in a 16.9 MB tensor file. There is no flag that raises them, and a launch-thread tester who recorded past the limit got a runtime error rather than a truncated transcript. So any clip longer than 30 seconds means you own the segmentation — and segmentation is where long-form ASR accuracy actually lives, because a cut through the middle of a word or a clause is an error the model cannot recover from. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Resample and downmix first⌄ 16 kHz mono is not a recommendation, it is the input contract. A 44.1 kHz stereo file needs converting before it reaches the model; the base install handles 16 kHz WAV and raw samples, and the [mic] extra adds resampling and microphone capture. ←PreviousNext→ 2Segment on silence, not on a timer⌄ Run a voice-activity detector and cut in the gaps. Fixed 30-second slices will eventually cut mid-word, and that error lands in your transcript permanently. Target 10–25 second segments so you keep headroom for a long final clause. ←PreviousNext→ 3Overlap the segments by about a second⌄ Give consecutive passes a shared region so you can stitch on agreement instead of trusting a hard boundary. The cost is re-decoding a second of audio; at 1,319 tokens/s decode that is not your bottleneck. ←PreviousNext→ 4Stitch with the word timestamps, not the text⌄ Every word comes back with a start and an end, so dedupe the overlap region by time rather than by string matching. This is the only reliable way to drop a doubled word without dropping a legitimately repeated one. ←PreviousNext→ 5Gate on probability and hand off⌄ Average the per-word probabilities over each segment. Low-confidence segments are your queue for a bigger model — on-device for free, off-device when it matters. Do not re-run everything. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: The 30-second wall is in the encoder, not in a config file

documents.t: The model card makes a specific and welcome claim: silence and steady noise return an empty transcript rather than an invented sentence, because silence detection runs before the beam search. That is a direct fix for Whisper's most notorious failure — confidently hallucinating subtitles over nothing. Read the claim precisely. It covers silence and steady noise. It does not cover quiet, distant or overlapping speech, and the thread contains exactly that failure: a tester reported the model emitting "Thank you." repeatedly for over a minute while real dialogue was playing, and another found a negation flipped — "can handle" for "can't handle" — plus a word invented outright. Those are the classic artefacts of training on web video captions, where "Thanks for watching" occupies an enormous share of the text, and they survive the silence gate because the gate was never aimed at them. If a dropped n't would change what your application does, a per-word probability check is not optional.
documents.s: Silence is handled; low-SNR speech is not

documents.t: A recurring complaint in the discussion was that Whistle cannot do live transcription, because the demo showed no partial text while speaking. The demo did not; the library does. needle.stream(chunks) takes live microphone input and commits words that consecutive overlapping passes agree on. That policy — decode an overlapping window repeatedly, emit only the prefix two passes agree on — is the LocalAgreement family of streaming ASR, and knowing that tells you the thing the spec sheet will not: Your perceived latency is not the 11.1 ms time-to-first-token. It is the agreement delay: how long a word has to wait before a second pass confirms it. TTFT is a decode-speed measurement on a complete 10-second clip. In a streaming loop the user-visible number is set by your window stride and how long you are willing to wait for stability, and it will be hundreds of milliseconds, not eleven. Fast is still fast — 11.1 ms against Whisper base's 73.2 ms and Moonshine's 22.8 ms, and 1,319 tokens/s decode against 266 and 262, measured on 10 s of audio on an Apple M4 Pro CPU. Just do not promise a product manager 11 ms of live captioning.
documents.s: Streaming exists — the launch thread concluded it did not

documents.t: Every depth from two layers up is a deployable model, selected at load time with --audio-depth. You download one 16.9 MB blob and choose your accuracy/latency point on the device, which is the right place to choose it — a watch and a phone can run the same artifact at different depths. For scale, the sibling Needle text model decodes at roughly 4,000 tokens/s at two layers and 400 at twenty on a Raspberry Pi 5.
documents.s: The decoder is laddered, so one file is a family

documents.t: The encoder output is available directly: one row per 80 ms frame, via needle.Whistle().embed(audio). That is wake-word spotting, command matching, audio deduplication and "find where in this recording someone said this" — without decoding text, without a language model, and without the error classes discussed above, because you never ask it to spell anything. For a lot of embedded jobs ("did the user say one of these eleven things?") this is the correct tool and transcription is the detour. Run it from the CLI, including the built-in three-way comparison CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ pip install cactus-needle # microphone playground needle whistle playground # put Whistle next to Whisper and Moonshine on YOUR audio needle whistle compare my-clip.wav # air-gapped / embedded: fetch a platform engine and the weights needle download macos-arm64 needle download whistle ./macos-arm64/needle --model whistle.cact --audio clip.wav --audio-word-timestamps The compare subcommand deserves a mention: the vendor ships the tool that checks its own claims against your audio. Given how sharply the WER spread above depends on recording conditions, running it on a representative clip of your audio is worth more than any table on this page.
documents.s: embed() gives you speech matching with no transcript at all

documents.t: The engine reads no environment variables. Every behaviour is a compiled default or an explicit flag. That means the same blob plus the same flags scores the same on any machine, which is a property most inference stacks cannot claim and which matters enormously when you are trying to work out whether last week's eval regressed or last week's shell did.

Your situation Pick Why Dictation on a phone or wearable, close mic, offline, 7 supported languages Whistle This is the design centre. 16.9 MB, no GPU, word timestamps, and it beats Whisper base on exactly this audio profile Wake words or fixed command sets on a microcontroller Whistle embed() Skip transcription entirely; match encoder frames Meeting recordings, multiple speakers, room mics Not Whistle Its own chart puts it last on AMI. Use a full-size Whisper, Parakeet, or a cloud ASR with diarization Any language outside the seven Not Whistle English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Dutch, Polish only. No Chinese, despite being the most-requested addition in the launch thread Best open-weight accuracy-per-second on a GPU, English Parakeet NVIDIA's parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2 was the practitioner favourite in the thread; CC-BY-4.0 Audio you cannot send anywhere, and accuracy matters more than size Whisper large, local Still the accuracy reference. You are trading ~100x the footprint for it Medical, legal or financial transcripts of record Cloud ASR with a human in the loop The negation-flip failure mode above is disqualifying on its own A hybrid is usually the right answer, and it is the same shape as every other local/remote split on this site: run the small model on everything, use the per-word probabilities as the gate, escalate the uncertain fraction. See Claude plus local models for the general pattern and a private local AI stack for where a transcription step belongs in it.
documents.s: Choosing: Whistle, Whisper, Parakeet, or a cloud API

documents.t: Whistle is a good instance of a pattern now showing up across small models: the capability is real and the operating envelope is narrow, and only the first half fits in a headline. The 2-bit quantization is not a cheat — the model genuinely works — but it buys its size by spending the capacity that would have handled hard audio, and the vendor's chart shows exactly where that bill lands while labelling only the rows where it does not. The practical rule generalises past ASR: when a small model publishes a wide benchmark spread, the spread is the specification. Find the row where it does worst, work out what that test set has that the others do not, and check whether your real input looks like that row. For Whistle the answer is distance and overlap. For a quantized language model it is usually long context — see what "98.2% retention" hides. Teams are discovering this the hard way: a coding agent left running racks up a bill that a human at a keyboard never would. The scary part isn't the average; it's that you can't predict it in advance, and the cost of the same task can swing wildly. This page explains why agents burn tokens (the mechanism is not what most people guess), shows the numbers that surprise even experienced builders, and gives you the four levers that actually cut the bill — the same levers whether you're on Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or a home-grown loop over any model. What you'll learn Explain the context snowball — why agent cost grows roughly QUADRATICALLY with steps, not linearly Cite the real multipliers: agentic tasks ~1000x a chat's tokens, and the SAME task varying up to 30x Know when a second agent is worth it — and the benchmark showing it usually isn't Pull the four cost levers that work: budget caps, prompt caching, model-tier routing, context pruning Diagnose a runaway agent bill and put a hard ceiling on it 最后验证时间：2026-07-15。 Per-token prices, per-developer monthly spend, and which model is cheapest change almost monthly — treat every dollar figure here as perishable and illustrative. The mechanism (context snowball, re-read tax) and the levers are durable; the exact ratios come from 2026 benchmarks and research linked in Sources. Confirm today's rates on each provider's pricing page before quoting a bill to anyone. 请对照以下来源核实： 官方来源.
documents.s: Why AI Agents Burn Tokens (and How to Cap the Bill)

documents.t: Here's the trap. A chat is one turn — one input, one output, done. An agent is a loop: it reads a task, takes an action, reads the result, takes the next action, and so on until the job is finished. The catch is that on every step, the model re-reads the entire accumulated conversation so far — the original prompt, every prior action, and every tool result — before deciding what to do next. So the input grows on every step, and you pay for the whole snowball again each time it rolls forward: Step 1 processes the prompt. Step 2 re-reads the prompt + step 1's action + result. Step 3 re-reads all of that + step 2's action + result. …and so on. Add up the input across a run and the total scales roughly with the square of the number of steps, not linearly. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab found agentic tasks to be "uniquely expensive, consuming 1000x more tokens than code reasoning and code chat" — and crucially, it's the input tokens that dominate, not the output. The agent isn't writing more; it's re-reading more. What you'll learn The cost driver is re-reading, not thinking. Each loop step re-processes the full transcript, so a 20-step run pays for early context ~20 times over. This is why 'just let the agent figure it out' is expensive: every extra step it takes multiplies against everything before it. Output-heavy tasks (write me an essay) are cheap by comparison; input-heavy loops (explore this repo, then fix the bug) are where the money goes.
documents.s: The context snowball: why cost grows quadratically

documents.t: Three figures reset most people's intuition: ~1000x. Agentic tasks can consume roughly a thousand times the tokens of an equivalent chat or code-completion, per the Stanford analysis — driven by the snowball above, not by a bigger model. Up to 30x variance on the same task. The same agent, run on the same task, can cost up to 30x more one time than another — because the path it takes (how many tools it calls, how far it wanders) is non-deterministic. You genuinely cannot know the bill until it's done. This is why "result-based pricing" for agents is so hard: you only see the cost after everything runs. More agents rarely pay for themselves. 2026 production benchmarks found that a multi-agent setup added only ~2.1% accuracy at 2x the cost versus a well-configured single agent on 64% of tasks. A hierarchical-supervisor pattern pushed a document task from 85% → 95% accuracy — but at roughly $0.15/task vs $0.003 for the single agent (~50x). More agents buys a little accuracy for a lot of money. Watch out Because the same task varies up to 30x, an average-based budget WILL be blown by the tail. Cap the ceiling, don't budget the mean. Adding agents to 'be safe' usually multiplies cost far faster than it adds accuracy. Reach for a second agent only when the task genuinely decomposes into parallel, independent subtasks.

Before the loop even starts, how the agent reaches its tools sets a floor on cost. Connecting a set of MCP servers can inject tens of thousands of tokens of tool definitions into every step of the snowball. A rough comparison many builders hit: a plain CLI command averages ~200 tokens, while the equivalent MCP operation can cost 32k–82k tokens once tool schemas and wrapping are counted. That gap rides along on every loop step. That doesn't make MCP wrong — it's the right choice for auth, multi-tenancy, and governed access. It means the tool surface is a cost lever you chose at design time. AILmanac has a dedicated deep-dive: The MCP Token Tax covers Tool Search, deferred loading, and code execution as the three fixes.
documents.s: Your tool surface is part of the bill

documents.t: Optimization advice is endless; only four levers move the number materially. In rough order of leverage: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Cap the budget — a hard ceiling, not a hope⌄ Set a per-run or per-user token/dollar cap that HARD-STOPS the agent. Because the same task can cost 30x more on a bad run, a ceiling is the only thing that bounds the tail. Most agent harnesses expose a max-tokens or max-steps limit — use it. This is the single most important control. ←PreviousNext→ 2Cache the stable prefix⌄ The system prompt, tool definitions, and house rules are re-sent on every loop step (the snowball). Prompt caching charges those repeated tokens at a fraction of the input rate. On a long agentic run this is often the biggest single saving, because the cached part is exactly what gets re-read the most. ←PreviousNext→ 3Route by model tier⌄ Don't run one frontier model for the whole loop. Use a cheap, fast model (Haiku-class, or a small open model) for the grunt work — reading files, formatting, routine tool calls — and reserve the expensive frontier model for the hard reasoning or the orchestrator role. Orchestrator-worker splits with cheaper workers cut cost 40–60% in production benchmarks at near-parity accuracy. ←PreviousNext→ 4Prune the context aggressively⌄ The snowball is the problem, so shrink it. Compact old turns, drop tool outputs the agent no longer needs, summarize instead of carrying raw transcripts, and start fresh sub-tasks with a clean context instead of one ever-growing thread. Every token you remove is a token you stop paying for on EVERY remaining step. ←PreviousNext→ Audit a runaway agent (paste your run's token breakdown) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ You are a cost engineer. Here is a token-usage breakdown of one agentic run (input vs output tokens per step, tool calls, model used). Diagnose where the money went, in priority order: 1. Is input or output driving cost? (Agents are almost always input-heavy.) 2. Which repeated content should be prompt-CACHED (system prompt, tools, rules)? 3. Which steps could run on a CHEAPER model without losing correctness? 4. Where is context snowballing — what can be pruned, compacted, or summarized? 5. What is a safe per-run token CAP that stops the worst tail without hurting the median run? Give me the estimated % saving per fix and the ONE change to make first.
documents.s: The four levers that actually cut the bill

documents.t: The cheapest agentic run is the one you don't make. If a task is a single, well-specified transformation — summarize this, classify that, rewrite this — a plain chat/completion call does it at a fraction of the cost, with no snowball at all. Reach for an agent when the work genuinely requires reading, deciding, acting, and re-checking in a loop against a changing environment (explore a repo, debug across files, drive a browser). If you can write the exact steps yourself, script them — don't pay a model to re-derive them every run. Check yourself 0/3
documents.s: When an agent is the wrong tool
